tooltip.semiconductor-lab.purity.hint: Transistors need 9N or better. Zone refining raises purity one step at a time (up to 10N for Ge).
tooltip.semiconductor-lab.oxide.hint: Colour is interference; it changes with thickness
assembly.semiconductor-lab.transistor_ra: Amplify (3 transistors): boost the weak radio signal
Tuning coil (copper): with the capacitor, picks a station
Tuning capacitor (Leyden jar): with the coil, picks a station
Speaker (magnet): the signal shakes a cone into sound
Battery case (zinc): − pole, gives off electrons
Battery rod (graphite): + pole, takes in electrons
assembly.semiconductor-lab.hf_oscillator: Oscillate (2 tubes): push and pull the current steadily
Tank coil: with the capacitor, sets the frequency
Tank capacitor (Leyden jar): trades charge with the coil
Wiring (copper): links the parts and the refiner's coil
Frame (4 iron): holds the parts and sheds heat
litho.semiconductor-lab.fail.size_mismat: Grid size differs from the last layer
item.semiconductor-lab.microscope.limit: 🔬 NA %s: finest resolvable line ~ %s (Abbe: lambda / 2NA, light 550 nm)
item.semiconductor-lab.microscope.hold: Hold a mask, original, design or process wafer in your other hand and right-click
item.semiconductor-lab.microscope.blurre: ✖ The lines are too fine and blur (needs a higher-NA objective or a shorter wavelength)
block.semiconductor-lab.test_power_sourc: A block for checking the game, not normally obtainable. It gives electricity forever without fuel.

Creative only, no recipe. Placed under (next to) a machine it sends 1 MW. The test site (/function semiconductor-lab:testworld) puts one under each machine. Check real power generation in the test site's steam engine area.

In the real world there is no power source that needs no fuel: electricity is converted from the energy of fuel, flowing water, light and so on (conservation of energy). This block is just a shortcut for testing.
Labs often test a device on a regulated bench power supply instead of its real power source. The test site uses the same idea.
For testing only: not a real technology (just for checking the game).
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge.hold: Hold a lathe-turned part (rotor, standard screw) in your other hand and right-click
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge.no_grade: This scale cannot read 0.01 mm differences -> grade with a micrometer
litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.diffus: A thin diffused strip resists current: a resistor. Kilby's first IC of 1958 (germanium) already had resistors made from the wafer itself.
litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.juncti: The border between p-type and n-type lets current through one way only. In 1940 Ohl found such a border by chance inside a silicon crystal.
litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.planar: Open windows in the oxide and diffuse n, p, n nested inside each other: a transistor. Hoerni's 1959 method keeps the surface flat.
litho.semiconductor-lab.discovery.rtl_no: A circuit of just a transistor and resistors that outputs 0 for input 1 and 1 for input 0 (RTL). One of the logic circuits announced as ICs in 1961.
Inventions from history hide in the chips you draw. Press Probe at the probe station.
gui.semiconductor-lab.blast_furnace.need: Add iron ore or iron sand
Blow air in through a tuyere
gui.semiconductor-lab.blast_furnace.out_: Take out pig iron and slag
block.semiconductor-lab.surface_plate.no: A perfectly flat iron table, the reference for measuring flatness and length.
Cast iron plates lapped three together until the warp is 1 um or less. It can be placed. Lapping it again against a warped plate can warp it again.
Inspection rooms still have cast iron or granite surface plates. In the 20th century granite, which does not rust and moves little with temperature, became common.
Precise measuring and assembly begin on a surface plate. Gauge blocks ([8-05]) and isolation tables ([8-07]) only make sense once there is a flat reference.
tooltip.semiconductor-lab.oxygen.cz: Oxygen about %s ppma (CZ: from the quartz crucible)
Chapter 1: The Birth of the Transistor
1947. Before silicon, there was germanium. Goal: build a transistor radio!
Ashes to Elements
Smelt coal into coal ash. Some coal deposits contain trace germanium.
Reduction
Reduce GeO2 with charcoal into metallic germanium. Still full of impurities - not nearly pure enough for a transistor!
Zone Refining
Refine germanium. A molten zone sweeps impurities to one end of the bar (Pfann, 1952).
The First Transistor
Two gold contacts pressed onto n-type germanium by a plastic wedge: the point-contact transistor (Bardeen and Brattain, 1947).
Music from Coal
Build a transistor radio. In 1954 this changed how the world listened.
Needle in a Haystack
Combine 8 coal ash into germanium concentrate. Only a tiny fraction is germanium.
Brimstone Chemistry
Burn sulfur powder in a furnace to get SO2, then dissolve it in water. Real plants oxidize SO2 to SO3 first (contact process).
Leaching
Dissolve the concentrate in acid to get germanium dioxide (GeO2).
Doping
Add a trace of phosphorus to make n-type germanium. Purify first, then add exactly the impurity you want.
The Sandwich
Indium on both sides of n-type germanium, then heat: a p-n-p alloy-junction transistor (1952).
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p1:
SEMICONDUCTOR LAB
Chapter 1: The Birth of the Transistor (1947)

Goal: build a transistor radio.

Everything here follows real chemistry. Where the game simplifies, this book says so.

Press L to see your next step.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p2:
1. GERMANIUM
Before silicon, there was germanium. It hides in two places: zinc ore (sphalerite, deep underground) and the ash of some coal.

Smelt coal for ash. Mine sphalerite with an iron pickaxe and roast it in a reverberatory furnace: every 4th gives germanium concentrate.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p3:
2. SULFURIC ACID
Burn sulfur powder (from sulfur caves) in a furnace: S + O2 -> SO2. Dissolve in water.

Simplified: real plants first oxidize SO2 to SO3 with a catalyst.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p4:
3. EXTRACT + REDUCE
Acid pulls germanium out of the concentrate as GeO2. Charcoal takes the oxygen away: metallic germanium, but still dirty.

Simplified: industry uses hydrogen, and chlorine distillation.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p5:
4. ZONE REFINING (Pfann, 1952)
Melt a narrow zone and move it along the bar. Impurities prefer the liquid, so they ride to the end.

Each pass: unrefined -> 6N -> 9N -> 10N. 9N = one impurity per billion atoms. 10N needs a synthetic graphite boat.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p6:
THE FURNACE
Graphite boat, quartz tube, copper induction coil, screw + motor.

HF oscillator (3 kW of electricity): 2 vacuum tubes + coil + Leyden jar. It ran on vacuum tubes!

Boat: clay-graphite = 9N max, synthetic graphite = 10N.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p7:
5. DOPING
Pure is not enough. Add ONE chosen impurity to the molten zone (zone leveling):
 phosphorus -> n-type (extra electrons)
 indium -> p-type (missing electrons)

Mixing solids would do nothing. Needs 9N or better.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p8:
6. TRANSISTORS
1947 point-contact: two gold contacts pressed onto n-type Ge by a plastic wedge.
1952 alloy-junction: indium on both sides of n-type Ge, then heat -> p-n-p sandwich.

A small base current controls a large current. That is the whole trick.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p9:
NO CLEAN ROOM?
Correct - in 1947 there were none. Laminar-flow clean rooms arrived in the 1960s, when one speck could kill a whole integrated circuit.

The surface of your germanium is dirty right now. Real labs etch it with acid before use.

guide2.semiconductor-lab.p1.title: Why Electricity?
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p1:
SEMICONDUCTOR LAB
Volume 2: Electricity (1830s-1900s)

Chapter 1 had two 'fakes': the furnace's power supply and its boat. Both need electricity.

Here you build a power grid, then use it to make what fire alone cannot.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p2.title: 1. Water Wheel
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p2:
1. WATER WHEEL
Put it next to FLOWING water: 500 W per side. Still water does nothing.

Power = flow x height of the fall. Many early power stations were hydro (Niagara, 1895).
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p3.title: 2. Steam
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p3:
2. STEAM
Coal boils water, steam pushes a piston, a dynamo turns: 50 kW.

One coal = 30 MJ of heat but only 1.5 MJ of electricity (5%). Watt's engines wasted most heat. The steam turbine reaches 30%.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p4.title: 3. Self-Excited Dynamo
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p4:
3. DYNAMO
Varley, Siemens and Wheatstone, 1866-67: no permanent magnet. Leftover magnetism in the iron core starts a small current, which makes the electromagnet stronger, and so on.

Right-click a water wheel or steam engine with it: 2x output.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p5.title: 4. Cables
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p5:
4. CABLES
Connected cables form one network. Cables store nothing: power goes straight from generators to machines.

Loss = 1% per cable on the longest path (P = I^2 R). Max 1 MW per network. Batteries take the surplus.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p6.title: 5. Electrolysis
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p6:
5. ELECTROLYSIS
Electricity splits water: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 (2:1 by volume). Sulfuric acid only carries the current.

Hydrogen reduces metals without carbon: tungsten, and the purest germanium.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p7.title: 6. Vacuum Tubes
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p7:
6. VACUUM TUBES
Pump the air out (hand pump, then a Sprengel mercury pump to 0.1 Pa), seal a hot tungsten filament, a grid and a plate in glass.

De Forest, 1906: a small grid voltage controls a big current. Two tubes make the HF oscillator for the zone refiner.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p8.title: 7. Electric Furnace
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p8:
7. ELECTRIC FURNACE
Current through graphite rods makes heat (Joule heat) up to ~1500 C, with no smoke from fuel.

Add a hydrogen tube: the hydrogen furnace.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p9.title: 8. Synthetic Graphite
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p9:
8. GRAPHITE
Acheson, 1896: pass current straight through packed coal + sand. Above 2500 C the carbon rearranges into graphite and impurities boil away.

Needs 500 kW: a steam turbine. Result: the 10N boat.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p10.title: 9. Chlorine
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p10:
9. CHLORINE
Electrolyze salt water: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH. Burn H2 in Cl2: hydrochloric acid.

GeO2 + HCl -> GeCl4 (boils at 83 C). Distill it, and only then can germanium reach 10N.
zukan.semiconductor-lab.root.title: Encyclopedia
zukan.semiconductor-lab.root.description: Every item you pick up unlocks its entry here: the adult (3) and deep-dive (4) notes in full.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p1.title: Why silicon?
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p1:
Semiconductor Lab
Vol. 3: Silicon (1950s)

Germanium is rare and dislikes heat. Silicon comes from ordinary rock (quartzite) and stands heat.

This volume turns rock into 11N silicon and then a solar cell.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p2.title: 1. Quartzite
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p2:
1. QUARTZITE
Quartz veins are everywhere (about 12% of the crust is SiO2). Mine with a stone pickaxe.

No nether quartz: it does not exist in reality.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p3.title: 2. Arc furnace
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p3:
2. ARC FURNACE
SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO (about 2000 C). Quartzite 2 + charcoal 1 + 12 kWh (500 kW) -> metallurgical silicon 98%.

Silicon holds oxygen very tightly, so it takes arc heat.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p4.title: 3. Trichlorosilane
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p4:
3. TRICHLOROSILANE
Si + 3HCl -> SiHCl3 + H2 (about 300 C). Dry HCl gas, not the acid.

SiHCl3 boils at 32 C. Each distillation stage adds one 9; 9 stages give 11N.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p5.title: 4. Siemens process
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p5:
4. SIEMENS PROCESS
SiHCl3 + H2 -> Si + 3HCl on a thin rod at about 1100 C. The rod grows.

500 kW x 648 s = 90 kWh/kg. The HCl goes back. Purity = the TCS purity, 9N-11N.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p6.title: 5. Czochralski
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p6:
5. CZ
Melt at 1420 C in a single-use quartz crucible, pull a turning seed under argon.

B2O3 -> p-type, phosphorus -> n-type. Boron spreads evenly (k 0.8), phosphorus piles up (k 0.35). Oxygen comes from the quartz.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p7.title: 6. Slices
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p7:
6. SLICES
A diamond disc cuts the crystal into thin plates: 1 ingot -> 8.

The blade width turns into powder. In 1954 Bell Labs cut long strips.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p8.title: 7. Diffusion
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p8:
7. DIFFUSION
At about 1000 C dopant soaks in from the surface. n-type slice + boron -> thin p-type top.

The boundary is the p-n junction, the heart of transistors too (Fuller 1954).
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p9.title: 8. Solar cell
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p9:
8. SOLAR CELL
8 p-n slices + copper cable. 60 W under the day sky (1000 W/m2 x 6%), about 20% in rain.

Bell Labs, 25 April 1954. Powered a satellite in 1958. Chapter 2 goal!

item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note1: Burn seashells or white stone and you get lime: the start of wall plaster.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note: CaO. Calcite (CaCO3) heated to about 900 C loses its carbon dioxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. A furnace (~1000 C) or blast furnace is hot enough. Seashells and limestone are also CaCO3 and burn the same way.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note3: Lime plaster is one of the oldest man-made materials: Natufian people in Israel already used burnt-lime plaster about 12,000 years ago, floors at Gobekli Tepe (from about 9500 BC) were made with burnt lime, and it spread widely about 10,000 years ago. People built lime kilns everywhere there was limestone or shells.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note4: Above about 900 C the pressure of CO2 released by CaCO3 exceeds 1 atm, so the reaction runs on its own. Burned too hot or too long, lime becomes 'dead-burned' (dense crystals that react slowly with water). The CO2 from lime kilns is still a big part of the cement industry's emissions.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.placeho: Omitted: the CO2 given off is not collected (a furnace has only one output).
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note1: Pour water on quicklime and it gets hot enough to steam, then falls into a white powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note: Ca(OH)2. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 gives off a lot of heat. Mixed as 'milk of lime' (about 2%), it binds silica sand into Dinas refractory bricks. In air it slowly takes back CO2: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, which is how lime plaster hardens.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note3: The Romans mixed slaked lime with volcanic ash (pozzolana) and got a concrete that sets even under water. Japanese castle walls (shikkui plaster) are slaked lime with seaweed glue and fibres.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note4: Slaking releases about 65 kJ per mole of CaO, enough to boil water or set wood on fire; self-heating meal boxes still use this reaction. Slaked lime is a strong base (pH about 12.4) used to causticize potash [2-02] and soda [2-08] and to neutralize acids.
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern.note1: The bitter liquid left after boiling seawater. It sets tofu.
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern.note2: Nigari: the mother liquor left after NaCl crystallises from boiled seawater. Mostly MgCl2 (plus MgSO4, KCl). Future raw material for magnesium [1-39].
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern.note3: Seawater is about 3.5% salt. When you boil it down, NaCl crystallises first and magnesium salts stay in the liquid. That bitter liquid is nigari, the traditional coagulant for tofu.
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern.note4: From 1941 Dow Chemical made aircraft magnesium from seawater in Freeport, Texas: Mg(OH)2 precipitated with lime, dissolved in HCl, then molten MgCl2 electrolysed. 1 L of seawater holds about 1.3 g of Mg.
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.note1: Makes salt from seawater using the sun. Put it on the beach next to water.
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.note2: Works only in ocean/beach biomes, with water beside it, open sky above and no rain. Makes 1 salt per minute and 1 bittern per 8 salt. Right-click to collect (holds up to 64 salt / 16 bittern). The boiling pot can be a cauldron or an earthenware pot [0-03].
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.note3: Agehama style: seawater is sprinkled on a sand bed, the sun dries it, the salty sand is washed to get strong brine (kansui), then boiled down in a pot. Noto in Japan still does it this way.
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.note4: Salt-making pottery from the late Jomon period has been found in Japan. In the Edo period the Seto Inland Sea used tidal 'irihama' pans. Since 1972 Japanese salt has been made by ion-exchange membrane electrodialysis instead.
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.placeho: Approximation: the fuel for boiling down the brine is skipped (it runs on sunshine alone).
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.worki: Salt pan: drying in the sun (%s%%)
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.not_s: Salt pan: not by the sea (needs an ocean or beach biome)
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.no_wa: Salt pan: no seawater beside it
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.no_sk: Salt pan: no sunlight (needs open sky above)
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.full: Salt pan: full - right-click to collect
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.note1: A round, hard river pebble. Strike flint with it and sharp pieces fly off.
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.note2: Sometimes found when breaking gravel. Right-click with flint in the other hand to knap 2 flakes. Right-click an obsidian block for an obsidian flake (the block stays). Ordinary stone will not give an edge. Returned when used in crafting.
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.note3: Striking stone with stone (direct percussion) is humanity's oldest technology. The oldest secure examples are Oldowan tools from Gona, Ethiopia, about 2.6 million years old. Tools from Lomekwi, Kenya, are dated to about 3.3 million years, but their age and whether they were made on purpose are still debated ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.note4: Knappers chose tough, hard-to-break hammerstones (quartzite or basalt cobbles). The striking angle (less than 90 degrees between platform and edge) and the spot matter: a good blow spreads as a cone of force (a Hertzian cone) and detaches a flake, leaving a bulb of percussion on its inner face.
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.place: Omitted: flake size, striking angle and failed fractures. The hammerstone comes from gravel (really you pick a rounded river cobble).
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.note1: Hit a stone with a stone and it breaks with a knife-sharp edge. Humanity's first blade.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.note2: Knap flint with a hammerstone (right-click or crafting table, 1 flint -> 2 flakes). A small blade for cutting and fighting. No handle, so it wears out fast. Repair with flint or obsidian. Right-click a spruce log to tap pine resin ([2-31]).
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.note3: Flint is made of extremely fine quartz (SiO2) grains, so it breaks like glass with a conchoidal (shell-like) fracture and a razor edge. The Oldowan toolkit (about 2.6 million years ago) is just such flakes plus the cores they came from. Silicon for chips is made from the same SiO2.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.note4: Cut marks on animal bones show what Oldowan flakes (named after Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania) were for: stripping meat and cracking bones for marrow. Oldowan tools about 2.9 million years old have been reported from Nyayanga, Kenya ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.place: Omitted: different flake tools (scrapers, points) are merged into one item.
item.semiconductor-lab.obsidian_flake.no: A flake of volcanic glass. Extremely sharp, but brittle.
Right-click an obsidian block with a hammerstone (the block stays). Sharper than a flint flake but chips quickly (half the durability). Right-click a spruce log to tap pine resin ([2-31]).

Obsidian is natural glass: lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. With no grains, its fractured edge is only a few nanometres thick, sharper than a steel scalpel. In Palaeolithic and Jomon Japan, obsidian from Wada Pass (Nagano) and Kozushima island travelled far.

Kozushima obsidian was carried across the sea to Honshu from around 38,000 years ago ⚠️. Obsidian blades are still used in some surgery. In 19th-century Australia, Aboriginal knappers made beautiful Kimberley points from discarded bottle glass: natural or man-made, glass breaks the same way.
item.semiconductor-lab.obsidian_flake.pl: Omitted: the obsidian block is not used up (one block counts as a big raw nodule).
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.note1: A teardrop-shaped stone knapped on both faces. No handle: you grip it in your hand.
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.note2: 3 flint + hammerstone (returned). Works as an axe (a little faster than a wooden axe, but swings slowly without a handle). Repair with flint or obsidian. The vanilla stone axe is the later hafted stone tool.
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.note3: The hand axe is the signature tool of the Acheulean (named after Saint-Acheul, France). It appeared in Africa about 1.7 million years ago and was made in nearly the same shape for over a million years. Knapping both faces symmetrically needs a picture of the finished tool in the maker's mind.
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.note4: The oldest Acheulean tools come from Kokiselei, Kenya (about 1.76 million years) and Konso, Ethiopia (about 1.75 million years). Hafting a stone point onto a wooden shaft is thought to date from about 500,000 years ago (Kathu Pan, South Africa) ⚠️; vanilla stone tools (cobblestone + stick) correspond to that stage.
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.placehol: Omitted: the second, shaping stage with a soft hammer (bone or wood).
message.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.gl: Crack! Glassy stone breaks like a shell - you got a sharp flake
message.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.gr: Thud... Coarse-grained stone just crumbles along its grains. No edge
message.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.fl: Clink! You knapped 2 flakes from the flint
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_clay_pot.note: A pot shaped from clay. It is not fired yet, so soaking it in water turns it back into clay.

Made from 5 clay balls. Fire it on a campfire for 30 s (open firing) or in a furnace for 10 s to get earthenware. With a water bucket on the crafting table it turns back into 5 clay balls (fired earthenware does not).

Clay is made of tiny plate-shaped crystals (clay minerals) stacked with water between them. The water lets the plates slide, so you can mould it into any shape. Merely dried clay soaks up water and softens again.
The 'cord marks' of Jomon pottery were made by rolling a cord over the half-dry surface. A pot must be dried well before firing, or the water inside turns to steam and cracks it.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_clay_pot.plac: Omitted: the drying step (firing a damp pot cracks it).
item.semiconductor-lab.earthenware_pot.n: Once fired, clay never turns back with water. People knew this 20,000 years ago.
Fire an unfired clay pot on a campfire (open firing) or in a furnace. Water no longer turns it back into clay. Can be used as the boiling pot of a salt pan (instead of a cauldron).

Clay minerals such as kaolinite lose the water (OH) inside their crystals at about 500-600 C and become something else (metakaolin). The change only goes one way: adding water will not make clay again. Open firing reaches about 600-900 C.

Among the oldest pottery is from Xianren Cave, Jiangxi, China (about 20,000 years ago). In Japan, sherds about 16,500 years old come from Odai Yamamoto, Aomori ⚠️. Hunter-gatherers made pottery before farming began. Late Jomon people also had pots for boiling seawater into salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.earthenware_pot.p: Omitted: uneven firing, cracking and leaky unglazed pots.
item.semiconductor-lab.polished_stone_ax: Grind a stone axe with sand and water and its edge stops chipping. Now it has a wooden handle.
Hand axe + sand + water bucket (returned) + stick. Lasts longer and cuts faster than a knapped axe (200 durability, a little faster than a stone axe). Repair with flint or obsidian.

A knapped edge is covered with small steps and scars where flakes came off, and cracks start there. Rubbing it for hours with sand (quartz, very hard) and water removes them, giving an edge that does not chip when chopping wood. Neolithic people cleared forests with these axes to make fields and houses.

A well lining near Leipzig, Germany, was cut in 5206-5098 BC (dated by tree rings) and joined with mortise-and-tenon joints, probably shaped with polished stone axes. Axes with only the edge ground have been found in Palaeolithic Japan (about 38,000 years ago), among the oldest in the world ⚠️.
Omitted: the grinding time (really hours to days) and choosing a good axe stone (greenstone, jadeite).
block.semiconductor-lab.wild_einkorn.not: Wild wheat. When ripe its ears fall apart. Now and then a seed whose ear does not fall appears - pick it and plant it.

Sometimes dropped when breaking grass (seeds). Plant on farmland. If left ripe, the ears shatter and it starts again from a sprout (no harvest). Harvest it while ripe: 10% of the time a mutant non-shattering seed (domesticated einkorn) comes with it.

The ear stalk of wild wheat is brittle: when ripe, the spikelets drop one by one to sow themselves. Rarely a mutant plant keeps its ears. When people reaped the plants, carried them home and sowed the grain, these mutants kept increasing. People were selecting wheat without knowing it.

DNA comparisons place einkorn domestication about 11,000 years ago near the Karacadag mountains in south-east Turkey. Ear stalks from sites suggest non-shattering wheat took 1,000-2,000 years to become the majority ⚠️ (experiments calculated that with the right harvesting it could take only 20-200 years).
block.semiconductor-lab.wild_einkorn.pla: Approximation: seeds come from grass (really grasslands of the Fertile Crescent). Mutant seeds appear 10% of the time (really far rarer).
block.semiconductor-lab.einkorn.note1: Fields began when people kept choosing and growing wheat whose ears did not fall.
block.semiconductor-lab.einkorn.note2: The non-shattering seed that sometimes comes from harvesting wild einkorn. Planted on farmland, its ripe ears stay on, so you can harvest whenever you like. Harvest gives wheat (vanilla wheat) and seeds.
block.semiconductor-lab.einkorn.note3: Einkorn ('one grain') bears a single grain per spikelet. With emmer, barley and lentils it was among the first crops grown in the Fertile Crescent. Its ears stay on because of mutations that switch off the genes making the ear stalk brittle.
block.semiconductor-lab.einkorn.note4: Einkorn has 2 sets of chromosomes (diploid). Today's bread wheat has 6 (hexaploid); it arose about 8,000-9,000 years ago when emmer crossed with wild goatgrass. Einkorn was even found in the gut of Otzi the Iceman, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago.
block.semiconductor-lab.einkorn.placehol: Approximation: the harvested ears count as vanilla wheat. Bread wheat is a different species from a later cross.
block.semiconductor-lab.flax.note1: A plant with blue flowers. Long threads for cloth hide inside its stem.
block.semiconductor-lab.flax.note2: Sometimes dropped when breaking grass. Plant on farmland; ripe flax gives 2 flax stalks and seeds. The seeds are also called linseed.
block.semiconductor-lab.flax.note3: Just inside the skin of a flax stem lie bundles of long, joined cells: bast fibres. Strong and up to tens of centimetres long, they are what linen is spun from.
block.semiconductor-lab.flax.note4: Linseed oil, pressed from flax seed, hardens in air (a drying oil). It is used in oil paint and in linoleum (linseed oil plus cork; the name comes from linum, flax).
block.semiconductor-lab.flax.placeholder: Approximation: seeds come from grass (the real ancestor is wild flax).
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_stalks.note1: The fibres will not come off like this. Throw them into water and wait a while.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_stalks.note2: From harvesting ripe flax. Dropped in water for about a minute they become Retted Flax (nothing happens on land). Unretted stalks give no fibre when beaten.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_stalks.note3: Inside the stem the fibres are glued to the skin and core by a jelly-like substance, pectin. Beat a dry stem and the fibres just break with it.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_stalks.note4: Flax was pulled up by the roots rather than cut, so the fibres stay long right to the base: the stem length is the fibre length.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_stalks.place: Omitted: pulling, drying and rippling off the seed heads.
item.semiconductor-lab.retted_flax.note1: Let flax stalks rot in water and you can get thread for cloth.
item.semiconductor-lab.retted_flax.note2: Drop flax stalks in water for about a minute. With a hammerstone on the crafting table it becomes flax fibre (the hammerstone is returned).
item.semiconductor-lab.retted_flax.note3: Bacteria and moulds in the water break down the pectin so the fibres come away from the skin and core. This is retting. Retting too long weakens the fibres too, so people checked it every day.
item.semiconductor-lab.retted_flax.note4: Water retting in rivers or ponds takes 1-3 weeks; dew retting on grass takes several weeks. Retting ponds stank, and some medieval European towns banned retting in rivers used for drinking water ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.retted_flax.place: Approximation: retting takes 1 minute (really 1-3 weeks) and over-retting is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_fiber.note1: Beat retted stalks and scrape off the broken core, and long strong fibres remain.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_fiber.note2: Retted flax + hammerstone (returned). 2 make Linen Thread.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_fiber.note3: Fibre is freed by breaking the core (braking), scraping the bits off with a wooden blade (scutching) and combing it straight (hackling). The fibre is mostly cellulose and is even stronger when wet.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_fiber.note4: Wild flax fibres about 30,000 years old, some dyed, have been reported from Dzudzuana Cave, Georgia ⚠️. Long before cloth, they may have been used for cords and bags.
item.semiconductor-lab.flax_fiber.placeh: Omitted: braking, scutching and hackling are merged into one step.
item.semiconductor-lab.linen_thread.note: Twist many fibres together and you get a long thread that is hard to break.
2 flax fibres (spun by hand, rolled on the thigh). 4 make Linen.
Twisting presses short fibres against each other so they stop sliding, so a thread can be longer than any single fibre. A spindle with a whorl twists much faster ([0-07]).
Thread can be twisted S-wise or Z-wise. Ancient Egyptian linen is almost all S-spun, perhaps the same way flax fibre naturally twists as it dries ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.linen_thread.plac: Approximation: spun by hand (the spindle whorl [0-07] is not implemented yet).
item.semiconductor-lab.linen_cloth.note1: Cloth woven from flax thread, with warp and weft. People were making it 9,000 years ago.
item.semiconductor-lab.linen_cloth.note3: Stretch the warp threads and pass the weft over-under-over-under: that is plain weave. Linen fabric and nets about 9,000 years old were found in Nahal Hemar Cave, Israel. Ancient Egyptian mummies were wrapped in linen.
item.semiconductor-lab.linen_cloth.note4: English line, lining and lingerie all come from Latin linum, flax. In old Japan, cloth was made the same way from the stems of hemp and ramie instead of flax.
item.semiconductor-lab.linen_cloth.place: Approximation: woven on the crafting table without a loom.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_clay_whorl.no: A flat round piece of clay with a hole in the middle. Fire it to make a spindle whorl.
1 clay ball. Fire on a campfire (30 s) or in a furnace (10 s) to get an earthenware whorl.
Unfired clay turns back in water (as with [0-03] pottery). A whorl needs its weight, so it is fired hard before use.
Broken pottery was sometimes ground round and pierced to make whorls.
item.semiconductor-lab.earthenware_whorl: A fired clay disc. Fixed to a spindle, it keeps spinning like a top: humanity's first flywheel.
Fire an unfired whorl. Add it to a spindle shaft to make a spindle with a whorl.

Spinning things keep spinning (inertia), and the farther the mass is from the axis, the bigger the effect (moment of inertia). With a disc whorl the spindle spins far longer than a bare stick, twisting the thread all the while.
Yayoi-period sites in Japan yield many clay and stone whorls. The same flywheel idea leads on to the potter's wheel and the flywheels of steam engines and motors.
Approximation: clay and stone whorls are treated as the same weight.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_whorl.note1: A stone disc with a hole in the middle, fixed to a spindle as a flywheel.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_whorl.note2: Stone + hammerstone (returned) + flint (as a drill). Add it to a spindle shaft to make a spindle with a whorl.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_whorl.note3: Holes were drilled bit by bit with a flint drill from both faces, so they end up hourglass-shaped, narrow in the middle.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_whorl.note4: Pebbles drilled from both sides at Nahal Ein Gev II, Israel (about 12,000 years old) were proposed in 2024 as the oldest spindle whorls ⚠️ (still debated). The researchers suggest that, as rotating tools, they may be a starting point of the idea of the wheel.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_whorl.place: Approximation: shaping the stone round and wearing out drills are skipped (one flint).
item.semiconductor-lab.spindle_shaft.not: A stick for spinning thread. But it stops almost at once. What happens with a heavy disc (a whorl)?
1 stick. Hold flax fibre or carded wool in the other hand and keep right-click pressed to spin it. It stops after 1 s: 1 thread per spin (2 fibre -> 1 thread). Add a whorl to make a spindle.
A thin stick is light, with all its mass close to the axis, so its spin dies quickly (small moment of inertia). There is little time to twist the thread.
Bare spindles and rolling fibre on the thigh are thought to be older than the whorl.
item.semiconductor-lab.spindle_shaft.pla: Approximation: spin time (1 s) and thread amounts are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.spindle.note1: A spindle with a whorl. It spins long like a top and makes lots of thread.
item.semiconductor-lab.spindle.note2: Spindle shaft + whorl (clay or stone). Hold flax fibre or carded wool in the other hand and keep right-click pressed: it spins for 4 s and makes 4 threads per spin (2 fibre -> 1 thread, the same as the bare shaft). Let go early and you get thread only for the time it spun.
item.semiconductor-lab.spindle.note3: Hung and spun, the spindle's own weight draws out the fibres while it twists them (a drop spindle). The flywheel keeps it turning, so both hands can feed the fibre.
item.semiconductor-lab.spindle.note4: The spinning wheel appeared in India or China about 1,000 years ago and in Europe around the 13th century ⚠️. For thousands of years before that, all the world's thread was made on spindles.
item.semiconductor-lab.spindle.placehold: Approximation: spin time (4 s) and thread amounts are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.carded_wool.note1: Wool teased apart with its fibres lined up. A spindle turns it into yarn.
item.semiconductor-lab.carded_wool.note2: 4 from 1 wool block (any colour). 2 make 1 woolen yarn (spun on a spindle).
item.semiconductor-lab.carded_wool.note3: Wool fibres have tiny scales and crimp, so they lock together and even short fibres make a yarn that holds. Before spinning, the dirt was picked out and the wool combed so the fibres lie the same way (carding).
item.semiconductor-lab.carded_wool.note4: The first domestic sheep (about 10,000 years ago) were not woolly: a coarse hairy coat over a short soft undercoat that fell out in spring. Wool breeds are thought to have appeared in south-west Asia around 4000 BC ⚠️ (some say around 6000 BC).
item.semiconductor-lab.carded_wool.place: Omitted: washing out the grease, and carding tools.
item.semiconductor-lab.woolen_yarn.note1: Thread spun from sheep's wool. It makes warm cloth.
item.semiconductor-lab.woolen_yarn.note2: Spin 2 carded wool on a spindle (cannot be spun by hand here).
item.semiconductor-lab.woolen_yarn.note3: Woolen yarn traps lots of air, so it conducts heat poorly and keeps you warm. Wool stays fairly warm even when wet.
item.semiconductor-lab.woolen_yarn.note4: Wool is made of a protein, keratin - a completely different material from flax (a plant, cellulose). In medieval England, wool exports were a major source of the kingdom's wealth.
item.semiconductor-lab.woolen_yarn.place: Approximation: twist and thickness are not modelled.
message.semiconductor-lab.spindle.no_fib: Hold at least 2 flax fibre or carded wool in your other hand
item.semiconductor-lab.rope.note1: Twist thin threads together and they become a thick rope that can lift heavy things.
item.semiconductor-lab.rope.note2: 3 linen threads (twisted together). To be used later with pulleys and cranes for lifting heavy loads.
item.semiconductor-lab.rope.note3: Fibres are twisted into yarns, then several yarns are twisted together the opposite way. The opposite twists balance each other, so the rope does not unravel. Under load the twist tightens and friction shares the force among the fibres.
item.semiconductor-lab.rope.note4: At Abri du Maras, France, a stone tool about 41,000-52,000 years old carried a fragment of cord: three twisted bundles plied together (Neanderthals, published 2020) ⚠️. Ancient Egyptians made thick ropes of papyrus and palm fibre to haul huge stones.
item.semiconductor-lab.rope.placeholder: Approximation: the twisting stages (yarn -> strand -> rope) are merged into one.
block.semiconductor-lab.assembly_bench.n: A desk for assembling machines from parts. It shows what each part is for.
Pick a product with < > on the left, put parts into the slot for each role, then press Build. Radios and HF oscillators are made here.
Factories keep a bill of materials (BOM) for each product: one list of which parts and how many. Orders, stock and repairs are all planned from it.

Sony's TR-55 of 1955 was a five-transistor radio. Around the same time, flow soldering spread: parts are pushed into the board, which then passes over a wave of molten solder to solder everything at once.
block.semiconductor-lab.pea.note1: Bacteria on pea roots turn nitrogen from the air into fertiliser, so the field does not wear out.
block.semiconductor-lab.pea.note2: Sometimes dropped when breaking grass (peas = seeds). Plant on farmland: when ripe, the farmland below becomes Nitrogen-Rich Farmland, where the next crop (such as wheat) grows faster (3 times). Compare it with farmland that had no peas.
block.semiconductor-lab.pea.note3: Peas, lentils and other legumes have lumps (nodules) on their roots. Rhizobia bacteria living inside turn nitrogen gas N2, about 80% of the air, into ammonia NH3 for the plant (nitrogen fixation); the plant gives the bacteria sugar in return. Peas and lentils were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent around the same time as wheat.
block.semiconductor-lab.pea.note4: In 1886 Hellriegel and Wilfarth in Germany showed that legumes can use nitrogen from the air only when they have nodules. Mendel discovered the laws of heredity by crossing peas for eight years (published 1865).
block.semiconductor-lab.pea.placeholder: Approximation: rhizobia are assumed to be present (really, no bacteria in the soil means no nodules). Seeds come from grass.
block.semiconductor-lab.nitrogen_farmlan: A field after growing peas. The next crop grows well here.

Farmland under ripe peas becomes this. The crop above (not peas) grows faster; each time a crop ripens it uses up one share of nitrogen, and after 3 it is ordinary farmland again. It gets wet and turns back to dirt when trampled, just like farmland.

Crops need lots of nitrogen to make proteins and chlorophyll. Growing wheat on the same field year after year drains the soil's nitrogen. Alternating legumes and grain (crop rotation) lets the grain use the nitrogen the legumes left. Roman farming books already say to sow grain after beans.

The 18th-century Norfolk four-course rotation (wheat, turnips, barley, clover - a legume) greatly raised English harvests. From 1913 the Haber-Bosch process [6-09] made ammonia from the air's nitrogen in factories.
Approximation: nitrogen is counted as '3 ripe crops'. Peas themselves do not grow faster.
block.semiconductor-lab.potters_wheel.no: A turntable for making pottery. It came before the wheel on carts. Throwing on a wheel makes a thinner pot from less clay.
3 stone + spindle shaft + 3 planks. Right-click with clay balls: 3 clay balls make one unfired clay pot (by hand on the crafting table it takes 5).

A heavy disc keeps turning once spun (a flywheel, just like the [0-07] spindle whorl). A finger against the spinning clay evens the wall all the way round, so a thin, tall wall can be drawn up - using less clay and time than building it up from coils.

The oldest potter's wheel is thought to come from the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture in Ukraine, around 4500 BC ⚠️. In the Near East slow turntables were used around 3500 BC, and the fast kick wheel (the flywheel principle) dates to the 3rd millennium BC. It reached Japan with Sue ware from the Korean peninsula around the 5th century AD.
block.semiconductor-lab.potters_wheel.pl: Approximation: wheel speed and centring the clay are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.wooden_wheel.note: Planks cut into a round wheel. An axle goes through the hole in the middle to make a cart.
3 planks + polished stone axe (returned, slightly worn). To be used for the cart [0-13].
The first wheels were heavy discs of joined planks cut round. When a wheel rolls, nothing rubs at the rim: only the axle rubs in its hole. So heavy loads move with far less force than dragging.

Pictographs from Uruk in Mesopotamia show wheeled vehicles around 3500-3350 BC. Among the oldest real wheels is the wooden wheel from the Ljubljana Marshes, Slovenia (about 3130 BC) ⚠️, whose wheel and axle turned together.
item.semiconductor-lab.wooden_wheel.plac: Approximation: the battens joining the planks and boring the axle hole are skipped.
You spun the wheel and threw an unfired pot from %s clay balls (5 by hand)
item.semiconductor-lab.dugout_canoe.note: Heavy stones and loads are far easier to move floating on water than over land.

5 logs + polished stone axe (returned, slightly worn). Place it on water and ride it. It has a hold where you can load stone loads. Carrying stone loads makes you walk slowly, but not while you are in the canoe. Try moving the same load by land and by water.

A boat made by hollowing out one thick log, charring it with fire and scraping it with stone axes and adzes. Water pushes up as much as the boat and load weigh (buoyancy), so the water carries the heavy load. Nothing drags on the ground, so a little force moves it.

The Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, made around 8040-7510 BC, is the oldest known boat ⚠️. Jomon-period dugouts have been found all over Japan. Ancient Egyptians moved huge pyramid stones by boat on the Nile.
item.semiconductor-lab.dugout_canoe.plac: Approximation: shape and handling are those of the vanilla chest boat (the hold = the hollowed space).
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_load.note1: Cut stone tied with rope. Carrying it on foot is heavy and slow.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_load.note2: 4 stone + rope. While it is in your inventory you walk slowly (1 load = level 1, 4 or more = level 4). Not while riding a boat or other vehicle. Load it into the dugout canoe's hold.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_load.note3: Over long distances a person can carry about half their body weight. The heavier the load, the more lifting each step needs, and you tire fast. On water, buoyancy carries the load, and paddling only has to push the water aside.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_load.note4: Until railways, rivers and canals were the cheapest way to move heavy goods (stone, timber, grain, later coal) far. On 18th-century English canals one horse is said to have pulled tens of times more than with a cart ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.stone_load.placeh: Approximation: weight is counted by number of loads (really it depends on the stone and the carrier's strength).
advancement.semiconductor-lab.domesticat: You bred cattle, sheep or goats. Now breed their young again (3 generations to domesticate)
You raised 3 generations of cattle. Their ancestor was the wild aurochs, nearly 2 m tall at the shoulder. About 10,000 years ago people in West Asia began keeping the calmest ones
You raised 3 generations of sheep. The first domestic sheep were not woolly; wool breeds appeared around 4000 BC after thousands of years of selection ⚠️
You raised 3 generations of goats. Goats, with sheep, were among the very first livestock (about 10,000 years ago, around the Zagros Mountains ⚠️), giving milk, meat, hair and hides
Generation %s is born (%s more to domestication - breed this one too)
Generation %s! They are now tame livestock
advancement.semiconductor-lab.domesticat: You made a wooden wheel. Four-wheeled carts pulled by oxen appeared around 3500-3000 BC (Mesopotamia and central Europe); axles were greased with animal fat
tooltip.semiconductor-lab.route.sulfate: Route: sulfuric acid, not distilled (up to 9N)
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note: Natural graphite from metamorphic rock (e.g. Sri Lanka vein graphite). Same stuff as pencil lead.
block.semiconductor-lab.magnetite_ore.no: Fe3O4, the natural magnet (lodestone). Found deep in ancient banded iron formations.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note: Magnetite grains washed out of rock and concentrated on beaches. Japanese tatara steel was made from this.
block.semiconductor-lab.wolframite_ore.n: (Fe,Mn)WO4. Forms in quartz veins at the edge of granite. 'Tungsten' is Swedish for 'heavy stone'.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note: PbS. Forms with sphalerite in the same hydrothermal veins - look near zinc ore. Often carries silver.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note1: Just blow air through iron and it becomes steel. The colour of the flame tells you when it's done.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note: Steel = iron with only about 0.1–0.5% carbon. Pig iron (≈4% C) is hard but brittle; nearly pure wrought iron is too soft. Steel, in between, is strong and tough. Made in the Bessemer converter by blowing air through molten pig iron, burning the carbon away: C+O2→CO2. Material for turbines, pressure vessels and lathes.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note3: Announced by Henry Bessemer (UK) in 1856. Steel had been a luxury made in small crucibles; a converter made several tonnes in about 20 minutes and the price of steel collapsed. Rails, bridges and ships turned to steel. William Kelly in the USA had noticed the same principle around the same time.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note4: Early Bessemer steel kept oxygen and sulfur and was brittle. In 1856 Robert Mushet found that adding spiegeleisen (an Fe-Mn-C alloy) at the end removed the oxygen and restored the carbon (omitted: manganese is not in the mod yet). The acid lining could not remove phosphorus, so phosphorus-rich ores were useless until Thomas and Gilchrist's basic converter of 1878 [3-08].
block.semiconductor-lab.bessemer_convert: No fuel: just blow air through iron and it becomes steel.

A vessel that blows air up through molten pig iron from tuyeres in the bottom (Bessemer, 1856). No fuel: first the silicon, then the carbon burn, and that heat alone keeps the iron molten. The flame shows the progress: 1) red sparks (silicon) → 2) long white flame (the carbon "boil") → 3) the flame drops: done. In game: one iron ingot (≈ pig iron) + blower power 20 kW × 20 s → one steel ingot.

A real converter is a pear-shaped iron vessel tilted on trunnions to pour iron in and out. The blast came from a steam blowing engine. The lining is acidic silica refractory (here: refractory silica bricks [3-12]; early converters rammed ganister, a siliceous rock with clay).

Inside, mostly 2C+O2→2CO; at the mouth the CO burns in air to CO2, making the long flame. Si+O2→SiO2 releases a lot of heat, so low-silicon pig iron does not get hot enough. The end of the blow (flame drop) was judged by eye, later with a spectroscope watching the flame's light.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note: Lead sulfide PbS, the main ore of lead. Smelt it to roast it into lead oxide (PbO), then smelt that again to get lead. Galena often contains a little silver (0.01-1%); extracting it (cupellation [1-32]) is not implemented yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note1: Burning galena in air drives the sulfur out as a choking gas and leaves a yellow powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note: PbO, made by roasting galena in air: 2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2. Smelt it again: carbon and CO from the fuel take the oxygen away, PbO + C -> Pb + CO. In a furnace the SO2 escapes; roast in a reverberatory furnace [3-06] to collect it for sulfuric acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note3: Litharge is Greek for 'silver stone': it was the yellow crust left over when silver was separated from lead. It was also used in glazes, in lead glass [7-01] and in old paints.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note4: Real roasting is done below the melting point of galena (about 600-800 C) with plenty of air, so the sulfur burns off without the ore melting. In real smelters, roasting and reduction are often joined (roast-reduction), and the SO2 is sent to an acid plant.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note1: The metal of old water pipes and printing type. It is bad for your body.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note: Pb. Soft, heavy (11.3 g/cm3) and melts at only 327 C, so people have smelted it since ancient times. It does not rust away in acid easily: used for sulfuric acid chambers [6-12], containers for hydrofluoric acid [2-10] and lead-acid batteries [4-07]. Lead is toxic: it builds up in the body and harms the brain and nerves.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note3: The Romans made water pipes from lead: the Latin word plumbum gave us 'plumbing' and the symbol Pb. Gutenberg's printing type (about 1450) was a lead-tin-antimony alloy. Leaded petrol and lead paint were banned in the 20th century because of lead poisoning.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note4: Galena often contains silver. Lead was smelted first, then silver was separated by cupellation: melt the lead in air so it becomes PbO and soaks into a bone-ash dish, leaving only silver [1-32]. Much of the silver of the ancient world (and of Iwami in Japan) was made this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_trioxide: A bright yellow powder. Tungsten is hiding inside it, bound to oxygen.

WO3, made by roasting tungstic acid (H2WO4 -> WO3 + H2O). Reduce it with hydrogen in the hydrogen furnace: WO3 + 3H2 -> W + 3H2O (about 700-1000 C). Carbon is not used, because tungsten would turn into tungsten carbide.

Tungsten was first isolated in 1783 by the Elhuyar brothers in Spain, from wolframite. The name wolfram (symbol W) comes from German miners: the ore 'ate' tin like a wolf when it was mixed in tin smelting.

Industrially the reduction goes step by step through blue and violet oxides (WO2.9, WO2.72, WO2) to W. The grain size of the powder is controlled by temperature, hydrogen flow and moisture: wet hydrogen gives coarse grains, dry hydrogen fine ones. Modern plants go through ammonium paratungstate (APT).
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_powder.n: Tungsten melts at about 3400 C. Nothing can melt it, so the powder is baked together.

Metal tungsten as a grey powder. No crucible survives 3400 C, so tungsten is made by powder metallurgy: press the powder into a bar and sinter it in hydrogen (hydrogen furnace: 2 powder + 1 H2 -> sintered bar).
Powder metallurgy is how the metals that are hardest to melt are made: tungsten, molybdenum [1-31], and tungsten-carbide cutting tools.

During sintering, atoms move across the contact points between grains (diffusion), so the gaps close and the bar shrinks by about 15% while becoming dense. The temperature must be close to the melting point for this to be fast.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_bar.note: A big electric current flowing through the bar itself heats it to about 3000 C.

Pressed tungsten powder sintered in hydrogen by passing a current straight through the bar (Coolidge's method). At this stage it is still brittle like glass. Hot swaging and wire drawing make it ductile. Craft it into tungsten wire.
Before Coolidge, tungsten filaments (Just and Hanaman, 1904) were squirted paste that broke easily. Coolidge found that working the hot metal again and again made it bendable at room temperature.

Swaging: the hot bar (about 1200-1500 C) is hammered thousands of times per minute by rotating dies, little by little thinner. The grains become long fibres, which is why worked tungsten is ductile but recrystallised tungsten (after overheating) becomes brittle again.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.not: The thin wire that glows inside light bulbs and vacuum tubes.

Ductile tungsten wire (Coolidge, GE, 1909-1910). It does not melt even when glowing white-hot, so it is used for light-bulb filaments [B-01], vacuum-tube cathodes [5-02], X-ray tubes [B-03] and the needles of point-contact diodes [9-05].
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.pla: Approximation: swaging and drawing through diamond / tungsten-carbide dies are skipped (the bar becomes wire in the crafting grid).
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.not: In 1910-1911 GE began selling lamps with drawn tungsten filaments. They gave about three times more light per watt than carbon filaments, and the tungsten bulb became the light of the 20th century.

Even tungsten slowly evaporates when it glows, darkening the glass and thinning the wire. Filling the bulb with argon (Langmuir 1913, from air separation [6-07]) slowed this down; halogen lamps go further by carrying evaporated tungsten back to the filament.
block.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_furnace: Tungsten is made by blowing hydrogen over hot yellow powder.

An electric furnace [4-12] with a steel tube carrying hydrogen. (1) Reduce: WO3 + 3 H2 + 3 kW x 30 s -> W powder. (2) Sinter: 2 W powder + 1 H2 + 10 kW x 20 s -> bar. (3) GeO2 + 2 H2 + 3 kW x 20 s -> germanium (high-purity GeO2 gives GeCl4-route Ge, refinable to 10N). Hydrogen from the bag slot or an adjacent hydrogen gas holder.

Hydrogen protects the hot metal from oxygen and takes the oxygen out of the oxide. The water vapour made by the reaction leaves with the gas stream; the exhaust hydrogen is burned at the furnace exit.

Hydrogen + air is explosive (4-75%), so real furnaces purge the air with nitrogen before letting hydrogen in, and keep a small flame burning at the exit. The same furnaces later reduced GeO2 for germanium and annealed metals.
gui.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_furnace.n: Insert WO3, W powder or GeO2
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnabar_dust.not: Red powder of mercury and sulfur. Roast it to get mercury.
Crushed cinnabar HgS (from a vanilla cinnabar block, 1 -> 2). Roast it: HgS + O2 -> Hg + SO2 at about 600 C. A furnace lets the SO2 escape; a reverberatory furnace collects it.
Cinnabar was also the red pigment vermilion. The Almaden mine in Spain was worked for over 2000 years and once produced a third of the world's mercury.

Roasting works because mercury boils at 357 C: it leaves the hot ore as vapour and condenses as liquid in the cool part of the retort. The sulfur leaves as SO2, which could become sulfuric acid [2-01].
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note1: The stuff inside old thermometers. Never touch it.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note: Hg, the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Made by roasting a retort charge (cinnabar dust with an empty iron flask) in a furnace. Used for the mercury vacuum gauge; later for Sprengel and diffusion pumps and mercury lamps.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note3: Mercury is 13.6 times heavier than water, so a column only 76 cm tall balances the whole atmosphere. A water barometer would need about 10 m.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note4: Mercury vapour is toxic and builds up in the body (Minamata disease was methylmercury). It was traded in iron flasks of 34.5 kg. Gallium [1-44] melts in your hand (30 C) but is solid at room temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.placehold: Omitted: the retort's condenser (the flask just catches it). In a furnace the SO2 escapes (a reverberatory furnace collects it). Warning only: real mercury vapour is poisonous.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite_soda_c: Tungsten ore mixed with soda, ready to be melted.
Wolframite + sodium carbonate (1:1). Smelt it: (Fe,Mn)WO4 + Na2CO3 -> Na2WO4 + (Fe,Mn)O + CO2 (soda fusion, about 800-900 C).
Fusing with soda turns the insoluble ore into sodium tungstate, which dissolves in water, while iron and manganese stay behind as insoluble oxides. This is how tungsten is separated from them.
The Elhuyar brothers (1783) treated wolframite with potassium carbonate in the same way. Modern plants digest the ore with NaOH under pressure instead of fusing it.
Tungsten that now dissolves in water.
Na2WO4, the water-soluble product of soda fusion. Add hydrochloric acid to precipitate tungstic acid: Na2WO4 + 2HCl -> H2WO4 + 2NaCl.
Iron and manganese oxides do not dissolve, so leaching the fused cake with hot water and filtering leaves almost pure sodium tungstate in solution.
Sodium tungstate solutions are very dense; related tungstate salts (sodium polytungstate) are used as 'heavy liquids' to separate minerals by density.
Simplified: leaching the cake with water and filtering off the Fe/Mn oxides is skipped (they just disappear). CO2 is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungstic_acid.not: A yellow powder that falls out when acid is added.
H2WO4 (WO3*H2O), precipitated from sodium tungstate with hydrochloric acid (1 bottle = 2 mol HCl, exactly the amount needed). Roast it in a furnace to get WO3.
Scheele obtained tungstic acid from the mineral now called scheelite in 1781, but could not reduce it to the metal; the Elhuyar brothers did that two years later with charcoal.
The salt left in the liquid (NaCl) washes away. Heating H2WO4 drives off water at a few hundred degrees and leaves yellow WO3.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_germanium_t: Germanium dissolved in hydrochloric acid turns into a liquid. It still has other things mixed in.
GeO2 + 4HCl -> GeCl4 + 2H2O (2 bottles of hydrochloric acid = 4 mol HCl). Still mixed with other chlorides (AsCl3 etc.). Distil it with a quartz still.
GeCl4 is a colourless liquid that boils at only 83 C. Most impurity chlorides boil at different temperatures, so distillation separates them.
Arsenic is the troublesome one: AsCl3 boils at 130 C, close enough that real plants add chlorine or oxidisers to keep arsenic as non-volatile As(V) during distillation.
Simplified: the impurity chlorides are only named; distilling removes them all at once.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_still.note: A quartz flask and a glass cooling tube. Boil a liquid and catch the vapour.
Use it in the crafting grid with crude GeCl4 to get distilled GeCl4. The still comes back (it is a tool, not an ingredient).
Quartz glass is used because hot HCl and chlorides do not attack it and it releases almost no impurities - ordinary glass would leach sodium and boron into the product.

The water-cooled 'Liebig condenser' was popularised by Justus von Liebig in the 1830s, although similar designs are older. Semiconductor-grade GeCl4 and SiCl4 are still purified by fractional distillation in quartz or PTFE columns.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_still.plac: Simplified: the heat source and cooling water are skipped (distillation is done in the crafting grid).
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_tetrach: Very pure germanium liquid made by boiling and cooling.
Distilled GeCl4 (bp 83 C). Add water to hydrolyse it: GeCl4 + 2H2O -> GeO2 + 4HCl, giving high-purity GeO2.
In the 1940s-50s, Eagle-Picher and Bell Labs made transistor germanium this way: GeCl4 distillation, hydrolysis, hydrogen reduction, then zone refining.
Today GeCl4 is also the raw material for optical fibre: it is burned with SiCl4 to put GeO2 into the fibre core, raising its refractive index.
item.semiconductor-lab.high_purity_germa: Very clean white powder. Germanium from this can be refined all the way to 10N.

GeO2 from hydrolysed GeCl4. Reduce it with hydrogen in the hydrogen furnace (GeO2 + 2H2 -> Ge + 2H2O): the germanium keeps the 'GeCl4 route' mark and can reach 10N in the zone refining furnace (sulfate-route germanium stops at 9N).
It is reduced with hydrogen, not charcoal, because carbon and its ash would put impurities back in.
Zone refining removes impurities whose segregation coefficient is far from 1. Those close to 1 (and silicon in germanium) must be removed chemically first - that is why the chloride route matters.
Simplified: the HCl released by hydrolysis is not recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnetite.note1: A black stone that pulls on iron. It is full of iron.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnetite.note2: Drops from magnetite ore or iron sand (mined without Silk Touch). Four of them make a natural magnet, used to build a dynamo.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnetite.note3: Fe3O4 = FeO·Fe2O3. It mixes Fe2+ and Fe3+ ions and is the most strongly magnetic (ferrimagnetic) natural mineral. At about 72% iron by weight it is the richest iron ore, and above about 580 °C (its Curie temperature) it stops being magnetic.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnetite.note4: The word "magnet" comes from Magnesia in Greece, either because lodestones were found there or from the legend of the shepherd Magnes, whose iron-nailed sandals stuck to a rock.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite.note1: A heavy black stone. It holds the metal used for light bulb filaments.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite.note2: Mix with sodium carbonate and fire in a furnace (soda fusion) → sodium tungstate → hydrochloric acid → tungstic acid → furnace → tungsten trioxide → hydrogen furnace → tungsten powder → tungsten wire, the filament of the vacuum tube.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite.note3: (Fe,Mn)WO4 + Na2CO3 → Na2WO4 + (Fe,Mn)O + CO2. Na2WO4 dissolves in water, separating it from iron and manganese. Hydrochloric acid precipitates H2WO4, which is fired to WO3 and reduced with hydrogen: WO3 + 3H2 → W + 3H2O.
item.semiconductor-lab.wolframite.note4: German miners called it "wolf's froth" (Wolf Rahm) because it ate up tin when mixed into the smelt. That is where the symbol W comes from. In 1783 the Elhuyar brothers in Spain first isolated tungsten metal from this mineral.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note1: A heavy silvery stone that breaks into little cubes.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note3: Roasting (heating in air without melting): 2PbS + 3O2 → 2PbO + 2SO2. Reduction: PbO + C → Pb + CO. In the reverberatory furnace the SO2 is collected and can become sulfuric acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note4: PbS is a semiconductor (a material that conducts only a little). In 1874 Braun found that metal sulfide crystals let current flow in only one direction. Early 20th-century crystal radios touched galena with a fine wire (a cat's whisker) to turn radio waves into sound: a distant ancestor of the transistor.
block.semiconductor-lab.magnetite_ore.no: Iron ore deep underground that can become a magnet.

Banded iron formations formed about 2.5 to 1.8 billion years ago. Oxygen released by cyanobacteria (photosynthetic bacteria) oxidized iron (Fe²⁺) dissolved in the sea and made it settle out, laying down stripes of iron oxide and quartz.

Tiny magnetite crystals exist in living things too: magnetotactic bacteria line up magnetite grains inside themselves as a compass needle. Near huge magnetite deposits such as Kiruna in Sweden, compasses go wrong.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note1: Black beach sand. It sticks to a magnet.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note3: In tatara ironmaking, iron sand and charcoal are fed in turns and reduced by carbon monoxide: Fe3O4 + 4CO → 3Fe + 4CO2. The iron does not fully melt; a lump called kera forms at the bottom, and its best part becomes tamahagane steel.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note4: One tatara run (three days and nights, called hitoyo) uses about 10 t of iron sand and 12 t of charcoal to make about 2.5 t of kera. The Nittoho tatara in Shimane still runs each winter to supply steel for Japanese swords.
block.semiconductor-lab.wolframite_ore.n: Ore holding tungsten, a very heavy metal.

As granite magma cools, the last hot water (hydrothermal fluid) carries dissolved tungsten and tin into cracks, where they crystallize in quartz veins as it cools. That is why wolframite is often found with tin ore (cassiterite).
Tungsten melts at 3422 °C, the highest of any metal, and its density (about 19.3 g/cm³) is almost the same as gold. Today China produces about 80% of the world's tungsten.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note1: Lead ore. Look for it near zinc ore.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note3: Lead and zinc dissolved in hot underground brines (hydrothermal fluids) precipitate as sulfides when they meet sulfur-bearing water: Pb²⁺ + H2S → PbS + 2H⁺. That is why galena (PbS) and sphalerite (ZnS) form together.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note4: Its crystals have the same cubic structure as table salt, so it cleaves into neat little cubes. Ancient Egyptians ground galena into kohl, the dark eyeliner painted around the eyes.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_ash.note1: What is left after burning coal. It holds a tiny bit of germanium.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_ash.note2: Smelt coal in a furnace. 8 of them make germanium concentrate.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_ash.note3: Germanium binds to the plant matter that became coal, so some coals hold a few hundred ppm. Burning sends the carbon off as CO2 while the Ge stays concentrated in the ash, especially the fine fly ash.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_ash.note4: In 1930 the Norwegian geochemist V. M. Goldschmidt reported that rare elements such as germanium are strongly enriched in coal ash. Coal from places like Lincang in Yunnan, China is still a major germanium source.
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_concent: A powder with the germanium gathered and concentrated.
From 8 coal ash, or as a by-product of roasting sphalerite in the reverberatory furnace. Combine with sulfuric acid to get germanium dioxide.
Real concentrate is a mix of oxides and sulfides with a few percent germanium (for example zinc-smelting residue). Acid dissolves it so the germanium can be separated from the other metals.

Germanium was discovered in 1886 by Clemens Winkler in the silver ore argyrodite (Ag8GeS6). It matched Mendeleev's 1871 prediction of 'eka-silicon' (atomic weight about 72, density about 5.5) and became proof that the periodic table worked.
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_dioxide: A white powder of germanium joined to oxygen.
Made from germanium concentrate + sulfuric acid (crude, up to 9N) or by breaking down GeCl4 with water (high purity, up to 10N). Reduce it with charcoal or in the hydrogen furnace to get germanium.

GeO2 is a sibling of SiO2 (quartz) and can take the same crystal form. Hydrogen reduces it: GeO2 + 2H2 -> Ge + 2H2O (about 600-700 °C). Charcoal also works (GeO2 + C -> Ge + CO2) but leaves a little carbon behind.
GeO2 is mixed into the core of optical fibres: it raises the refractive index so light stays trapped in the core. Pure GeO2 glass passes infrared well and is used in infrared optics.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note1: Black, slippery carbon - the same stuff as pencil lead.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note3: Sheets of hexagonal carbon nets stacked in layers. The layers are held only by weak van der Waals forces, so they slide off onto paper. It does not melt at normal pressure: it sublimes (solid straight to gas) at about 3600 °C.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note4: In the 1560s a large vein of pure graphite was found at Borrowdale in England, and the pencil was born. People thought it was a kind of lead and called it 'plumbago'. In 1789 Abraham Werner named it graphite, from the Greek graphein, 'to write'.
block.semiconductor-lab.graphite_ore.not: Mine it for graphite, used for electrolyzer electrodes and boats.
Natural graphite is carbon from ancient living things rearranged into graphite by heat and pressure (metamorphism). It comes as flake, lump (vein) and amorphous graphite.
Sri Lankan vein graphite is a rare lump graphite over 90% pure. It is thought to have been deposited from hot underground fluids.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium.note1: A soft silver metal you can scratch with a fingernail.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium.note2: A by-product of roasting sphalerite in the reverberatory furnace. As a dopant in the refiner it makes p-type germanium; sandwich n-type Ge with it and fire to make an alloy-junction transistor.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium.note3: Indium is in group 13 (the boron family) with 3 outer electrons. Inside 4-electron germanium it leaves one bond short - a 'hole' - which makes p-type material. Its low melting point (about 157 °C) makes it easy to melt onto Ge as an alloy.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium.note4: Discovered in 1863 by Reich and Richter in sphalerite; its indigo spectral line gave it the name. Bend it and it 'cries' like tin. Today it is essential for the transparent electrodes (ITO, indium tin oxide) in phone screens.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_germanium.not: Made by reducing germanium dioxide with charcoal or in the hydrogen furnace. Refine it in the zone refining furnace: 6N -> 9N -> 10N.
At this stage the purity is about 99-99.9% (2N-3N). A transistor needs 9N (99.9999999%) or better: at most one impurity atom per billion.

Germanium looks like a metal but is a semiconductor, with the same crystal structure as diamond - hard and brittle. It melts at about 938 °C and, like water, expands when it freezes (the solid floats on the liquid).
item.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite.note1: An ore of zinc and sulfur, with a few rare metals mixed in.
item.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite.note2: Drops from sphalerite ore. A furnace gives zinc; roasting in the reverberatory furnace gives zinc oxide + SO2, with germanium concentrate or indium as by-products.
item.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite.note3: ZnS. Roasting: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. Elements similar to zinc - germanium, indium, cadmium, gallium - hide in its crystal and collect in the residue after the zinc is taken out.
item.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite.note4: The name comes from the Greek sphaleros, 'deceptive': it looks like lead ore (galena) but yields no lead. Its German name, blende, also means 'the deceiver'.
block.semiconductor-lab.sphalerite_ore.n: Mine it for sphalerite. Found at the same depths as galena.
Sphalerite and galena usually precipitate together from hot underground water (lead-zinc deposits). Iron-rich sphalerite is black; iron-poor crystals are clear yellow or red.
The zinc-blende crystal structure is shared by many compound semiconductors such as gallium arsenide (GaAs). It is the diamond structure of Ge and Si with its two sites filled by different elements.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_ingot.note1: A bar of zinc, used for galvanized iron and batteries.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_ingot.note2: Smelt sphalerite in a furnace, or roast it to zinc oxide in the reverberatory furnace and then reduce that in a furnace.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_ingot.note3: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. The roughly 1000 °C needed is above zinc's boiling point (about 907 °C), so the zinc comes off as vapour. It burns back to oxide in air, so it has to be condensed away from air.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_ingot.note4: Zinc distillation began at Zawar in India (worked from around the 12th century to the early 19th); in Europe William Champion patented it in 1738. Galvanized iron is iron plated with zinc: the zinc corrodes first and protects the iron (sacrificial protection).
block.semiconductor-lab.borax_deposit.no: A layer of white crystals at the bottom of a dried-up desert lake.
Found near the surface of deserts (y56-76) in sand and sandstone, a little rarer than trona. A wooden pickaxe gives borax; silk touch gives the block.

In dry regions boron leached from volcanic rocks drains into lakes; when the water evaporates it crystallizes as an evaporite. At Searles Lake in California trona and borax come out of the same lake bed.
In the 1880s borax from Death Valley was hauled about 260 km to the railway in huge wagons pulled by twenty mules (the '20 Mule Team'). Today Turkey holds most of the world's boron reserves.
item.semiconductor-lab.borax.note1: A white mineral with boron in it. It is also used to make slime.
item.semiconductor-lab.borax.note2: Mined from borax deposits. With sulfuric acid it gives 2 boric acid (1 item = 2 mol).
item.semiconductor-lab.borax.note3: Na2B4O7·10H2O (sodium tetraborate decahydrate). Sulfuric acid, the stronger acid, drives out the weak boric acid: Na2B4O7·10H2O + H2SO4 -> 4H3BO3 + Na2SO4 + 5H2O.
item.semiconductor-lab.borax.note4: In the Middle Ages borax (tincal) from Tibetan lakes travelled the Silk Road. Molten borax dissolves the oxide film on metals, so it has long been the flux for brazing gold and silver.
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.note1: A very weak acid, once used in eye wash and in cockroach bait.
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.note2: Borax + sulfuric acid gives 2. 1 item = 2 mol. Bake it in a furnace to get boron trioxide (the water comes off).
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.note3: H3BO3 = B(OH)3. Instead of giving off H+ like an ordinary acid, it takes OH- from water and becomes B(OH)4- (a Lewis acid, pKa about 9.2). Heating drives off water: 2H3BO3 -> B2O3 + 3H2O (in the game 1 item = 2 mol, so 1 -> 1).
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.note4: In Tuscany, Italy, steam jets from the ground carry boric acid; from 1818 it was boiled down there (Larderello). The same steam ran the world's first geothermal power generator in 1904.
item.semiconductor-lab.boric_acid.placeh: Omitted: the sodium sulfate (Na2SO4) and water formed along with it are discarded.
item.semiconductor-lab.boron_trioxide.no: A glassy lump of boron and oxygen - the stuff that makes silicon p-type.

Bake boric acid in a furnace. 1 item = 1 mol. A p-type dopant for silicon (used in the v0.2b silicon chapter), and an ingredient of heat-resistant borosilicate glass [2-15]. In silicon, put it in the CZ puller [9-08] dopant slot (p-type).

B2O3 melts into a glass at about 450 °C. Boron is in group 13 with 3 electrons; inside silicon (group 14, 4 electrons) it leaves one bond short - a hole - making p-type. Its segregation coefficient in silicon is about 0.8, close to 1, so the concentration barely changes along a pulled crystal - which is why boron is the p-type dopant of choice for silicon.

Elemental boron was isolated almost simultaneously in 1808 by Gay-Lussac and Thénard and by Davy, but pure boron was not made until Weintraub in 1909. In the 1950s Bell Labs diffused boron into silicon surfaces with heat to make p-type layers (the diffusion process) - a foundation of how integrated circuits are made.
block.semiconductor-lab.quartz_vein.note: A crack in the rock filled with white quartz.
Common everywhere in stone and deepslate (y-56 to 96). Mine with a stone pickaxe or better for vein quartz; silk touch gives the block.

Hot water deep underground (hydrothermal fluid) dissolves SiO2 from the rock and deposits it as quartz in cracks when it cools or the pressure drops. About 12% of the Earth's crust is quartz, the most common mineral after feldspar. Quartz veins sometimes carry gold (gold-quartz veins).
Where a vein has open space, quartz grows into clear hexagonal crystals - rock crystal. In Kofu, Yamanashi, crystal has been mined since the Edo period, and crystal carving became a local industry.
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.note1: A white stone of almost pure silicon dioxide (SiO2) - the starting point for glass and silicon.
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.note2: Mined from quartz veins. Melt it in the oxyhydrogen burner to get fused quartz. Also the raw material for metallurgical silicon [1-15] later on.
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.note3: SiO2 is a crystal of tetrahedra - one silicon surrounded by four oxygens - linked by sharing their corner oxygens. It melts at about 1713 °C, far beyond a furnace (about 1000 °C). Fused quartz is made from quartz low in iron, aluminium and other impurities (natural rock crystal or selected vein quartz).
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.note4: The purest natural quartz today comes from pegmatites (very coarse granite) at Spruce Pine, North Carolina, with under 100 ppm impurities. It becomes the quartz crucibles that silicon single crystals are pulled from - holding up the world's semiconductor industry.
item.semiconductor-lab.vein_quartz.place: Omitted: real quartz is crushed and acid-washed to remove iron and other impurities before melting (the purification steps).
item.semiconductor-lab.metallurgical_sil: Shiny grey silicon made from stone, charcoal and a lot of electricity.

From the arc furnace: 2 vein quartz + 1 charcoal or coal. 98% pure (metallurgical grade) - still far too dirty for semiconductors, so it is purified via trichlorosilane [1-16] and the Siemens process [1-17]. Each kg takes over 10 kWh of electricity. Modern plants use AC submerged-arc furnaces; the game approximates it with DC until AC arrives in v0.4.

SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO. Silicon and oxygen are bound so tightly that ordinary furnace temperatures cannot separate them; the arc's ~2000 °C is needed. Remaining impurities are iron, aluminium, calcium and so on (from the raw materials and electrodes).

Most metallurgical silicon goes into aluminium alloys and silicone resins, not semiconductors. Because it uses so much electricity, plants have been built where hydropower is cheap, such as Norway. The fine SiO2 dust from the furnace (silica fume) is used to make high-strength concrete.
Omitted: carbon monoxide (CO) and SiO fumes are not collected. Industrial production in electric furnaces began in the early 20th century (c. 1900; no exact year is known).
block.semiconductor-lab.trichlorosilane_: Turns hard silicon into a liquid, then boils it again and again to clean it.

Synthesis (10 kW, 60 s): metallurgical silicon 1 + dry hydrogen chloride 3 → crude trichlorosilane 1 (99%) + hydrogen 1. Distillation (20 kW, 30 s per stage): put trichlorosilane in the bottom-left slot; each stage removes 9/10 of the impurities (one more 9), up to 11N. If the distillation slot has something, it distils; otherwise it synthesizes. Use dry HCl gas from the HCl burner with no water, not hydrochloric acid.

Si + 3HCl → SiHCl3 + H2 at about 300 °C (the reaction gives off heat). SiHCl3 boils at 32 °C, BCl3 at 12 °C and PCl3 at 76 °C, so a distillation column can separate the boron and phosphorus chlorides by their boiling points.

Boron and phosphorus are the hardest impurities, because they are the very elements that set a semiconductor's type. Real plants use tall columns with many trays and repeat the distillation. It is the same idea as distilling GeCl4 for germanium.

Approximation: real plants use a fluidized-bed reactor plus separate tall distillation columns; here it is one block. ⚠️ Amounts are symbolic (1 silicon ≈ 1 kg but 1 gas bag = 1 mol). ⚠️ Power and time are for gameplay. By-product SiCl4 and waste chlorides are not shown.
gui.semiconductor-lab.trichlorosilane_re: Needs Si 1 + HCl gas 3, or TCS to distil
