item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_chloride: The sharp-smelling gas that becomes hydrochloric acid when it dissolves in water. Here it is kept dry.
From the HCl burner with no water: H2 1 mol + Cl2 1 mol → hydrogen chloride 2 bags (1 bag = 1 mol). Used for trichlorosilane [1-16]. The Siemens reactor [1-17] gives it back.
HCl is a colourless gas that dissolves very easily in water (that is hydrochloric acid). Trichlorosilane reacts with water, so silicon refining needs dry HCl gas, not the acid.

Wet HCl eats through steel, but dry HCl hardly does, so keeping the gas dry protects the plant too. In real plants the HCl from the Siemens reactor is separated and sent back to make more trichlorosilane.
Approximation: real HCl is stored in cylinders or piped; here it is a 1 mol bag.
item.semiconductor-lab.trichlorosilane.n: Silicon turned into a liquid. It boils at a bath-like temperature, so it is easy to clean by distilling.
SiHCl3. From the trichlorosilane reactor: crude is 99%. Put it back in the distillation slot: each stage adds one 9 (up to 11N). Feed it to the Siemens reactor [1-17] to make polysilicon.
A colourless liquid that boils at 32 °C. It fumes in moist air (it reacts with water and gives off HCl), so it is handled sealed and dry.
Solid silicon cannot be distilled, but its chloride can. The trick of 'make it a liquid, distil it, turn it back' is the key to ultra-pure silicon, just like GeCl4 for germanium.
item.semiconductor-lab.trichlorosilane.p: Approximation: 1 item is a symbolic amount (enough for about 1 kg of silicon). ⚠️ Crude purity 99% is a game stage.
Thin silicon rods glow hot inside a bell, and grow fatter and fatter from the gas.

500 kW (one steam turbine). Trichlorosilane distilled to 9N or more 1 + hydrogen 1 → polysilicon 1 (same purity, 9N–11N) + hydrogen chloride gas 3 (648 s = 90 kWh). The HCl goes back to the trichlorosilane reactor [1-16]. Not enough power → stops (the rods cannot stay at 1100 °C).

SiHCl3 + H2 → Si + 3HCl at about 1100 °C. Electricity flows through the silicon rods themselves to heat them, so the walls stay cooler and add little dirt. Only silicon sticks to the rods, layer by layer.

11N means one foreign atom in a hundred billion, like one stranger among more than ten times the people on Earth. A rod grows about 1 mm per hour and takes days to reach 15–20 cm thick. Siemens developed the method in the mid-1950s (basic patent filed 1956, published 1959).

Omitted: the thin seed rods (slim rods) and pre-heating them (cold silicon barely conducts). ⚠️ Amounts are symbolic (1 polysilicon ≈ 1 kg but 1 gas bag = 1 mol). 90 kWh/kg is a patent comparative example; modern reactors use less ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.note1: The cleanest stuff people make in large amounts: silicon with almost nothing else in it.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.note2: From the Siemens reactor [1-17]: same purity as the trichlorosilane (9N–11N). Made of many tiny crystals. Next it becomes one big crystal (CZ [9-08], FZ [9-09]) and then wafers.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.note3: "Poly" means many crystals: the silicon that piles up on the rod grows as countless small grains facing different ways. For transistors it must be melted and regrown as a single crystal.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.note4: Most polysilicon goes to solar cells (lower purity is enough); the purest goes to chips. Every year the world makes over a million tonnes ⚠️, mostly by the Siemens method.
item.semiconductor-lab.polysilicon.place: Approximation: 1 item ≈ 1 kg (symbolic amounts, Q22-1). Real rods are crushed into chunks for the crucible.
block.semiconductor-lab.malachite_ore.no: Rock with green banded stone in it, the same green as rusted copper.
In stone near the surface (y40-110). A stone pickaxe or better drops malachite. It forms in the 'oxidized zone' at the top of a copper deposit, exposed to rain and air.

Deep copper ore (chalcopyrite, the vanilla copper ore) turns into green malachite and blue azurite near the surface where it meets water and carbon dioxide. People once looked for copper by this eye-catching green.

Below the oxidized zone lies an 'enriched zone' where dissolved copper settled, and below that the original sulfide ore. When ancient mines exhausted the surface malachite they hit sulfide ore, which is harder to smelt [1-04].
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.note1: A green stone. Bake it with charcoal and copper comes out.
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.note2: Basic copper carbonate Cu2CO3(OH)2. Furnace (faster in a blast furnace) -> copper ingot. Heat splits it into CuO, CO2 and H2O, and carbon (CO) from the fuel takes the oxygen: CuO + C -> Cu + CO.
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.note3: At Belovode in Serbia, slag from copper smelting about 7000 years ago (around 5000 BC) has been found. The smelters used a manganese-rich, greenish-black oxidized copper ore, and kept pure malachite for beads. In ancient Egypt malachite was also ground and worn as eye paint.
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.note4: Malachite decomposes into black copper oxide at about 300 C, and carbon monoxide in a charcoal fire reduces it from about 800 C. Copper melts at 1085 C, so a furnace blown with bellows was needed to melt it into a lump. Having no sulfur, it is easier than sulfide ore and became the first copper ore used.
item.semiconductor-lab.malachite.placeho: Approximation: the furnace (~1000 C) does reduction and melting in one step (reduced by the fuel's C/CO, as in CHEMISTRY #38). CO2 and steam are not collected.
Granite with dark, heavy grains in it. Tin ore.
Only in granite (y-10-70, the same belt as wolframite). An iron pickaxe or better drops cassiterite.
Tin and tungsten often settle together in the same veins from the last hot water left as granite cools. Cornwall in England has produced tin since the Bronze Age.

Cassiterite is very heavy (density about 7) and does not weather. When rock breaks down it stays behind and gathers in river sand (placer deposits). Big tin mines in Malaysia and Indonesia dig such river and sea sands (in the game it is only in granite).
item.semiconductor-lab.cassiterite.note1: A dark, heavy stone. Bake it with charcoal and tin comes out.
item.semiconductor-lab.cassiterite.note2: Tin(IV) oxide SnO2. Hard (Mohs 6-7). Bake it in a furnace with charcoal (the fuel's carbon) for a tin ingot [1-30].
item.semiconductor-lab.cassiterite.note3: The name comes from the Greek for tin (kassiteros). To make bronze with copper, ancient people carried tin long distances and traded it.
item.semiconductor-lab.cassiterite.note4: SnO2 hardly dissolves in water or acids; it is a very stable oxide, so it survives weathering at the surface. Thin transparent SnO2 films conduct electricity, and are used today for insulating window coatings and solar cell electrodes (FTO).
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.note1: A soft, silvery metal. Mixed with copper it makes bronze.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.note2: Cassiterite -> furnace (faster in a blast furnace). SnO2 + 2C -> Sn + 2CO (reduced by the fuel's carbon). Melts at only 232 C. A material for bronze [1-05] and speculum metal [7-05].
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.note3: Bend a tin bar and it creaks (the 'tin cry'): crystals rubbing against each other. Left in the cold for a long time it crumbles into grey powder (tin pest, a change that happens below 13 C).
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.note4: Tin, a bronze material 5000 years ago, is now the main part of electronic solder and even the light source of cutting-edge EUV lithography [7-18]: droplets of molten tin about 30 um across are hit by a laser tens of thousands of times a second, becoming a plasma that emits 13.5 nm light.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_ingot.placeho: Approximation: the furnace (~1000 C) does reduction and melting in one step (reduced by the fuel's C/CO, as in CHEMISTRY #38). CO2 is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.bronze_charge.not: Copper and tin weighed and mixed. Melt it and it becomes bronze.
8 copper ingots + 1 tin ingot -> 9 (about 11% tin). Melt in a furnace (faster in a blast furnace) for bronze ingots.
Ancient founders varied the copper-tin ratio: about one tenth tin for tools and swords, over one fifth for bells (hard, ringing bell metal).
Tin dissolves readily in molten copper. The alloy melts lower (copper 1085 C -> bronze about 950 C) and flows into every corner of a mould, so it casts well.
item.semiconductor-lab.bronze_ingot.note: Copper with one tenth tin: a metal that melts easily yet is hard.
Cu-Sn about 11%. Much harder than pure copper and corrodes less. c:ingots/bronze. With more tin, speculum metal makes mirrors [7-05].

From about 3000 BC people made tools, weapons, mirrors and bells of bronze (the Bronze Age). Before that, copper containing arsenic (arsenical bronze) was also used (⚠️ timing and spread differ by region).
Large tin atoms in the copper crystal distort the lattice and hinder the slipping of crystal planes (solid-solution strengthening), so the alloy is harder than the pure metal.
item.semiconductor-lab.bronze_ingot.plac: Approximation: melting in a furnace stands in for a crucible furnace (CHEMISTRY #38).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_ash.note1: White ash from burnt bone. It soaks up molten metal oxides well.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_ash.note2: Bone meal -> furnace. Mostly calcium phosphate. 4 make a cupel.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_ash.note3: Besides cupels, bone ash goes into English 'bone china' (white porcelain with bone ash in it).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_ash.note4: Burning removes the bone's organic part (collagen), leaving porous hydroxyapatite Ca5(PO4)3(OH). Molten lead oxide wets it and soaks in by capillary action, but molten silver is repelled and stays on the surface.
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel.note1: A small dish of pressed bone ash. Heat silver-bearing lead on it and only the silver remains.
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel.note2: 4 bone ash. Combine with 8 lead ingots into a cupel charge (the dish soaks up lead oxide and is used up).
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel.note3: 'Cupel' comes from the Latin for 'little cup'. The same dishes have long been used in assaying, testing the purity of gold and silver.
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel.note4: A cupel must weigh about as much as the lead oxide it absorbs. Old mines also used hearths of pressed wood ash or lime besides bone ash.
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel_charge.note: Silver-bearing lead on a cupel. Heat it in a blast furnace and silver comes out.
8 lead ingots + cupel. Blast furnace (blown with air), about 1000 C -> silver nugget. A plain furnace does not give enough air.

At Iwami Ginzan in Japan, silver was extracted by cupellation introduced from the Korean peninsula in 1533, and in the 16th-17th centuries it produced a large share of the world's silver (⚠️ the share varies by source).

Air on molten lead gives 2Pb + O2 -> 2PbO. PbO melts at 888 C and soaks into the cupel or runs off. Silver hardly oxidizes, so when all the lead is gone a bright silver bead appears (the 'flash' or 'blick').
item.semiconductor-lab.cupel_charge.plac: Approximation: all galena is treated as silver-bearing, 1 silver nugget per 8 lead (about 1.4%). Real silver content is about 0.01-1% and varies. The PbO (litharge) absorbed by the cupel is not recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.silver_nugget.not: A bead of silver left by cupellation. 9 make a silver ingot.
Cupel charge -> blast furnace. Used in vacuum evaporation [5-14] to coat glass thinly for half-mirrors and mirrors.
Much of the silver in old coins and silverware was extracted from galena by cupellation.
Silver reflects visible light better than any other metal (over 95%), but it tarnishes black with sulfur compounds (silver sulfide).
item.semiconductor-lab.silver_ingot.note: A shining white metal. It conducts electricity and heat best of all.
9 silver nuggets (an ingot can be split back into 9). c:ingots/silver.
Used for photographic emulsions (silver bromide and iodide), mirrors and electrical contacts.

Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of all metals (slightly above copper), yet copper is the main wiring metal because it is far cheaper. Chip wiring moved from aluminum to copper, and silver is hardly used.
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorite.note1: A glassy purple or green stone. It contains fluorine.
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorite.note2: Calcium fluoride CaF2. Mined from fluorite ore with a stone pickaxe or better. Raw material for hydrofluoric acid [2-10] (fluorite + sulfuric acid).
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorite.note3: The first record is 'fluores' in Agricola's 1530 book: a flux that made ores melt and flow more easily in the furnace, from Latin fluere, to flow. The element fluorine is named after it.
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorite.note4: Some fluorite glows blue under ultraviolet light; in 1852 Stokes named this glow 'fluorescence' after it. The Japanese name means 'firefly stone' because it glows when heated. Large fluorite crystals later became lenses and windows for excimer laser lithography [7-20].
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorite_ore.not: Stone with purple and green grains in it. Mining it gives fluorite.
Found in stone and deepslate at the same depth as galena (Y −16 to 64), less often than galena. Stone pickaxe or better. Silk Touch keeps the ore block.
Fluorite usually forms in veins left by hot water flowing through cracks in rock (hydrothermal veins), together with galena and sphalerite. Lead and zinc mines often produce fluorite too.
Most fluorite today becomes hydrofluoric acid, the starting point of almost all fluorine chemistry (fluoropolymers, refrigerants, etching gases for chips).
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorite_ore.pla: Approximation: real fluorite occurs in veins with galena and sphalerite; in the game it is scattered at the same depth.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_flask.note1: An iron bottle for mercury. Mercury does not dissolve iron.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_flask.note2: Roast it together with cinnabar dust and the mercury that comes out collects in this flask.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_flask.note3: Mercury mixes with gold, silver, copper and zinc to form amalgams, but hardly with iron. That is why mercury is kept in iron.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_flask.note4: Mercury is still traded by the flask: one flask is 76 pounds (about 34.5 kg), and prices are quoted per flask.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_bottle.note1: A lead bottle for hydrofluoric acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_bottle.note2: Hydrofluoric acid dissolves glass, so it cannot go in a glass bottle.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_bottle.note3: ⚠️ Hydrofluoric acid used to be kept in lead, wax (ceresin) or gutta-percha (a tree resin) containers. Today it comes in polyethylene bottles.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_bottle.note4: A thin film of lead fluoride (PbF2) forms on lead and slows further attack. Sulfuric acid forms a lead sulfate film, which is why lead lined the chambers of the lead-chamber process.
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnabar_retort_c: Cinnabar dust packed with an empty iron flask. Roast it to collect mercury.
Roast it in a furnace or a reverberatory furnace to get an iron flask of mercury (the reverberatory furnace also gives SO2).
HgS + O2 → Hg (gas) + SO2. Mercury boils at 357 °C, so it leaves as vapour; it is cooled back to liquid and caught in the flask.
At the Almadén mine in Spain, mercury vapour was cooled and collected for centuries in rows of clay pipes called aludels. The vapour is very toxic and ruined the health of the workers.
item.semiconductor-lab.coke.note1: What is left after baking coal: a light, grey, holey kind of charcoal.
item.semiconductor-lab.coke.note2: The gas works retort [2-20] turns 4 coal into 3 coke. It fuels the retort and the blast furnace [1-09] in place of charcoal (the coke blast furnace [1-10]).
item.semiconductor-lab.coke.note3: Raw coal gives off smoke and sulfur that make iron brittle. Baking off the volatile part leaves almost pure carbon, a strong fuel. In 1709 Darby made iron with coke, ending the worry of using up the forests.
item.semiconductor-lab.coke.note4: In a blast furnace, coke does three jobs: fuel, carbon that reduces the iron ore, and a frame that holds up the charge. Because it is full of holes, the air blast can pass through it.
item.semiconductor-lab.bauxite.note1: A reddish-brown, earthy rock. The raw material of aluminium.
item.semiconductor-lab.bauxite.note2: A mixture of aluminium hydroxides (gibbsite Al(OH)3 and others) and red iron rust (iron oxide). Mined from bauxite ore. Dissolved in sodium hydroxide to extract alumina (Bayer process [1-14]).
item.semiconductor-lab.bauxite.note3: Where it is hot and rainy, rock washed by rain for a very long time loses its soluble parts, leaving aluminium and iron behind (residual weathering). The red is the colour of iron rust.
item.semiconductor-lab.bauxite.note4: In 1821 Berthier found it near the village of Les Baux in southern France and named it after the village. Today tropical and subtropical countries such as Australia and Guinea are the big producers.
block.semiconductor-lab.bauxite_ore.note: A reddish-brown ore near the surface in jungles and savannas.
Only in jungles and savannas, replacing dirt, coarse dirt and stone at Y 56–90. Mine with a pickaxe (wood is fine). Silk Touch keeps the ore block.
Bauxite usually lies near the surface like a blanket rather than deep underground, so it is dug in open pits.
The 'red mud' left after extracting aluminium is strongly alkaline. As the 2010 reservoir collapse at Ajka, Hungary showed, how to store it is a serious problem.
block.semiconductor-lab.bauxite_ore.plac: Approximation: it appears as lumps in dirt and stone rather than as a real surface layer (laterite).
block.semiconductor-lab.bayer_digester.n: A vessel that dissolves bauxite in hot caustic soda and takes out only the aluminium part.

2 kW. 2 bauxite → 1 aluminium hydroxide + 1 red mud (30 s). The liquor is 1 sodium hydroxide dissolved in 1 water bucket and lasts 4 runs (the empty bucket goes to the output). Bake aluminium hydroxide in a furnace to get alumina.

Al(OH)3 + NaOH → NaAl(OH)4. The aluminium dissolves, but iron rust does not and stays behind as red mud. Cooling the filtered liquor and adding seed crystals brings aluminium hydroxide back out. The liquor is used again and again.

Karl Josef Bayer devised it in 1888 while working for textile mills in Russia. Paired with the Hall–Héroult process of two years earlier, these two methods still make almost all the world's aluminium. Gallium collects in the liquor, and most gallium today comes from here.
block.semiconductor-lab.bayer_digester.p: Omitted: heating is an electric heater (the real one is a steam-heated pressure vessel at about 150–250 °C). Amounts are symbolic (really about 2–3 tonnes of bauxite per tonne of alumina). Gallium in the liquor is not extracted.
item.semiconductor-lab.aluminium_hydroxi: A white powder. Baking it gives alumina.
Al(OH)3, from the Bayer digester [1-14]. Bake it in a furnace or blast furnace to get alumina Al2O3 (the water leaves). Also used to make cryolite [1-38].
2Al(OH)3 → Al2O3 + 3H2O. Real plants bake it at over about 1000 °C (calcination).
It is also used in antacids and as a flame retardant (it releases water when heated and cools the fire).
item.semiconductor-lab.alumina.note1: White powder of aluminium oxide. The raw material of aluminium.
item.semiconductor-lab.alumina.note2: Al2O3, made by baking aluminium hydroxide. Its melting point (about 2050 °C) is too high, so it is dissolved in molten cryolite and electrolysed (Hall–Héroult process [1-29]).
item.semiconductor-lab.alumina.note3: Alumina crystals are very hard; the gems ruby (with chromium) and sapphire (with iron and titanium) are alumina too. It is also used as an abrasive and refractory.
item.semiconductor-lab.alumina.note4: Aluminium is the most common metal in the Earth's crust, but it holds oxygen so tightly that it was very hard to extract before electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_mud.note1: The red mud left after taking out aluminium. It is strongly alkaline, so do not touch it with bare hands.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_mud.note2: Residue of the Bayer digester [1-14]: iron oxides (the red colour), silicon and titanium compounds and leftover caustic soda. No use yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_mud.note3: About 1–1.5 tonnes of red mud come out per tonne of alumina. It is dried in ponds, which take up space and must be watched so the alkali does not leak.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_mud.note4: In October 2010 a red mud reservoir burst at Ajka, Hungary, and strongly alkaline mud flowed into villages and rivers (ten people died). Since then, drying it into solid blocks and reusing it for cement and iron have been studied more.
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.note1: An icy, white, see-through mineral. It becomes the 'hot bath' for making aluminium.
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.note2: Na3AlF6. At the crafting table: 3 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles come back) + 1 aluminium hydroxide + 3 sodium hydroxide → 1 cryolite (6HF + Al(OH)3 + 3NaOH → Na3AlF6 + 6H2O). The bath for the Hall–Héroult process [1-29].
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.note3: Alumina only melts at about 2050 °C, but it dissolves well in cryolite melted at about 1000 °C, so it can be electrolysed at about 960 °C. That is the key idea of the Hall–Héroult process.
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.note4: Natural cryolite was mined in quantity only at Ivittuut, Greenland, and ran out in 1987. Today it is all made chemically (this way). ⚠️ The year synthetic production became industrial is not yet checked.
item.semiconductor-lab.cryolite.placehol: Approximation: mixed at the crafting table (really reacted in lead- or rubber-lined tanks, then the crystals are filtered and dried).
block.semiconductor-lab.hall_heroult_cel: A cell that dissolves alumina in molten cryolite and takes out aluminium with electricity. It eats a lot of power.

100 kW. 2 alumina → 1 aluminium (about 1 kg, 540 s = 15 kWh). 1 cryolite gives a bath for 16 runs; 1 graphite rod (anode) lasts 2 runs. 2Al2O3 + 3C → 4Al + 3CO2. The current's own heat keeps the bath at about 960 °C.

In 1886 Charles Martin Hall (22, USA) and Paul Héroult (23, France) found the same method independently. Both were born in 1863 and both died in 1914. Before that, aluminium cost more than gold or silver, and Napoleon III is said to have served only his most honoured guests on aluminium plates.

About 13–15 kWh (roughly a household's daily use) goes into 1 kg of aluminium, so smelters were built near hydropower (Niagara, Norway, Canada). Aluminium is called 'packaged electricity'; recycling it needs only about 5% of the energy of making it new.

Omitted: CO2 and fluoride exhaust are not modelled, nor current and voltage (really about 4–5 V DC at tens to hundreds of thousands of amperes). One block stands for a whole potline of dozens of cells.
item.semiconductor-lab.aluminium_ingot.n: A light, silvery metal that hardly rusts.
Made in the Hall–Héroult cell [1-29]. Later used for chip wiring (vacuum evaporation [9-25]) and machine parts.
In air, aluminium quickly grows a thin oxide film (alumina) that protects the metal underneath, so rust does not spread, the same trick silicon uses with its oxide.
In 1959 Noyce's integrated circuit was wired with aluminium evaporated onto the chip. IC wiring stayed aluminium until copper took over in the 1990s.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_tetrachlo: A liquid made alongside trichlorosilane. It fumes white in air. ⚠ Reacts with water, releasing hydrochloric acid gas.
SiCl4. One per 4 syntheses in the trichlorosilane reactor (Si + 4HCl -> SiCl4 + 2H2). Burned in the oxyhydrogen burner into synthetic quartz; later a material for epitaxy [9-30]. Boils at 57.6 C.

Polysilicon plants produce several times more SiCl4 than trichlorosilane as a byproduct. Rather than dump it, they turn it into synthetic quartz and optical-fibre feedstock, or convert it back to trichlorosilane with hydrogen.
SiCl4 reacts with moisture in air to give fine SiO2 particles and HCl (the white fumes). Done inside a flame, this reaction yields an extremely pure glass powder that is fused into synthetic quartz.
Approximation: one per 4 syntheses is a game value (in reality 10-20% of the product). No bottle.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_grain.no: Tiny grains of platinum mixed into river and beach sand. Very rare.
Native platinum (Pt with palladium, iridium, iron and others). Digging beach iron sand with a shovel rarely (about 3%) gives some (not with Silk Touch). Refined by dissolving in aqua regia [1-18].

Platinum is heavy and never rusts, so when rock breaks down it stays metal and settles with iron sand and gold in riverbeds and beaches (placer deposits). It came from rivers in Colombia and the Urals.
Gold miners in Colombia threw away the hard-to-melt white grains as 'platina' (little silver). In 1748 Ulloa's travel account first described it in Europe.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_grain.pl: Approximation: in the game it comes from beach iron sand (really mostly from river sands in Colombia and the Urals).
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroplatinic_ac: An orange liquid: platinum dissolved in aqua regia.

H2PtCl6 in water (glass bottle). Crafting: 2 placer platinum + 3 hydrochloric acid + 1 nitric acid (aqua regia; bottles come back) + 1 empty glass bottle → 1. Mixed with 2 ammonium chloride it gives a yellow precipitate. GHS: corrosive, respiratory sensitiser.

Platinum resists every single acid but dissolves in aqua regia, 3 parts hydrochloric to 1 part nitric. The nitric acid oxidises the platinum and chloride ions grab it into solution. The name ('royal water') comes from dissolving gold, the king of metals.
Repeated contact with platinum salts can cause a serious allergy (platinosis), so refineries take care not to breathe them in.
Approximation: evaporating the aqua regia, filtering and separating palladium and the other platinum metals are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonium_chloropl: A yellow powder that settles out of the platinum solution. Baking it gives platinum.
(NH4)2PtCl6. Crafting: 1 chloroplatinic acid solution + 2 ammonium chloride → 1 (the glass bottle comes back). Baked in a furnace it becomes platinum sponge.
H2PtCl6 + 2NH4Cl → (NH4)2PtCl6↓ + 2HCl. It hardly dissolves, so it sinks, while iron, copper and other metals stay in the liquid: this is where platinum is separated.
Heating breaks it down, roughly (NH4)2PtCl6 → Pt + 2NH4Cl + 2Cl2, leaving a porous, sponge-like platinum.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_sponge.n: A porous lump of platinum, like a sponge.
Left after baking the yellow precipitate in a furnace. Press 2 into a compact and forge it at white heat in a blast furnace to get a platinum ingot.
Its huge surface makes it a good catalyst: hydrogen meeting oxygen on it catches fire by itself (Döbereiner's lamp, 1823).
Platinum melts at about 1768 °C, beyond early-19th-century furnaces, so a way to consolidate the powder without melting was needed.
2 platinum sponge → 1 (crafting). Heated to white heat in a blast furnace, the grains bond (sintering) into a platinum ingot.

Around 1800 Wollaston pressed fine platinum powder with a screw press, heated it white-hot and hammered it, making workable platinum that nobody else could. This was the beginning of powder metallurgy.
Wollaston kept the method secret for life and made a fortune from platinum, discovering palladium and rhodium along the way.
Approximation: pressed at the crafting table instead of a screw press.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_ingot.no: A heavy, silvery-white metal that never rusts and resists acids.
Made by heating the platinum compact in a blast furnace (c:ingots/platinum). Becomes the anode in the hydrogen peroxide cell [2-19].
Platinum barely dissolves even where oxygen is produced in electrolysis, so it was essential for strongly oxidising electrolysis (persulfate, hydrogen peroxide).
From 1889 to 2019 the kilogram was defined by a cylinder of 90% platinum and 10% iridium (the International Prototype Kilogram).
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.note1: A clay furnace. Roasting iron ore with charcoal gives a lump of iron that never melts.
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.note2: Load iron ore (or iron sand) and charcoal, then keep pumping the bellows beside it to pass 1100 °C. Fire alone stops at about 800 °C. Heat the bloom red-hot in a furnace and hammer it with a hammerstone to get wrought iron (an iron ingot).
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.note3: Carbon monoxide from the burning charcoal takes the oxygen from the ore (Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2). At about 1200 °C iron (melting point 1538 °C) stays solid and forms a spongy lump full of slag.
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.note4: Iron smelting began around 1400–1200 BC. Anatolia and its surroundings are among the proposed places, but nothing is certain. Iron hammered free of slag is low in carbon and soft (wrought iron).
block.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.placeho: Approximation: temperatures and times are game values; vanilla raw iron is treated as hematite Fe2O3
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.note1: A spongy lump of iron from the bloomery.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.note2: Reheat it red-hot in a furnace, then hammer it with a hammerstone in the crafting grid to get wrought iron (an iron ingot). It can't be forged cold.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.note3: It is full of holes because it was reduced as a solid, without melting. Glassy slag (silicates) fills the gaps.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.note4: Smiths reheated the bloom red-hot and hammered and folded it again and again to squeeze the slag out. The 'kera' of Japanese tatara iron-making is also iron that never melted.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_bloom.placeh: Approximation: one reheating in a furnace
gui.semiconductor-lab.bloomery.need_ore: Add iron ore or iron sand
block.semiconductor-lab.blast_furnace_he: The lowest opening of a tall brick furnace. Molten iron flows out here.

Place it at the bottom middle of the front and build bricks around it, 3×3×4. The four sides of the 2nd layer are tuyeres; keep the inside empty. Put a water-powered bellows outside a tuyere for a steady blast. Opening the screen lights up missing spots.

A tall furnace with a strong, steady blast reaches about 1500 °C. Carbon dissolves into the iron and lowers its melting point to about 1150 °C, so the iron runs out as liquid (pig iron, about 4% carbon). Limestone turns the ore's earth into slag that separates from the iron.

China made pig iron in blast furnaces from about the 5th century BC and cast it in molds. Europe took it up around the 14th century. In 1709 Darby used coke instead of charcoal so forests no longer had to be cut (this furnace also runs on coke).
Approximation: temperatures, times and the limestone amount are game values; the lining is fired brick (refractory brick [3-12] comes with later furnaces)
block.semiconductor-lab.tuyere.note1: A fired clay pipe that blows the bellows' air into the furnace.
block.semiconductor-lab.tuyere.note2: Put them on the four sides of the blast furnace's 2nd layer. A bellows outside sends its air into the furnace.
block.semiconductor-lab.tuyere.note3: Right in front of the tuyere is the hottest place in the furnace. Charcoal burns hard there, and the carbon monoxide rises and takes the oxygen from the ore.
block.semiconductor-lab.tuyere.note4: Later big blast furnaces made tuyeres of copper cooled by flowing water, and preheated the blast (hot blast, 1828).
item.semiconductor-lab.pig_iron.note1: Iron that ran out of a blast furnace. Lots of carbon: hard but brittle.
item.semiconductor-lab.pig_iron.note2: Blow air through it in a converter and the carbon burns away, giving steel.
item.semiconductor-lab.pig_iron.note3: With about 4% carbon it melts about 400 °C below pure iron (1538 °C), which is why it flows out of the blast furnace as liquid. It cracks when hammered, so it is cast in molds.
item.semiconductor-lab.pig_iron.note4: The name comes from the sand molds: thin bars of iron branching off a main channel looked like piglets lined up at a sow.
item.semiconductor-lab.blast_furnace_sla: Stony waste that separates from the iron in a blast furnace.
Limestone and the ore's earth (silica) melt together into it. It is lighter than iron and floats on the molten metal.
CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3. Without slag, the earth would set inside and choke the furnace.
Today blast furnace slag is ground up for cement and used under roads.
item.semiconductor-lab.hot_iron_bloom.no: A bloom heated until it glows red. Now it can be hammered.
Put it in the crafting grid with a hammerstone to beat the slag out and get wrought iron (an iron ingot). The hammerstone comes back.
Above about 1000 °C the slag in the gaps softens. Hammering welds the iron grains together and squeezes the slag out. Wrought iron has under 0.1% carbon and is soft and tough.

Heating wrought iron packed in charcoal for a long time lets carbon soak into the surface (carburizing); quenching it in water then makes a blade. Wrought iron dates from the start of iron smelting, around 1400–1200 BC ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.hot_iron_bloom.pl: Approximation: heat once, hammer once (really heated and hammered again and again)
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_crucible.note: A crucible shaped from clay, not yet fired.
5 clay + refractory brick (crushed as grog). Fired in the blast furnace it becomes a fire-clay crucible.
Huntsman made his own crucibles from Stourbridge fire clay mixed with coke dust and ground old crucibles, kneaded by treading.
Mixing in already-fired clay (grog) reduces shrinking and cracking in the kiln, a basic trick of refractory making.
item.semiconductor-lab.clay_crucible.not: A clay pot that does not crack even when hot enough to melt iron.
A raw crucible fired in the blast furnace. Add 2 wrought iron and charcoal to make a crucible charge.
Iron melts at about 1500 C. Ordinary pottery softens before that, so heat-resistant fire clay was needed.
Real crucibles lasted about three heats, wearing each time the steel was poured, until they cracked.
item.semiconductor-lab.crucible_charge.n: A crucible filled with iron and charcoal and lidded. Melting it in the blast furnace makes steel.
Fire-clay crucible + 2 wrought iron (iron ingot) + charcoal. Melted in the blast furnace -> 2 crucible steel (the crucible breaks). An ordinary furnace is not hot enough.
Around 1740 the clockmaker Huntsman, wanting even steel for springs, found how to melt steel completely in a lidded crucible.
The lid keeps air out, so carbon does not burn away and mixes evenly into the molten iron. Indian wootz steel was also made by sealing iron with plant matter (carbon) in crucibles.
item.semiconductor-lab.crucible_charge.p: Approximation: the real charge was carburized blister steel melted over a coke fire (about 1550 C). Here wrought iron and charcoal go in together and the blast furnace melts them. The crucible breaks after one heat (really about three).
item.semiconductor-lab.crucible_steel.no: Fine steel with even carbon. Quenched, it becomes very hard.
Steel from melting a crucible charge (about 1% carbon). For clock springs, blades and precision parts (gauge blocks [8-05]).
Sheffield crucible steel, called 'cast steel', was the finest steel for blades and tools for over a century.
Earlier blister steel had more carbon at the surface than inside. Fully melted steel is equally hard wherever you cut it, an evenness that precision gauges depend on.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus.note1: A waxy, glowing element. It catches fire by itself in air, so it is kept under water.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus.note2: White phosphorus, P4 (Wöhler process: bone ash + sand + carbon). Burns spontaneously in air at about 30 C and glows in the dark (slow oxidation). Real labs store it under water. Used here as the n-type dopant. In silicon, put it in the CZ puller [9-08] dopant slot (n-type).
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus.note3: Hennig Brand discovered phosphorus in 1669 by boiling down urine — the first element found by a known person. The name means 'light-bearer' in Greek because it glows.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus.note4: White phosphorus is P4 tetrahedra and is very toxic (the 'phossy jaw' disease of match-factory workers). Heating it to about 250 C without air turns it into red phosphorus, a stable polymer used on matchbox strikers and as a getter in vacuum tubes [5-16] (red phosphorus is not in the mod yet). Germanium was doped with Sb/As at first; phosphorus became the main n-type dopant for silicon.
block.semiconductor-lab.trona_deposit.no: Salt left behind when a desert lake dried up. Found in the sand and sandstone of deserts.

Trona, Na2CO3·NaHCO3·2H2O, an evaporite from dried-up salt lakes. Generates only in desert biomes, from the surface to shallow depth (y 52-76), replacing sand and sandstone. Mine with any pickaxe (soft, Mohs 2.5-3) for trona; silk touch gives the block.
Desert lakes with no outlet lose their water to evaporation, so dissolved salts pile up as layers: first carbonates, then sulfates, then halite. Egypt's Wadi El Natrun gave its name to natron.

The world's largest trona beds lie in the Green River Formation of Wyoming, laid down in an Eocene lake about 50 million years ago and found in 1938 while drilling for oil. Today most US soda ash is mined there instead of made by the Solvay process.
item.semiconductor-lab.trona.note1: A salt the ancient Egyptians used to make mummies.
item.semiconductor-lab.trona.note: Na2CO3·NaHCO3·2H2O (natural soda). Heat it in a furnace to get sodium carbonate: 2 trona -> 3 Na2CO3 + CO2 + 5 H2O (about 150-200 C is enough).
item.semiconductor-lab.trona.note3: Ancient Egyptians used natron (a natural soda mixture containing trona) to dry bodies for mummies from about 2600 BC (the 4th Dynasty), and to make glass and faience. Pliny the Elder recorded natron glass in his Natural History (77 AD).
item.semiconductor-lab.trona.note4: 'Natron' comes from the Arabic natrun, and the chemical symbol Na (natrium) comes from natron. The name 'trona' is also thought to come from natrun.
item.semiconductor-lab.trona.placeholder: Approx: really 2 trona give 3 sodium carbonate; here 1 -> 1. The CO2 and water vapour are not collected.
Washing soda. Added to sand, it lets glass melt at a much lower heat.
Na2CO3 (soda ash). Made by heating trona. Flux for soda-lime glass: sand + soda + lime. Later also for refining tungsten ore (soda fusion).
Before 1800, soda came from natural deposits or from the ashes of seaweed and salt-marsh plants. The Leblanc process (1791) and the Solvay process (1860s) made it from salt.

Soda lowers the melting point of silica from about 1700 C to about 1000 C by breaking up the Si-O network (Na2O is a 'network modifier'). Too much makes glass dissolve in water (water glass), which is why lime is added too.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_batch.note1: Sand mixed with soda and lime, ready to be melted into glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_batch.note: Sand x6 + sodium carbonate + quicklime -> 6 batch. Roughly SiO2 72%, Na2O 14%, CaO 10% by weight, like real window and bottle glass. Melt it in a furnace (or faster in a blast furnace) to get soda-lime glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_batch.note3: Glassmakers have weighed out sand, flux and lime as a 'batch' for thousands of years. Broken glass (cullet) is added too, because it melts first and helps the rest melt.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_batch.note4: In the melt, Na2CO3 + SiO2 -> Na2SiO3 + CO2 and CaCO3/CaO join the network. The CO2 bubbles must rise out ('fining'), which is why real tanks are run hotter (about 1500 C) than the softening point.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_batch.place: Omitted: the CO2 released in the melt is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.soda_lime_glass.n: Ordinary glass, made properly from sand, soda and lime. Used for lab equipment.

Na2O-CaO-SiO2 glass. The soda lowers the melting point from about 1700 C to about 1000 C; the lime keeps it from dissolving in water. Needed for the vacuum chamber, mercury gauge and Leyden jar. (Windows and building glass stay vanilla.)

Glass was first made in Mesopotamia around 2500-2000 BC, as beads ⚠️ (large finds begin in the 15th-14th centuries BC). Pliny the Elder tells of merchants who set their cooking pots on blocks of natron on a beach and found glass in the morning - probably a legend, but the recipe is right.

It expands about 9 x 10^-6 per K, so it cracks if heated unevenly - that is why heat-resistant lab glass later used borosilicate (Schott, 1880s-1890s; Pyrex 1915). The faint green tint of thick glass comes from iron in the sand.
item.semiconductor-lab.sulfur_dioxide.no: The sharp-smelling gas you get by burning sulfur.
Burn sulfur powder in a furnace (roasting sulfide ores in the reverberatory furnace also gives it). Combine with water for sulfuric acid.

S + O2 -> SO2. Real sulfuric acid plants first oxidize it to SO3 over a vanadium pentoxide (V2O5) catalyst, then absorb it (the contact process). SO2 in water alone only gives sulfurous acid, H2SO3 (skipped in the game).
It is part of the smell of volcanoes and, as sulfites, protects wine from oxidation. SO2 from smelter smoke causes acid rain; it stripped the hills around Japan's Ashio copper mine bare.
item.semiconductor-lab.sulfur_powder.not: Made from pointed sulfur, sulfur blocks or potent sulfur. Burn it in a furnace for sulfur dioxide.
Sulfur normally forms rings of 8 atoms (S8). It melts at about 115 °C and burns with a blue flame.
Sulfur around volcanic vents forms when hydrogen sulfide meets sulfur dioxide: 2H2S + SO2 -> 3S + 2H2O. Meiji-era Japan exported large amounts of volcanic sulfur.
item.semiconductor-lab.sulfuric_acid.not: A very strong acid, used for electrolysis and more.
Made from sulfur dioxide + water. Used to dissolve germanium concentrate into GeO2, and as the electrolyte in the electrolyzer (not used up).

H2SO4. Mixing with water releases a lot of heat, so always add acid to water slowly (the other way round it boils and spatters). Concentrated acid pulls water out of things - it turns sugar into black carbon.

Sulfuric acid output was once called the yardstick of a nation's industry. The 18th century used the lead-chamber process; the catalytic contact process took over from the late 19th century. About 250 million tonnes are made each year - one of the biggest chemicals of all.
block.semiconductor-lab.wood_retort.note: A furnace that bakes wood without air and cools the smoke. Besides charcoal you get a sour-smelling liquid and black tar.

Put in logs and burn coal or charcoal (1 lasts 8 logs, 10 s per log, no electricity). 1 log -> 1 charcoal, plus 1 wood vinegar every 2 logs and 1 wood tar every 4 logs. An iron pot (retort) is heated from outside and the smoke is cooled in a copper pipe.

Charcoal burners once let the smoke escape. In the 19th century iron retorts distilled wood and recovered acetic acid, methanol (wood spirit) and acetone from the smoke: the wood chemical industry. It was replaced in the 1920s by synthesis from coal and natural gas.

Above about 270 C wood decomposes on its own, giving off heat (cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin break down). One tonne of dry wood gives about 300 kg charcoal, a watery liquor containing about 50 kg acetic acid and 16 kg methanol, and about 240 kg tar (FAO, hardwood). The rest is combustible gas, which real retorts also burned as fuel.
block.semiconductor-lab.wood_retort.plac: Omitted: the combustible gas (CO, methane, etc.) is not collected. Yield does not depend on the kind of wood.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_vinegar.note: A brown liquid from cooling the smoke of baked wood. It has the same acetic acid as vinegar and smells sour.
1 per 2 logs in the wood retort. Mostly water, a few % acetic acid CH3COOH and a little methanol CH3OH (⚠️ about 1-3%). Later the source of methanol and acetone.
In 1661 Boyle recorded a 'wood spirit' (methanol), different from the spirit of wine, from the liquid of distilled wood. Methanol is still called wood alcohol.
Neutralizing the acetic acid with slaked lime gives calcium acetate, and heating that gives acetone (a solvent for smokeless powder in World War I). Methanol is a poison that can cause blindness.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_vinegar.plac: Approximation: carried without a bottle until the container system (v0.3).
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_tar.note1: A black, sticky liquid that comes out when wood is baked. It smells smoky.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_tar.note2: 1 per 4 logs in the wood retort. A mixture of phenols, resin acids and more. Boil it down in a furnace and the light parts escape, leaving hard pitch.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_tar.note3: At Campitello in Italy, about 200,000 years ago, Neanderthals put tar made from birch bark on stone tools. It is one of the oldest materials humans made by a chemical change.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_tar.note4: Heating birch bark without air releases betulin and other compounds as tar. Whether it was made on purpose or happened by chance in a fire is debated (a 2019 study showed it can form simply on a stone beside a smouldering fire). Nordic pine tar waterproofed ships and was exported as 'Stockholm tar'.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_tar.placehol: Approximation: carried without a bottle until the container system (v0.3).
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch.note1: A black lump made by boiling down tar. It softens when warm and hardens when cool.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch.note2: Wood tar boiled down in a furnace (the light parts escape). Used to waterproof ships and for the polishing lap that shapes lenses [7-03].
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch.note3: The seams of wooden ships were packed with oakum and sealed with hot pitch. Tar and pitch were 'naval stores' that supported navies from the 17th to the 19th century.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch.note4: Pitch looks solid but is a very viscous liquid. In the University of Queensland pitch drop experiment, started in 1927, a drop falls from the funnel about once a decade. In lens polishing this slow flow lets the pitch lap mould itself exactly to the lens.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_ash.note1: The ash left after burning wood completely in a campfire. It contains a water-soluble salt (potassium carbonate).
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_ash.note2: Put a log on a campfire for 30 s. The potassium and calcium in the wood remain as carbonates and oxides. 4 + a water bucket make lye.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_ash.note3: Ash has long been spread on fields as fertilizer and used as a detergent: water with ash dissolved in it washed cloth.
item.semiconductor-lab.wood_ash.note4: Wood ash is mainly calcium carbonate and potassium carbonate. Potassium carbonate dissolves well in water but calcium carbonate hardly at all, so soaking the ash and taking the clear liquid separates the potassium salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.lye.note1: The clear liquid from soaking wood ash in water. It feels slippery and stings the skin (alkaline).
item.semiconductor-lab.lye.note2: 4 wood ash + water bucket (the bucket comes back) -> lye. Contains dissolved K2CO3. Boil it down in a furnace for potassium carbonate.
item.semiconductor-lab.lye.note3: In Japan, ash lye was used to prepare indigo dye vats, to set konjac, and to take the bitterness out of wild vegetables.
item.semiconductor-lab.lye.note4: K2CO3 partly hydrolyses in water and releases OH-, so lye is alkaline (around pH 11). Boiled with fat it makes soap (saponification). In English, lye now also means sodium hydroxide solution.
item.semiconductor-lab.lye.placeholder: Approximation: carried without a bottle until the container system (v0.3). Concentration control is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.potash.note1: The white powder left after boiling down lye. A material for glass and soap.
item.semiconductor-lab.potash.note2: Lye -> furnace (10 s) -> K2CO3. In glass it lowers the melting point (a flux). Used in the flint glass batch (Ravenscroft's lead glass used potash too).
item.semiconductor-lab.potash.note3: It was made by boiling lye down in iron pots, so 'pot ash'. In 1807 Davy extracted a new metal from it by electrolysis and named it potassium.
item.semiconductor-lab.potash.note4: In the 18th and 19th centuries forests in North America and Russia were burned in huge amounts and potash was exported (for glass, soap and gunpowder). The first US patent (1790) was for a way of making potash. Today potash comes from mined potassium chloride.
item.semiconductor-lab.potash.placeholde: Not yet: causticizing with slaked lime to potassium hydroxide KOH (added when something needs it).
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_bottle.note: A bottle for acids. Glass does not dissolve in most acids.
Holds sulfuric and hydrochloric acid. Filled with water it can also store white phosphorus. The bottle comes back after use.
Glass (mostly SiO2) resists hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acid, so chemicals have long been kept in glass. Only hydrofluoric acid dissolves it.
4HF + SiO2 → SiF4 + 2H2O. This reaction is used to etch patterns into glass, and later to clean semiconductor wafers.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_retort.note1: A furnace that bakes coal without air. You get coke, black coal tar and water that smells of ammonia.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_retort.note2: Put in coal and burn coal, charcoal or coke (1 fuel lasts 8 coal, 10 s each, no electricity). 4 coal → 3 coke, plus 1 ammoniacal liquor every 4 coal and 1 coal tar every 8. A refractory-brick vessel (retort) is heated from outside to about 1000 °C and the gas is cooled in a copper pipe.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_retort.note3: In 1792 Murdoch lit his house with gas from baked coal. By 1812 London had a gas company and streets lined with gas lamps. The coal tar left over was a nuisance until, from about 1850, it became a raw material for dyes and medicines.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_retort.note4: One tonne of coal gives about 700 kg of coke, 50 kg of coal tar, 100 L of ammoniacal liquor and 300 m³ of coal gas (mostly hydrogen and methane). Selling gas was the business; coke and tar were by-products. Later the by-product coke oven [3-19] recovered the same things.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_retort.place: Omitted: the coal gas is not collected (the real purpose was fuel for gas lamps). The gas cleaning plant that separates tar and liquor, and differences between coals, are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_tar.note1: A black, sticky liquid from baking coal. It is harmful, so do not touch it with bare hands.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_tar.note2: From the gasworks retort [2-20], 1 per 8 coal. Separated, it gives benzene [2-24], phenol [2-25], naphthalene and xylene, the materials of photoresists [2-30][2-32] (the separating machine comes later). GHS: health hazard (may cause cancer).
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_tar.note3: In 1856, 18-year-old Perkin used a substance from coal tar to make mauve, the first synthetic dye. The chemical industry of dyes, drugs and plastics grew from here.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_tar.note4: In 1775 Pott noticed that boy chimney sweeps often got cancer from soot. In 1915 Yamagiwa Katsusaburo and Ichikawa Koichi painted coal tar on rabbits' ears for months and produced cancer in an experiment for the first time, evidence that chemicals can cause cancer.
item.semiconductor-lab.coal_tar.placehol: Approximation: there is no machine yet to separate it into fractions (fractional distillation).
item.semiconductor-lab.ammoniacal_liquor: Water that collects when coal gas is cooled. It smells of ammonia.
From the gasworks retort [2-20], 1 per 4 coal. About 1–2% ammonia is dissolved in it. Treated with lime it gives ammonia water [2-21] (to come).
Coal contains a little nitrogen, which comes out as ammonia when coal is baked. Most ammonia in the 19th century was a by-product of gasworks.

Until the Haber–Bosch process made ammonia from the nitrogen in air (1913), ammonia for fertiliser and chemicals came from gasworks and Chilean saltpetre. Ammonia water is later used in the RCA clean of wafers [9-14].
Approximation: hydrogen sulfide and other dissolved gases are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.lead_retort.note: Heats fluorite with sulfuric acid in a lead vessel to make hydrofluoric acid. HF dissolves glass, so everything is made of lead.

1 fluorite + 1 sulfuric acid (the glass bottle pops out on top) + 1 empty lead bottle → 1 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottle) + 1 gypsum (10 s, 1 fuel lasts 8 runs, no electricity). The gas is absorbed in water in the receiver: 1 water bucket lasts 4 runs (the empty bucket goes to the output). CaF2 + H2SO4 → CaSO4 + 2HF.

In 1771 Scheele heated fluorite with sulfuric acid in a glass retort and found a new acid. The glass was eaten away and clouded from inside, showing that this acid dissolves glass. So factory vessels, pipes and bottles were made of lead (later wax, rubber and polyethylene).

Modern plants react them in long, slowly turning kilns (rotary kilns) at about 200–250 °C and cool the hydrogen fluoride into a liquid. About 3.6 tonnes of gypsum come out per tonne of hydrogen fluoride.
block.semiconductor-lab.lead_retort.plac: Omitted: amounts are symbolic (really 1 fluorite gives 2 HF). Acid strength (really about 40–70%) and the absorption tower are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrofluoric_acid: A very dangerous acid that even dissolves glass. Kept in a lead bottle.

Hydrogen fluoride HF in water. Made in the lead retort [2-10]. It dissolves silicon oxide (SiO2) but hardly touches silicon itself (oxide etching [9-06]). Using it gives back the empty lead bottle. GHS: skull (acute toxicity), corrosive.
4HF + SiO2 → SiF4 + 2H2O. Because it reacts with SiO2, the main part of glass, it has long been used to etch patterns into glass. In a glass bottle, the bottle would dissolve.

HF passes through skin and binds the body's calcium, so even a small splash can later harm bones and the heart (it may not hurt at first, which is what makes it dangerous). Factories always keep special gloves and a calcium remedy (calcium gluconate gel) at hand. Some 19th-century chemists who tried to isolate fluorine itself were badly poisoned, and some died.
Approximation: the strength (percent) is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.calcium_sulfate.n: A white powder left over from making hydrofluoric acid.
Calcium sulfate CaSO4, a by-product of the lead retort [2-10]. No use yet (later: plaster building materials).
Gypsum with water in it (CaSO4·2H2O), baked to drive off water, sets hard again when mixed with water: plaster casts, plasterboard, chalk.
An HF plant produces about 3.6 tonnes of gypsum per tonne of hydrogen fluoride. Where to put it, and how to reuse it as building material, are still open problems.
gui.semiconductor-lab.lead_retort.need_i: Put in fluorite and sulfuric acid
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphoric_acid.n: A syrupy acid. Used to cut the aluminium wiring of chips into shape.

H3PO4 (in a glass bottle; the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 bone ash + 3 sulfuric acid + 2 empty glass bottles → 2 phosphoric acid. In the etching tank [9-06] it dissolves only the aluminium where a developed wafer has no resist [9-25]. GHS: corrosive.
Ca3(PO4)2 + 3H2SO4 → 2H3PO4 + 3CaSO4: sulfuric acid on bone ash (calcium phosphate). 2Al + 2H3PO4 → 2AlPO4 + 3H2 dissolves aluminium but hardly touches oxide or silicon.
1960s chip plants etched aluminium with warm phosphoric acid mixed with a little nitric and acetic acid. Phosphoric acid also gives cola its tang and is used in fertiliser and rust removers.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphoric_acid.p: Approximation: the gypsum by-product does not appear. Plain phosphoric acid instead of the nitric/acetic etching mixture.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_silicate.n: Glass made from sand and caustic soda that dissolves in water.
Na2SiO3. Crafting: 1 sand + 2 sodium hydroxide → 1 water glass (2NaOH + SiO2 → Na2SiO3 + H2O). Neutralised with sulfuric acid it becomes colloidal silica.
Ordinary glass does not dissolve in water, but glass with a lot of sodium does. The solution is called 'water glass' and was used as glue and to preserve eggs.
Silica gel (the drying sachets in snack bags) is also made by setting water glass with acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_silicate.p: Approximation: mixed at the crafting table (really sand and soda ash are melted at about 1300 °C, or sand is dissolved in caustic soda in a pressure vessel).
A liquid with invisibly tiny glass particles spread through water. Used to polish wafers.

SiO2 particles (a few to 100 nm) dispersed in water (glass bottle; the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 water glass + 1 sulfuric acid (bottle back) + 1 empty glass bottle → 1. Used for the final polish in the wafer polisher [9-13].
The particles are so small that they do not settle, giving a milky liquid. They are softer than silicon, so they polish without scratching.

In 1941 DuPont removed sodium from water glass by ion exchange to make a stable silica sol (Ludox). Today's chip plants use the same kind of liquid for CMP. ⚠️ The sodium sulfate by-product is not modelled.
Approximation: really sodium is removed by ion exchange. Here it is just neutralised with sulfuric acid, and no sodium sulfate comes out.
block.semiconductor-lab.ammonia_still.no: Heats gasworks liquor to drive out the ammonia and absorbs it in water to make ammonia water.

1 kW. 4 ammoniacal liquor + 1 slaked lime + 1 empty glass bottle → 1 ammonia water (20 s). The absorber water is 1 water bucket per 4 runs (the empty bucket goes to the output). 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2NH3 + 2H2O.
The liquor holds free ammonia and ammonia bound as salts. Heating drives out the free part; adding slaked lime makes the liquid strongly alkaline so the bound part comes out as ammonia gas too.

Most 19th-century ammonia was a gasworks by-product. From 1913 the Haber–Bosch process made it from the nitrogen in air, and mass-produced fertiliser came to feed much of the world (the same ammonia also became a raw material for explosives and is known to have prolonged the First World War).
block.semiconductor-lab.ammonia_still.pl: Omitted: electric heating (real stills blow steam through a column). No calcium chloride waste liquor.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonia_water.not: An alkaline water with a sharp smell. Do not sniff it directly.

About 25% NH3 in water (glass bottle; the bottle comes back). Made in the ammonia still [2-21]. Used for wafer cleaning [9-14] and platinum refining [1-18] (ammonium chloride). GHS: corrosive, hazardous to the aquatic environment.
NH3 + H2O ⇄ NH4+ + OH-. Part of it becomes ammonium ions, making the water alkaline. Ammonia dissolves extremely well (about 500 L of gas in 1 L of water at 20 °C).

In 1965 Werner Kern at RCA devised a wafer cleaning recipe (RCA clean). Its first liquid, SC-1, is ammonia water, hydrogen peroxide and water 1:1:5 at about 75 °C, removing organic dirt and tiny particles.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_ash.note1: Ash from burnt kelp. Soaked in water it gives soda, and iodine can be taken from the liquid too.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_ash.note2: Burn dried kelp on a campfire (30 s). 4 + water bucket make kelp-ash liquor.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_ash.note3: In 18th-century Scotland the 'kelp industry' gathered and burned shore seaweed and sold the ash for glass and soap. In Spain the ash of saltwort plants, 'barilla', was famous.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_ash.note4: Ash from land trees is rich in potassium (K2CO3), but ash from sea plants is rich in sodium (Na2CO3), taken up from seawater. Kelp also concentrates seawater's iodine thousands of times.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_liquor.note1: The clear liquid from soaking kelp ash in water. Boil it down for soda, or add sulfuric acid for iodine.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_liquor.note2: 4 kelp ash + water bucket (the bucket comes back). Boil it in a furnace for (impure) sodium carbonate, or combine with sulfuric acid for iodine (the bottle comes back).
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_liquor.note3: In 1811 Courtois, at a French saltpeter works, added sulfuric acid to kelp-ash liquor and saw a beautiful violet vapor that left dark crystals on cool surfaces: the discovery of iodine (Greek for 'violet').
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_liquor.note4: Iodide ions I- in the liquid are oxidized by concentrated sulfuric acid to I2, which heat turns into violet vapor (sublimation). In reality soda and other salts were crystallized first, and iodine was taken from the remaining mother liquor.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_liquor.place: Approximation: one liquor gives either soda or iodine, not both (in reality both). No bottle.
item.semiconductor-lab.iodine.note1: Dark violet crystals. Warmed, they give off violet vapor. ⚠ Do not breathe it or get it on skin.
item.semiconductor-lab.iodine.note2: Kelp-ash liquor + sulfuric acid. A daguerreotype [B-02a] silver plate held over its vapor gains a light-sensitive silver iodide film. ⚠ GHS: harmful if inhaled or on skin, toxic to aquatic life.
item.semiconductor-lab.iodine.note3: Iodine is familiar from wound disinfectant (tincture of iodine) and the blue-black starch test. Japan extracts it from underground brine (ancient seawater) in Chiba and is one of the world's top iodine producers.
item.semiconductor-lab.iodine.note4: Iodine readily turns straight from solid to gas (sublimation). This let a thin, even silver iodide film form on a silver plate. In the body it is needed to make thyroid hormone.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonium_chloride: A white salt used when extracting platinum.
NH4Cl (sal ammoniac). Crafting: 1 ammonia water + 1 hydrochloric acid → 1 (both bottles come back). NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl. Makes the yellow precipitate in platinum refining [1-18].
Long known as sal ammoniac; it dissolves metal oxides, so it was a flux for soldering and brazing.
The paste inside old zinc–carbon dry cells also contained ammonium chloride.
block.semiconductor-lab.peroxide_cell.no: Electrolyses sulfuric acid with a platinum electrode to make hydrogen peroxide, used for cleaning wafers.

3 kW. 1 empty glass bottle → 1 hydrogen peroxide (about 30%) + 1 bag of hydrogen (60 s). 1 water bucket lasts 4 runs, 1 sulfuric acid 8 runs (mostly recovered; the bottle pops out on top), 1 platinum ingot (anode) 32 runs. Overall 2H2O → H2O2 + H2.

Electrolysing cold, strong sulfuric acid hard at a platinum anode makes persulfate (S2O8^2-) instead of oxygen. Warming it with water gives hydrogen peroxide and returns the sulfuric acid. Carbon or lead anodes do not make persulfate; it takes platinum.

In 1818 Thénard discovered hydrogen peroxide by treating barium peroxide with acid. In 1908 an electrolytic plant was built at Weissenstein, Austria; from the 1930s the anthraquinone process took over. ⚠️ Sources differ slightly on the plant's year (1908–1910).
block.semiconductor-lab.peroxide_cell.pl: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Cooling the electrolyte and the vacuum distillation that separates the peroxide are not modelled. Thénard's barium peroxide method is not used because there is no barium.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_peroxide: A strongly oxidising liquid, a stronger relative of the antiseptic for cuts. Keep it off eyes and skin.

About 30% H2O2 (glass bottle; the bottle comes back). Made in the peroxide cell [2-19]. Used for wafer cleaning (SC-1 and SC-2 of the RCA clean [9-14]). GHS: corrosive (serious eye damage), acute toxicity (swallowed).
H2O2 is water with one extra oxygen. It breaks down as 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2, oxidising organic dirt away, and leaves only water and oxygen, which makes it ideal for cleaning.

Pharmacy peroxide is about 3%. Strong solutions (especially above 60%) can suddenly decompose when metals or dirt get in, releasing heat and oxygen and bursting containers; such accidents are why factories keep it in clean, dedicated containers.
item.semiconductor-lab.distilled_water.n: Water boiled into steam and cooled back, leaving no salt behind.

In a glass bottle (the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 water bucket + quartz still (kept) + 3 empty glass bottles → 3 distilled water (the bucket comes back). Used to rinse wafers after cleaning [9-14].
Water turns to steam at 100 °C, but dissolved salts and minerals do not. Cooling the steam gives water without them. Very pure water hardly conducts electricity.

Alexandria in the 1st–3rd centuries had three-armed stills (traditionally credited to Maria, though this is uncertain). ⚠️ 1950s semiconductor plants moved to ion-exchange deionised water, cheaper in large amounts than distillation.
item.semiconductor-lab.distilled_water.p: Approximation: the heat is represented by using the quartz still (no furnace fire shown).
A black, sticky rock that seeps out of the ground. People used it as glue and waterproofing long ago.
Found near the surface (Y 56-90) in badlands and deserts, inside sand, sandstone and terracotta. Mining it gives bitumen (asphalt); with Silk Touch you keep the block.

Natural asphalt (bitumen) forms when underground oil rises near the surface and its light parts evaporate, leaving only the heavy parts. Famous places: the Dead Sea (once called Lake Asphaltites), the Pitch Lake of Trinidad and the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles.
In Mesopotamia, bitumen was used for over 5,000 years to set bricks and waterproof boats. Mammoths and sabre-toothed cats that got stuck in the La Brea tar pits survive as fossils.
Approximation: no crude oil or petroleum distillation (only natural surface asphalt).
item.semiconductor-lab.asphalt.note1: A black, sticky natural material. It hardens when light shines on it.
item.semiconductor-lab.asphalt.note2: From mining natural asphalt. Dissolved in turpentine it becomes a light-hardening varnish.
item.semiconductor-lab.asphalt.note3: Bitumen is a mixture of many kinds of large hydrocarbon molecules. Sunlight with ultraviolet links the molecules together (oxidative cross-linking) so they no longer dissolve in oil. Only the lit parts remain - the same idea as a photoresist.
item.semiconductor-lab.asphalt.note4: Niepce used 'bitumen of Judea' from around the Dead Sea. Light-hardening bitumen was later used for making printing plates too.
item.semiconductor-lab.asphalt.placehold: Approximation: differences between sources are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.pine_resin.note1: A sticky sap that oozes from a cut in a conifer trunk.
item.semiconductor-lab.pine_resin.note2: Right-click a spruce log (with bark) with a flint or obsidian flake (the flake wears a little; wait a moment before the next). Distil it in a furnace to get turpentine.
item.semiconductor-lab.pine_resin.note3: Trees make resin to seal wounds. It is a mix of a volatile oil (turpentine) and a hard resin (rosin). When heated, the oil evaporates first.
item.semiconductor-lab.pine_resin.note4: Resin tapping was done all over the world. Rosin is still used on violin bows and as solder flux.
item.semiconductor-lab.pine_resin.placeh: Approximation: the resin comes at once (really it oozes out over days and is collected).
item.semiconductor-lab.turpentine.note1: A sharp-smelling oil made from pine resin. It dissolves bitumen well. It burns easily - keep away from fire.
item.semiconductor-lab.turpentine.note2: Distil pine resin in a furnace. Mixed with bitumen it makes the varnish; right-click a heliograph plate with it to wash it. ⚠ GHS: flammable, harmful (treated only as an industrial solvent).
item.semiconductor-lab.turpentine.note3: Turpentine is a mixture of small hydrocarbons such as pinene. It dissolves loose bitumen molecules but not light-cross-linked bitumen. That difference makes the image.
item.semiconductor-lab.turpentine.note4: Niepce washed his plates with oil of lavender mixed with white petroleum. Turpentine has long been the thinner for oil paint.
item.semiconductor-lab.turpentine.placeh: Approximation: turpentine replaces Niepce's lavender oil (it dissolves bitumen the same way). The distillation residue (rosin) is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.bitumen_varnish.n: Bitumen dissolved in turpentine. Paint it on a plate and light hardens it.
Bitumen + turpentine. With a pewter plate it makes a heliograph plate.
Once painted, the solvent evaporates and a thin bitumen film remains - the same job as spin-coating photoresist on a wafer in a chip factory today.
Coat a light-sensitive film, expose it, dissolve with a developer: these three steps have not changed from Niepce in 1826 to today's EUV lithography.
item.semiconductor-lab.bitumen_varnish.p: Approximation: concentration and film thickness are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.pewter_plate.note: A plate of soft grey metal: tin mixed with lead.
2 tin ingots + 1 lead ingot make 3. Coated with bitumen varnish it becomes a heliograph plate; you get it back when washing leaves no image.
Pewter is mostly tin, and old pewter contained a lot of lead. It was used for tableware and plates. Lead is harmful, so modern pewter is lead-free.
Niepce's oldest surviving photograph (about 1826-27) is on a pewter plate, now kept at the University of Texas at Austin.
item.semiconductor-lab.pewter_plate.plac: Approximation: melting the metals together is merged into the crafting table.
block.semiconductor-lab.heliograph_plate: A plate coated with light-hardening bitumen. Put it in the sun and wait a few minutes.

In strong daylight with open sky it slowly hardens (it gets lighter; done after 4 steps). It works under glass but not in the shadow of a block. Right-click with turpentine to wash: a fully exposed plate keeps an image, an under-exposed one dissolves completely and returns the pewter plate.
Lit bitumen becomes cross-linked and stops dissolving, while shaded bitumen dissolves and bares the metal. This is how a negative photoresist works: the lit parts remain.
Niepce's exposure took at least eight hours of sunshine, some say several days ⚠️. It was too slow, and Daguerre's silver plates (1839) replaced it.
Approximation: exposure takes minutes (really hours to days). The image is a fixed picture (the view from a window).
block.semiconductor-lab.heliograph.note1: A picture drawn by light. The oldest surviving photograph was made this way.
block.semiconductor-lab.heliograph.note2: Wash a fully exposed heliograph plate with turpentine. You can keep it as decoration.
block.semiconductor-lab.heliograph.note3: 'Heliograph' is Greek for 'sun drawing'. The oldest photograph, View from the Window at Le Gras (about 1826-27), was taken by Niepce from his own window.
block.semiconductor-lab.heliograph.note4: The first photograph and the making of ICs share one principle: coat a light-hardening film, expose it, dissolve to leave a pattern. Even the name lithography ('stone printing') comes from printmaking.
block.semiconductor-lab.heliograph.place: Approximation: the image is a fixed picture.
message.semiconductor-lab.heliograph_pla: The light-hardened bitumen stayed - an image appeared! (only the shaded parts dissolved)
Not enough light: all the bitumen dissolved. You got the pewter plate back
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.note1: A rubber tree that grows in the jungle. Cut the trunk and white sap oozes out.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.note2: Grows in jungles. Right-click with a flint or obsidian flake to tap latex (the flake wears a little). Also works as fuel or for charcoal.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.note3: The Para rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) comes from the Amazon. Tubes inside its bark carry a white milky fluid, latex - rubber particles floating in water - which oozes out when cut.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.note4: In 1876 Wickham took seeds out of Brazil; seedlings raised at Kew Gardens were planted in Southeast Asia. Most natural rubber today comes from Southeast Asian plantations.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.place: Approximation: latex comes at once (really it drips from slanted cuts into a cup over hours).
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_leaves.no: Rubber tree leaves. Breaking them sometimes gives a sapling.
Rubber tree leaves. Sometimes drop a rubber tree sapling (shears keep the leaves).
Para rubber leaves come in sets of three leaflets. The tree sheds them once in the dry season.
In its native South America a leaf disease (South American leaf blight) made large plantations impossible - one reason plantations succeeded in disease-free Asia.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_sapling.n: Plant it and it grows into a rubber tree.
From rubber tree leaves. Plant on grass or dirt (bone meal works).
A rubber tree can be tapped about 6-7 years after planting.
Rubber seeds are oily and soon lose the ability to sprout, which made carrying them far very hard.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_sapling.p: Approximation: grows as fast as an ordinary tree.
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.note1: White sap from the rubber tree. Add acid and it sets into rubber.
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.note2: Tap a rubber tree log with a flake. 3 latex + wood vinegar make raw rubber.
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.note3: Latex is tiny particles of rubber (polyisoprene, (C5H8)n) floating in water. Their surface charges keep them apart; acid cancels the charges, so the particles stick together and set (coagulation).
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.note4: Rubber plantations still set latex with acetic or formic acid. Over 3,500 years ago, Mesoamerican peoples mixed latex with morning-glory juice to make bouncing balls ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.placeholder: Approximation: water content and concentration are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.note1: Untreated rubber. Sticky when hot, hard when cold.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.note2: 3 latex + wood vinegar (acetic acid). Carry it somewhere hot (jungle, desert) and it becomes 'Sticky Raw Rubber'; somewhere cold (snowy biomes) it becomes 'Stiff Raw Rubber'. Mix with sulfur and bake to vulcanize it.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.note3: Raw rubber is just long chain molecules tangled together: warm them and they slide and flow, cool them and they freeze stiff. Old rubberized coats were sticky in summer and cracked in winter.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.note4: Rubber goods boomed in America in the 1820s-30s, but they melted and stank in summer and the craze soon collapsed. Goodyear spent years looking for a cure.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.placeh: Approximation: stickiness and stiffness are shown only in the name (uses do not change). Temperature is the biome's base temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.rubber_compound.n: Raw rubber with sulfur kneaded in. Bake it to get tough rubber.
Raw rubber + sulfur. Bake in a furnace to get vulcanized rubber.
The sulfur atoms are ready to link the long rubber molecules together here and there when heated.
Modern tyre rubber also contains accelerators to speed up the reaction and carbon black to make it stronger.
item.semiconductor-lab.rubber_compound.p: Approximation: kneading is merged into the crafting table.
item.semiconductor-lab.vulcanized_rubber: Heat rubber with sulfur and it becomes tough rubber that stays non-sticky even when hot.
Bake the rubber compound in a furnace. It does not change in hot or cold places (compare with raw rubber). Used for seals, and the starting point for cyclized rubber, a negative-resist material.

Sulfur bridges (cross-links) turn the rubber molecules into a network, so it no longer flows when warm and springs back when stretched (elasticity). Goodyear is said to have found it in 1839 when he dropped sulfur-mixed rubber on a hot stove.
Goodyear's patent dates from 1844; Hancock in England patented vulcanization in 1843. The name comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.
Approximation: sulfur amount, temperature and time are not modelled.
message.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.sti: The heat made the raw rubber sticky... (vulcanized rubber does not change)
The cold made the raw rubber stiff... (vulcanized rubber does not change)
message.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.nor: The raw rubber is back to normal
item.semiconductor-lab.cyclized_rubber_m: Raw rubber dissolved with an acid added. Heat it and the rubber turns into a hard resin.

Raw rubber + sulfuric acid + turpentine (the acid bottle is returned). Heat in a furnace to get cyclized rubber. Vulcanized rubber does not dissolve, so it cannot be used. ⚠ GHS: corrosive (sulfuric acid), flammable (turpentine). Treated only as an industrial material.
Rubber molecules (polyisoprene) carry many double bonds. With an acid, neighbouring double bonds join up and six-carbon rings form inside the chain (cyclization).
Vulcanized rubber is a network linked by sulfur bridges, so it does not dissolve. That is why cyclized rubber is made from unvulcanized raw rubber.
Approximation: real processes also use benzene or xylene as solvents. Concentration, temperature and time are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.cyclized_rubber.n: Rubber changed by acid into a hard resin. It no longer bounces. It is the base of a light-hardening resist.
Heat the cyclization mix in a furnace. Mixed with a sensitizer (a bis-azide) it becomes a negative photoresist ([2-30]).
The rings stiffen the molecules, so the rubber loses its bounce (elasticity). In return it dissolves well in solvents and makes thin, even films - ideal as a photoresist base.
Rubber cyclization was studied from the 1910s; Harries published a sulfuric-acid method in 1919. From about 1957, Kodak's KTFR (cyclized rubber + bis-azide) became the main resist for early ICs.
item.semiconductor-lab.cyclized_rubber.p: Approximation: degree of cyclization and molecular weight are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.limed_wood_liquor: Wood vinegar with lime added. The sour part sticks to the lime, so the rest is easier to distil.
4 wood vinegar + 1 slaked lime make 4. Distil in a furnace to get methanol.

Wood vinegar is water with acetic acid (about 5-10%), methanol (a few %) and more. Slaked lime turns the acetic acid into calcium acetate, a salt that does not evaporate, so methanol comes over first when distilled.
The leftover calcium acetate (grey acetate of lime) was heated to make acetone. In World War I acetone for smokeless-powder solvent ran short and wood distillation was expanded.
Omitted: the calcium acetate is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.note1: Distil the liquid from burning wood and you get methanol (wood spirit). Drinking it can make you blind - dangerous.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.note2: Distil limed wood vinegar in a furnace. Oxidized over hot copper gauze it gives formaldehyde ([2-27]). ⚠ GHS: flammable, acutely toxic, specific target organ toxicity (optic nerve). Never drink it (it cannot be drunk in the game). Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.note3: Methanol, CH3OH, is the smallest alcohol. In the body it turns into formaldehyde and formic acid, which damage the optic nerve. It looks just like the ethanol in drinks, so mistaken drinking has long caused accidents.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.note4: In 1834 Dumas and Peligot identified wood spirit; the name methyl comes from Greek for 'wine' + 'wood'. From 1923 BASF synthesised it from carbon monoxide and hydrogen under high pressure.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.placehol: Approximation: the rough wood-spirit distillation is merged into one step (really repeated to raise purity).
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_gauze.not: Methanol reacts with air on hot copper gauze. The gauze itself is not used up.
4 copper ingots. Put it on a lit campfire and right-click with methanol to get formalin. A cold gauze (not over fire) does nothing. The gauze can be used again and again (a catalyst).
