Methanol and oxygen stick to the hot copper surface, react, and leave as formaldehyde and water: 2CH3OH + O2 -> 2HCHO + 2H2O. The copper only speeds the reaction up and stays the same - that is a catalyst.
In 1867 Hofmann confirmed formaldehyde by oxidizing methanol over a hot platinum spiral. Industry later mostly used silver gauze at about 600 C.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_gauze.pla: Approximation: gauze temperature and air supply are not modelled (it reacts when over a campfire).
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.note1: Formaldehyde dissolved in water. A raw material for plastics. Very harmful.
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.note2: Oxidize methanol on hot copper gauze. React with phenol to make phenolic resin ([2-28]). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, skin sensitization, carcinogenicity, mutagenicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.note3: Formaldehyde, HCHO, is the smallest aldehyde. It links proteins together and sets them, so it was used to preserve specimens and disinfect. The same linking makes it join with phenol into a resin.
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.note4: Formaldehyde released from building materials caused eye and throat pain (sick building syndrome), so Japan regulated it in building materials from 2003. Butlerov first made it in 1859.
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.placehol: Approximation: concentration (real formalin is about 37%) is not modelled.
message.semiconductor-lab.copper_gauze.r: Methanol oxidized on the hot copper gauze: formalin! (the gauze is not used up)
message.semiconductor-lab.copper_gauze.c: The gauze is cold - no reaction. Put it on a lit campfire
item.semiconductor-lab.carbolic_oil.note: An oil distilled from coal tar. It contains phenol and more.
Distil coal tar in a furnace. Washed with sodium hydroxide, only the phenol moves into the water (adding acid straight away does not get it out). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion.
Heated coal tar gives, in order of boiling point, light oil, middle oil (about 170-230 C), heavy oil and anthracene oil, leaving pitch. Middle oil is rich in phenol and naphthalene.
Coal tar was a nuisance waste of coal-gas (gaslight) works, but in the 19th century it became a treasure trove of dyes, drugs, explosives and plastics.
item.semiconductor-lab.carbolic_oil.plac: Approximation: the other fractions (light, heavy oil...) and pitch are omitted.
Middle oil washed with alkali: only the phenol dissolved out into the water.
Middle oil + sodium hydroxide. Add sulfuric acid to get phenol back (the acid bottle is returned). ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion.

Phenol is a weak acid, so it reacts with sodium hydroxide to form a water-soluble salt (phenoxide): C6H5OH + NaOH -> C6H5ONa + H2O. Naphthalene and the rest are not acids, so they stay in the oil and can be separated.
Separating things by their acid-base behaviour is a basic trick of chemical plants. The same idea returns in resist development (positive resists dissolve in alkali).
Approximation: the separated oil layer (naphthalene etc.) is thrown away.
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.note1: Phenol, found in coal tar, was used to disinfect surgery. It burns the skin - dangerous.
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.note2: Sodium phenoxide solution + sulfuric acid. React with formalin to make phenolic resin ([2-28]). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, mutagenicity, specific target organ toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.note3: Phenol, C6H5OH, is a benzene ring with one OH. Acid turns the salt back, and phenol, which dissolves poorly in water, separates out (white needle crystals melting at about 41 C).
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.note4: Runge found it in coal tar in 1834. In 1867 Lister used it to disinfect surgery, and deaths after operations fell sharply. Today it is mostly made by the cumene process (1940s).
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.placeholde: Approximation: the sodium sulfate by-product is omitted. Purity is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.note1: Extra phenol with an acid added. Heat it to get a resin that melts with heat.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.note2: 2 phenol + 1 formalin + hydrochloric acid (the bottle is returned). Heat in a furnace to get 2 novolac. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, carcinogenicity (phenol, formalin).
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.note3: With acid, formaldehyde links phenol rings with CH2 bridges. With extra phenol there are not enough bridges for a network, so it stops as chains.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.note4: In 1907 Baekeland made both a melting resin and a setting resin just by changing acid/base and the mixing ratio.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.place: Approximation: the ratio (really about 0.8 formaldehyde per phenol) and temperature are symbolic.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.note1: A yellowish phenolic resin that melts with heat. The main material of resists that copy patterns with light.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.note2: Heat the novolac reaction mix in a furnace. Mixed with DNQ (a sensitizer) it becomes a positive photoresist ([2-32]). It does not set when heated (it can be melted again and again).
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.note3: Novolac is short chains of phenol joined by CH2. Many OH groups remain, so it dissolves a little in alkaline water. DNQ makes it dissolve less - until light hits it and it dissolves more: the mechanism of positive resists.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.note4: From the late 1970s novolac/DNQ positive resists became the workhorse of chip making, through the g-line and i-line era (down to about 0.35 um).
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.placehold: Approximation: molecular-weight distribution is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.note1: Extra formalin with alkali added. Heat it and it sets into a resin that never melts again.
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.note2: 1 phenol + 2 formalin + sodium hydroxide. Heat in a furnace to get 2 Bakelite. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, carcinogenicity (phenol, formalin).
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.note3: With alkali, plenty of formaldehyde attaches to phenol, giving CH2OH arms. With extra formaldehyde, heating joins the arms and the whole thing becomes one network.
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.note4: Baekeland set resol in moulds in a 'Bakelizer' that heated it under pressure so no bubbles formed (patent 1909).
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.placeho: Approximation: the pressure step (Bakelizer) is merged into the furnace.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.note1: The first synthetic plastic, made from phenol and formaldehyde. Once set it never melts.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.note2: Heat the resol reaction mix in a furnace. It does not melt in a furnace (compare with novolac). It does not conduct electricity, so radio and telephone cases and wiring parts were made of it.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.note3: Its molecules are bridged in three directions (a thermoset), so it does not flow when hot, hardly burns and does not conduct electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.note4: Invented by Baekeland in 1907, the world's first fully synthetic plastic, called 'the material of a thousand uses'. Radios and black telephones of the 1930s-40s were made of Bakelite.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.placehol: Approximation: no filler (such as wood flour) is added.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_etch.note: A very dangerous acid mixture that dissolves silicon itself. Kept in a lead bottle.

Crafting: 1 hydrofluoric acid + 1 nitric acid + 1 empty lead bottle → 1 (bottles come back). In the etching tank [9-06] it cuts away unwaxed silicon to form mesas. GHS: skull (acute toxicity), corrosive, oxidising.
Nitric acid oxidises silicon to SiO2 and hydrofluoric acid dissolves that SiO2; repeating the two eats into the silicon.
In the 1950s a liquid called CP-4 (HF, nitric, acetic acid and a little bromine) was used to smooth germanium and silicon surfaces.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_etch.plac: Approximation: no acetic acid or bromine (not CP-4 itself).
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.note1: Warm coal tar gently over a low fire and only the light oil comes out first.
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.note2: Heat coal tar on a campfire (a furnace heats it so strongly that heavier parts come over too, giving middle oil). Distil it again on a campfire for benzene, or in a furnace for xylene. ⚠ GHS: flammable, carcinogenic (contains benzene).
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.note3: When a mixture of liquids is heated, the ones with the lowest boiling points evaporate first. Collecting them by temperature is fractional distillation. In coal tar, the part up to about 170 C is light oil, containing benzene, toluene and xylene.
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.note4: In 1849 Mansfield worked out how to get benzene industrially by fractionating coal-tar light oil. He later died of burns from a benzene fire.
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.placeho: Approximation: fractionation is shown as 'campfire = low temperature, furnace = high temperature'. Toluene is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzene.note1: A molecule of six carbons in a ring. The source of many drugs and dyes. Very harmful.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzene.note2: Distil light oil on a campfire, at low temperature (boiling point 80 C, it comes over first). ⚠ GHS: flammable, carcinogenic (category 1A), mutagenic, specific target organ toxicity (blood), aspiration hazard. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzene.note3: Benzene, C6H6, has six carbons in a regular hexagon with electrons spread around the whole ring (aromatic). Kekule proposed the ring in 1865 (the story goes he dreamt of a snake biting its tail).
item.semiconductor-lab.benzene.note4: Faraday found it in gaslight oil in 1825. It was long used as a solvent until it was found to cause leukaemia; today toluene, xylene and others replace it. In 1856 Perkin made mauve, the first synthetic dye, from coal-tar chemicals, starting the chemical industry.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.note1: An oil related to benzene. It dissolves rubber well, so it is the solvent and developer for negative resists.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.note2: Distil light oil in a furnace, at higher temperature (boiling point about 140 C). Dissolves negative resists (cyclized rubber type) and is the developer that washes away the unexposed parts ([9-21]). ⚠ GHS: flammable, acutely toxic (inhalation, skin), skin irritant, specific target organ toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.note3: Xylene, C6H4(CH3)2, is a benzene ring with two methyl groups (ortho, meta and para forms). It dissolves oils and rubber well but not water.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.note4: Negative resists swell slightly in the xylene developer, so lines finer than about 2 um were impossible. That is why positive resists (developed in alkaline water) took over.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.placeholde: Approximation: the three xylene isomers are not separated.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.note1: White crystals that smell of mothballs. They appear when tar oil is cooled.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.note2: Middle oil + ice (crystals come out on cooling). Sulfonate it to start on the road to DNQ. ⚠ GHS: flammable solid, acute toxicity, carcinogenicity (category 2), aquatic hazard.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.note3: Naphthalene, C10H8, is two benzene rings joined. It is the most abundant compound in coal tar; cooling middle oil makes it separate as white plate crystals.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.note4: It was once used as mothballs. As a dye raw material it carried the 19th-century chemical industry, and sensitizers like DNQ belong to the naphthalene family.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.place: Approximation: the remaining oil is thrown away.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalenesulfon: Naphthalene with a sulfuric-acid arm (sulfo group) attached.
Naphthalene + sulfuric acid (the bottle is returned). With 2 sodium hydroxide and baking it gives 2-naphthol. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, serious eye damage.
The SO3H of sulfuric acid replaces a hydrogen on the naphthalene ring (sulfonation). At high temperature it prefers position 2.
Sulfonation is a basic reaction of the chemical industry, for detergents and dyes.
Approximation: the position change with temperature is not modelled (only the 2-acid).
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol_melt.not: Naphthalenesulfonic acid mixed with strong alkali. Bake it to get 2-naphthol.
Naphthalenesulfonic acid + 2 sodium hydroxide. Bake in a furnace for 2-naphthol. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion (alkali).
In molten sodium hydroxide the sulfo group is swapped for OH (alkali fusion).
The same reaction as the old way of making phenol (sulfonate benzene, then alkali fusion).
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol_melt.pla: Approximation: the sodium sulfite by-product is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol.note1: White crystals: naphthalene with an OH. A dye raw material.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol.note2: Bake the alkali fusion mix in a furnace. With sulfuric acid, ammoniacal liquor and sulfur dioxide it gives Tobias acid. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, aquatic hazard.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol.note3: 2-Naphthol, C10H7OH, is the naphthalene version of phenol, a material for azo dyes (reds and oranges).
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol.note4: The late-19th-century German dye industry made thousands of colours from tar compounds such as naphthols.
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.note1: Naphthalene carrying a sulfo group and an amino group. The last raw material before DNQ.
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.note2: 2-Naphthol + sulfuric acid + ammoniacal liquor + sulfur dioxide. With potassium nitrite, hydrochloric acid and ice it gives DNQ. ⚠ GHS: eye and skin irritant.
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.note3: 2-Amino-1-naphthalenesulfonic acid. The OH of naphthol is turned into NH2 with the help of ammonia and sulfite (the Bucherer reaction, 1904).
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.note4: Named after the German chemist Tobias, who patented its preparation in the 1890s. It was originally a dye raw material.
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.place: Approximation: sulfonation and amination are merged into one step.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.note1: Saltpeter mixed with lead. Heated, the lead takes one oxygen and leaves potassium nitrite.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.note2: Saltpeter + lead ingot. Bake in a furnace for potassium nitrite. ⚠ GHS: oxidizer (saltpeter), reproductive toxicity (lead).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.note3: KNO3 + Pb -> KNO2 + PbO. In molten saltpeter the lead steals one oxygen and becomes lead monoxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.note4: An old way to make nitrites. Today nitrogen oxides are absorbed in alkali instead.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.place: Approximation: the lead monoxide by-product is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_nitrite: Saltpeter with one oxygen less. Used for diazotization.
Bake the saltpeter-lead mix in a furnace. With hydrochloric acid it gives nitrous acid, which diazotizes Tobias acid into DNQ. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing solid, acute toxicity, aquatic hazard.
Nitrous acid, HNO2, is unstable, so it is made from a nitrite and an acid just before use. It turns an amino group NH2 into N≡N+ (a diazo group): diazotization (Griess, 1858).
Tiny amounts of nitrite keep the colour of ham and sausages. Too much is poisonous.
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.note1: A yellow powder that breaks down in light - the 'eye' of a resist that copies patterns with light. Carry it into the sun and it decomposes.
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.note2: Tobias acid + potassium nitrite + hydrochloric acid + ice (diazotize while cold). If you stand in sunlight (day, open sky above) holding it, it turns into 'Light-Decomposed DNQ'. Safe in a chest or indoors. Mixed with novolac it makes a positive resist ([2-32]). ⚠ GHS: self-reactive (decomposes easily with heat or light), skin sensitizer. Treated only as an industrial material (a sensitizer).
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.note3: In light, DNQ loses N2 and rearranges (Wolff rearrangement) into an indene carboxylic acid, which dissolves in alkaline water. So a film of novolac + DNQ dissolves only where light fell: a positive resist.
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.note4: Invented by Suss at Kalle in the 1940s for diazo copying paper. Clean-room lights in chip fabs are yellow because they leave out the UV-to-blue light that DNQ and other sensitizers react to.
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.placeholder: Approximation: converting it to the sulfonyl chloride and binding it to novolac is omitted. Decomposition shows only in the name (uses do not change).
message.semiconductor-lab.dnq.decomposed: Sunlight decomposed the DNQ! (nitrogen escaped) Carry sensitizers in the shade
item.semiconductor-lab.positive_resist.n: A liquid that, where light hits it, later dissolves in alkaline developer. Carrying it in sunlight ruins it.

In a glass bottle (the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 novolac + 1 DNQ + 1 xylene + 1 empty glass bottle → 1. Spread on wafers with the spin coater [9-19]. Holding it in sunlight (daytime, open sky above) exposes it and spoils it (chests and indoors are safe). GHS: flammable (solvent).

Novolac resin alone dissolves a little in alkali, but DNQ mixed in holds it back. Ultraviolet light breaks DNQ down into an acid, so exposed areas dissolve readily: what light touches disappears, hence 'positive'.

Süs at Kalle devised it in the 1940s for diazo copying paper. It became the main IC resist only in the late 1970s with projection printing (before that, negative KPR and KTFR). ⚠️ The game uses positive resist first to match the v0.3 lithography flow (LITHO_DESIGN). Fab lighting is yellow so the resist is not exposed.
item.semiconductor-lab.positive_resist.p: Approximation: the solvent is xylene (real positive resists use cellosolve acetate and others). Resist made from exposed DNQ is not told apart at the crafting table.
message.semiconductor-lab.positive_resis: Sunlight exposed the resist! (keep it indoors or in a chest)
item.semiconductor-lab.cation_exchange_r: Resin beads that catch metal ions (such as sodium) in water and swap them for hydrogen ions.
Bakelite + sulfuric acid (the bottle is returned) make 2. With anion exchange resin and glass it makes an ion exchange column. ⚠ GHS: eye irritant (acidic).
A phenolic resin with sulfuric-acid arms (sulfo groups, SO3H): R-SO3H + Na+ -> R-SO3Na + H+. When every site is taken it is saturated; running acid through turns it back to H+ (regeneration).
In 1935 Adams and Holmes in Britain made ion exchange resins from Bakelite-type resins. Before that, natural minerals (zeolites) were used.
Approximation: sulfonation conditions are not modelled. Modern resins are polystyrene-based (D'Alelio, 1944).
item.semiconductor-lab.anion_exchange_re: Resin beads that catch chloride and other ions in water and swap them for hydroxide ions.
Novolac + ammoniacal liquor (ammonia) + formalin make 2. ⚠ GHS: skin irritant (alkaline).
A resin with amino groups: R-OH + Cl- -> R-Cl + OH-. The H+ from the cation side and the OH- from this side combine into water, H2O, so the ions disappear.
Adams and Holmes also made anion exchangers from phenylenediamine-formaldehyde resins.
Approximation: made with ammoniacal liquor (ammonia) instead of an amine.
block.semiconductor-lab.ion_exchange_col: A column packed with resins related to Bakelite. It removes the last salts from water to make it very pure.

6 soda-lime glass + cation exchange resin + anion exchange resin. Right-click with distilled water to get deionized water (8 times). When the cation side is spent, right-click with sulfuric acid; when the anion side is spent, with sodium hydroxide, to regenerate.
Cation exchange swaps metal ions for H+, anion exchange swaps chloride and others for OH-, and H+ and OH- become water. It removes even the traces of ions that distillation leaves.
From the 1950s chip factories rinsed wafers with water purified by ion exchange. Today's ultrapure-water plants stack reverse osmosis, ion exchange, UV and more ([2-18]).
Approximation: water volume, flow rate and resin amount are symbolic (1 use = 1 bottle).
item.semiconductor-lab.deionized_water.n: Very pure water with almost no salt or ions.
Pass distilled water through an ion exchange column (in a glass bottle). The starting point for ultrapure water [2-18] and wafer cleaning.
Pure water hardly conducts electricity. The fewer ions, the higher the resistance; 18.2 MOhm-cm at 25 C is the theoretical limit (water itself splits slightly into H+ and OH-).
In chip factories a single stray ion such as sodium can spoil a transistor, so wafers are rinsed with huge amounts of ultrapure water.
message.semiconductor-lab.ion_exchange_c: The cation exchange resin is spent (%s / %s / %s) - regenerate with sulfuric acid
The anion exchange resin is spent (%s / %s / %s) - regenerate with sodium hydroxide
Regenerated the cation exchange resin with sulfuric acid (%s / %s / %s)
Regenerated the anion exchange resin with sodium hydroxide (%s / %s / %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.calcium_acetate.n: The grey powder left when limed wood vinegar is boiled down. The source of acetic acid and acetone.
Boil limed wood vinegar down on a campfire (distilling it in a furnace gives methanol instead). + sulfuric acid -> glacial acetic acid; bake in a furnace -> acetone ([2-40]).
The salt formed when the acetic acid in wood vinegar meets lime: 2CH3COOH + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(CH3COO)2 + 2H2O. Driving off the water and wood spirit leaves a powder (grey acetate of lime).
Around 1850 Turnbull in the USA ran the first successful works making acetate of lime from wood distillation. Until the early 20th century most industrial acetic acid and acetone were made this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.note1: The sour part of vinegar, concentrated. It freezes when it is just a little cold - hence 'glacial'.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.note2: Calcium acetate + sulfuric acid make 2 (the bottle is returned). Take it somewhere cold (snowy biomes, mountain tops) and it becomes 'Frozen Glacial Acetic Acid', melting again where it is warm. ⚠ GHS: flammable, skin corrosion.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.note3: The strong acid (sulfuric) drives the weak acid (acetic) out of its salt: Ca(CH3COO)2 + H2SO4 -> 2CH3COOH + CaSO4 (gypsum). Acetic acid with almost no water freezes at about 17 C.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.note4: Vinegar is about 4-5% acetic acid. It is a raw material for cellulose acetate ([2-18] reverse-osmosis membranes, photographic film) and vinyl acetate (glues). Today it is mostly made from methanol and carbon monoxide (Monsanto process, 1960s).
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.place: Approximation: the gypsum by-product is not collected. Freezing is shown by biome temperature.
message.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.fr: The cold froze the glacial acetic acid (it sets at about 17 C)
message.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.me: The glacial acetic acid melted again
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.note1: The main part of nail-polish remover. It dissolves many things and dries fast.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.note2: Bake calcium acetate in a furnace. A raw material for bisphenol A (epoxy resin [2-41]) and a solvent for stripping resist and cleaning equipment. ⚠ GHS: flammable, eye irritant, specific target organ toxicity (drowsiness).
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.note3: Heated calcium acetate breaks down into calcium carbonate and acetone: Ca(CH3COO)2 -> CaCO3 + (CH3)2CO. Acetone is the smallest ketone and mixes with both water and oil.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.note4: In World War I acetone, the solvent for cordite (smokeless powder), ran short; Weizmann developed a way to make it by bacterial fermentation (ABE fermentation, 1915). He later became the first president of Israel.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.placehold: Approximation: the calcium carbonate by-product is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.note1: Fat from cows, pigs and sheep. Used to make soap and candles.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.note2: Sometimes dropped by cows, pigs and sheep. 3 of them with sodium hydroxide and water make a soap batch.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.note3: Fats are molecules of one glycerol with three fatty acids attached (triglycerides). Animal fat is rich in saturated fatty acids (such as stearic acid) that are solid at room temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.note4: In 1823 Chevreul showed that fats are made of fatty acids and glycerol. Tallow candles were later replaced by stearin and paraffin candles.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.placeholde: Approximation: rendering fat from meat is skipped (the fat itself drops).
item.semiconductor-lab.soap_batch.note1: Fat, strong alkali and water in a pot. Boil it to make soap.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap_batch.note2: 3 tallow + sodium hydroxide + water bucket (returned). Boil on a campfire to get saponified tallow. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion (alkali).
item.semiconductor-lab.soap_batch.note3: Alkali cutting the links (esters) in a fat is called saponification - 'soap-making'.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap_batch.note4: Long ago the alkali came from potash in wood-ash lye plus slaked lime. In the 19th century industrial soda became cheap and soap became everyone's.
item.semiconductor-lab.saponified_tallow: Boiled into soap, with glycerin still mixed in. Add salt and only the soap floats up.
Boil the soap batch on a campfire. With salt it gives 3 soap and leaves the spent lye (glycerin water) in the grid (salting out).
(C17H35COO)3C3H5 + 3NaOH -> 3C17H35COONa (soap) + C3H5(OH)3 (glycerin). Plenty of salt makes the soap insoluble, so it sets and floats off (salting out).
Soap works long made soap by 'kettle boiling + salting out'.
Approximation: repeated salting and washing is merged into one step.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap.note1: Mix fat with strong alkali and you get soap. It lets water wash away greasy dirt.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap.note2: Saponified tallow + salt make 3 (made with sodium hydroxide, so it is hard soap; potassium hydroxide would give soft soap). The first step into cleaning equipment.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap.note3: A soap molecule has a water-loving head (-COO-) and a long oil-loving tail. The tails surround grease in tiny balls (micelles) that float in water and wash away.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap.note4: The oldest evidence of a soap-like substance is from Babylon around 2800 BC ⚠️. Chip wafers are not washed with soap but with RCA cleaning (1965, ammonia and hydrogen peroxide etc., [9-14]).
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.note1: The liquid left after the soap is separated. Sweet glycerin is dissolved in it.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.note2: Left in the grid when making soap from saponified tallow. Bake in a furnace to get glycerin.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.note3: Spent lye contains glycerin, salt and a little alkali. Evaporating and distilling it yields glycerin.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.note4: It used to be thrown away; from the 19th century the glycerin was recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.placeho: Approximation: the salt is not recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerin.note1: A sweet, syrupy liquid. Used in skin lotions and medicines too.
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerin.note2: Bake spent lye in a furnace. Reacted with hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide it gives epichlorohydrin (a raw material for epoxy resin [2-41]).
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerin.note3: Glycerin, C3H5(OH)3, is an alcohol with three OH groups. It dissolves in water and holds moisture, so it is a humectant.
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerin.note4: Scheele found it in 1779 by boiling oil. Today it comes in huge amounts as a by-product of biodiesel.
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.note1: A weak alkaline water that dissolves only the resist that light has hit.
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.note2: About 1% sodium hydroxide in water (glass bottle; the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 sodium hydroxide + 1 water bucket + 3 empty glass bottles → 3 (the bucket comes back). Used in the developer bench [9-21]. GHS: corrosive (eyes, skin).
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.note3: In exposed positive resist the DNQ has turned into an acid, which reacts with the alkali and dissolves. Unexposed resist stays.
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.note4: Sodium that gets into oxide upsets MOSFETs, so later fabs switched to metal-free TMAH (2.38% solution is standard).
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.placeho: Approximation: made from a water bucket (really from pure water).
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.note1: White crystals: two phenols joined by acetone. One half of epoxy resin.
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.note2: 2 phenol + acetone + hydrochloric acid (the bottle is returned). ⚠ GHS: serious eye damage, skin sensitizer, reproductive toxicity.
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.note3: With acid, two phenol rings join onto one carbon of acetone: 2C6H5OH + (CH3)2CO -> (HOC6H4)2C(CH3)2 + H2O. The 'A' stands for acetone.
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.note4: First made by Dianin in Russia in 1891. It is also the raw material of polycarbonate (CDs, glasses); because it acts somewhat like a hormone, its use in food containers is regulated.
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.place: Approximation: heating conditions and purity are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.dichlorohydrin.no: Glycerin with two OH groups swapped for chlorine. One step before epichlorohydrin.

Glycerin + 2 hydrochloric acid (bottles returned). + sodium hydroxide -> epichlorohydrin. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, skin sensitizer, carcinogenic (category 1B), flammable. Treated only as an industrial material.
Two of the OH groups of glycerin, C3H5(OH)3, are replaced by Cl from hydrogen chloride.
Making it from glycerin is an old route; for a long time it came from propylene (petroleum). Since the 2000s glycerin from biodiesel is used again.
item.semiconductor-lab.epichlorohydrin.n: The other half of epoxy resin. It has a triangular ring (an epoxy group). Very harmful.

Dichlorohydrin + sodium hydroxide. React with bisphenol A and NaOH for epoxy resin. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, skin sensitizer, carcinogenic (category 1B), flammable. Treated only as an industrial material.
When the alkali pulls off one hydrogen chloride, a three-membered ring of oxygen and two carbons (the epoxy group) forms. The ring opens easily and links to other molecules.
First made by Berthelot in 1854. A raw material for epoxy resins, synthetic rubbers and water-treatment chemicals.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.note1: A sticky resin that has not set yet. Mix in a hardener and heat it to make it hard (like two-part glue).
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.note2: Bisphenol A + 2 epichlorohydrin + sodium hydroxide make 2. With novolac (the hardener) it becomes a molding compound. Heated alone it does not set. ⚠ GHS: skin irritant, skin sensitizer.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.note3: Bisphenol A with an epoxy group at each end. The OH of a phenolic hardener (or NH2 of an amine) opens the epoxy rings and links them into a network.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.note4: Around 1936 Castan in Switzerland (working on dental fillings) and Greenlee in the USA made it independently. Used for glues, paints and encapsulating electronics.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.place: Approximation: molecular weight (degree of polymerization) is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_molding_com: A black mix of epoxy resin and hardener. It becomes the case that wraps an IC.
Uncured epoxy resin + novolac (hardener). Heat in a furnace to get cured epoxy. Material for IC encapsulation ([9-34]).
The black case of an IC is epoxy resin + phenol-novolac hardener + silica powder (so it barely expands with heat) + carbon black (to block light), heated and set in a mould.
In the 1960s-70s IC packages moved from costly ceramic to cheap moulded epoxy (transfer moulding), so ICs could be made cheaply in huge numbers.
Approximation: no silica powder or carbon black.
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.note1: Set epoxy resin. It keeps out water and electricity and protects the IC.
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.note2: Heat the epoxy molding compound in a furnace. It does not melt when heated (a thermoset).
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.note3: Epoxy groups and the novolac OH groups have linked into a 3D network, so it is hard, resists heat and chemicals, and does not conduct.
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.note4: Almost every IC today sits inside this black epoxy, which protects the chip and its fine gold wires from moisture and knocks.
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.place: Approximation: shaping in a mould is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.refractory_brick_: Mostly quartz sand, shaped into a brick. It still has to be fired very hot.

Silica sand (SiO2) bound with a little slaked lime (about 2%, as milk of lime), pressed into shape. An ordinary furnace (~1000 C) is not hot enough: fire it in a blast furnace (~1450 C). During firing, quartz slowly turns into other crystal forms (tridymite, cristobalite), which is why silica bricks grow slightly instead of shrinking.
Ordinary bricks melt in a furnace. Only bricks full of quartz can take the heat.

Silica brick, about 95% SiO2. Fire-clay bricks soften around 1600 C, but silica bricks stay hard almost up to their melting point (~1700 C), so they were used for the roofs of steel furnaces. Silica is acidic: it is the right lining for an acid Bessemer converter.

1822: William Weston Young made bricks from the quartz-rich 'Dinas' rock of the Vale of Neath in Wales, so silica bricks are still called Dinas bricks. They made the hot open-hearth furnaces of the 1860s possible.

Silica bricks are acidic and are eaten by basic slag (CaO, MgO). That is why the Thomas converter (1878) needed a basic dolomite lining to remove phosphorus. Quartz changes crystal form near 573 C with a sudden size change, so silica bricks crack if heated or cooled quickly at low temperature.
Bake charcoal with electricity way too hard and it turns into graphite.

Resistance furnace where the charge itself is the heater: current flows from graphite electrodes straight through the packed carbon. 4 coal/charcoal + 1 sand -> 2 synthetic graphite, after the furnace reaches 2500 C. Needs 500 kW (about 10 steam engines); with less power it settles at a lower temperature and never graphitizes.

Edward Acheson found silicon carbide (carborundum) in 1891 while trying to make diamonds, and patented synthetic graphite in 1896. Heated far enough, SiC loses its silicon as vapour and leaves graphite behind - he thought the sand acted as a catalyst.

Game model: temperature rises with power in and falls with heat lost (proportional to temperature above 20 C), tuned so 500 kW settles at 2600 C. Real furnaces were tens of metres long, ran on Niagara hydroelectric power at hundreds of kW to MW, and one cycle took days. Today it is known that soft carbons (petroleum coke) graphitize without any catalyst.
item.semiconductor-lab.synthetic_graphit: Graphite made by people. Purer than the graphite you dig up.

Made in the Acheson furnace above 2500 C. At that heat the carbon atoms rearrange into graphite layers, and impurities (ash, sulfur, metals) boil away. Machined into high-purity boats for zone refining.

Natural graphite carries the minerals it grew in (clay, iron, silica). Synthetic graphite became the standard for electrodes, crucibles and later nuclear reactor moderators (the 1942 Chicago Pile used hundreds of tonnes).

Graphitization: carbon atoms in coke are arranged in small, misaligned layers. Above about 2500 C they move enough to stack into the ordered hexagonal layers of graphite. Electrical resistance drops and the material becomes soft and slippery.
block.semiconductor-lab.reverberatory_fu: Roasting ore sends its sulfur up the chimney as smoke. It used to be poison gas; collected, it becomes sulfuric acid.

Burns coal or charcoal (1 piece = 8 roasts, 10 s each) and roasts sulfide ores in air without melting them. Galena -> lead oxide + SO2; cinnabar dust -> mercury + SO2; sphalerite -> zinc oxide + SO2, plus germanium concentrate every 4th and indium every 8th. SO2 + water -> sulfuric acid.

The fire burns in a separate firebox; the flame and hot gas sweep over the hearth and the low roof reflects ('reverberates') the heat down onto the ore. English smelters used it for lead and copper from the 1690s, and Henry Cort used it for puddling iron in 1784. The Nirayama reverberatory furnace in Japan (Egawa Hidetatsu, finished by his son Hidetoshi in 1857) cast cannons and is a World Heritage site.

Because the fuel never touches the ore, the ash and sulfur of coal do not get into the metal. Roasting itself gives off heat (sulfur burns), so little fuel is needed. Smelter smoke (SO2) once killed forests around mines, such as Ashio in Japan; today smelter gas is sent to contact-process sulfuric acid plants, and smelters are major acid producers.

Approximation: a real furnace is a large brick building (firebox, hearth, flue, chimney); shrunk to one block. Ge and In really come from zinc-refining residues (leach residue, flue dust), not straight from roasting; here they come out as roasting by-products.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note1: A white powder: old white paint (zinc white) and the white in sunscreen.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note: ZnO, made by roasting sphalerite: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. Smelt it to reduce it with the fuel's carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note3: Zinc white became an artists' paint in 1834 ('Chinese white', Winsor & Newton). Unlike lead white it is not poisonous and does not darken.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note4: ZnO is itself a semiconductor (band gap about 3.3 eV). It absorbs UV, which is why it is in sunscreen, and it is used in varistors (surge protectors) and transparent electronics.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.placeh: Approximation: reducing ZnO needs about 1000 C, above zinc's boiling point (907 C), so real zinc escapes as vapour and must be condensed (distillation smelting [1-13]). Done in one furnace step here.
item.semiconductor-lab.refractory_brick_: The lime binder sets in air (Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O), and on firing reacts with quartz to form calcium silicate (CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3), welding the sand grains together. Above about 870 °C quartz turns into tridymite and above about 1470 °C into cristobalite, both bulkier crystals.

Silica bricks are also called Dinas bricks, after the Dinas rock, a quartzite in Wales from which they were made in the 1820s. Because they do not shrink when hot, they were used for open-hearth and glass furnace roofs and in coke ovens.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_furnace.note: A furnace that uses an electric spark (an arc) to get hot enough to melt almost anything.

Needs 500 kW (one steam turbine). Top left: vein quartz; middle: charcoal or coal; bottom left: graphite rods (electrodes, one used up every 8 runs). 2 vein quartz + 1 charcoal or coal -> 1 metallurgical silicon (about 86 s). It stops when power is short. Modern metallurgical silicon is made in AC submerged-arc furnaces; the game approximates it with DC until AC arrives in v0.4.

A huge current between two electrodes turns the gas (and charge) into glowing plasma at 2000-3000 °C (an arc discharge). At that temperature carbon can pull oxygen even off silicon, which holds it very tightly: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO.

The arc was found by Petrov in 1802 (published 1803) and also shown by Davy around 1808-1810 ⚠️. In 1892 Henri Moissan melted many substances in his electric arc furnace, and that same year Thomas Willson made calcium carbide (CaC2) by accident in the USA. Around 1900 Paul Héroult made the arc furnace practical for melting steel.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_furnace.plac: Approximation: real furnaces are large multi-block structures and today run on AC (high current from a transformer [4-10]). Here it is one block on DC (⚠️ whether Moissan's early furnace was DC is unconfirmed). Temperature changes are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.note1: Put it beside a furnace and pump it to blow air and make the fire hotter.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.note2: Each right-click with an empty hand gives about a second of air. With a turning water wheel beside it, it becomes a water-powered bellows that blows all the time. Place it next to a bloomery or blast furnace.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.note3: Blowing in more oxygen makes charcoal burn hard, reaching about 1200–1300 °C. An open fire (about 800 °C) can't make iron. The tomb of Rekhmire in Egypt (about 1450 BC) shows foot-operated bellows.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.note4: In AD 31 Du Shi of the Eastern Han dynasty in China drove bellows with a water wheel. The 'tatara' of Japanese iron-making was originally the name of a big foot bellows.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.placehol: Approximation: one pump gives about a second of air (game value)
message.semiconductor-lab.bellows.air: Air %s%% (keep pumping to keep it going)
item.semiconductor-lab.induction_coil.no: High-frequency current in the coil heats only the germanium itself, melting a narrow zone. Real coils are water-cooled.
item.semiconductor-lab.electric_motor.no: Turns the lead screw. Real zone refiners move a few cm per hour.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: Connected cables form one network: generators and discharging batteries feed machines directly (cables store nothing). Loss is 1% per cable along the longest path; at most 1 MW flows through a network, shared in proportion to demand. Right-click: network info.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note: Magnetite that nature magnetized (lightning does it). Known since antiquity as lodestone.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note: Faraday 1831: spin a coil in a magnetic field and current flows. Early dynamos used permanent magnets; from 1866-67 (Varley, Siemens and Wheatstone, almost simultaneously) the iron core's residual magnetism was enough.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_wheel.note: Needs FLOWING water beside it (500 W per side). Still water does nothing: power = flow x head. Early power stations were hydro.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_engine.not: Coal boils water, steam pushes a piston, the dynamo turns: 50 kW. Watt's engine converted only 2-5% of the coal's heat into work; ~30% only came with steam turbines. One water bucket = 2 coal's worth of steam.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note1: A glass jar wrapped in metal inside and out stores electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note: The first capacitor (Kleist and Musschenbroek, 1745): metal foil on the inside and outside of a glass jar, the glass between them as insulator. Charge piles up on the two foils. With a coil it forms the tuned circuit of the HF oscillator.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note3: Early radio transmitters used racks of Leyden jars as their capacitors. A coil (L) and a capacitor (C) together ring at one frequency, f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)) - the same idea as tuning a radio.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note4: Musschenbroek got such a shock from his jar that he wrote he would not repeat it for the whole kingdom of France. Benjamin Franklin later showed the charge sits on the glass surfaces, not in the water the first jars held.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.placeh: Approximation: the foil was tin foil (tin [1-30] not implemented) - copper here (copper-foil capacitors are real too).
item.semiconductor-lab.hf_oscillator.not: The machine that makes transistors ran on vacuum tubes - the very parts transistors would replace.

Two triode tubes + coil + Leyden jar + power input. The tubes keep the coil-capacitor circuit ringing at radio frequency (hundreds of kHz) and feed it to the induction coil of the zone refining furnace, where eddy currents melt only the germanium.

A tube amplifier whose output is fed back to its own grid keeps itself oscillating (Meissner and Armstrong, 1912-1913). Induction heaters of the 1950s that melted germanium were exactly such tube oscillators, with big water-cooled triodes.

Bell Labs' zone refiners (Pfann, 1952) were heated by RF induction of a few hundred kHz to MHz. Only the material inside the coil heats, so the graphite boat and quartz tube stay cooler - a clean way to melt one narrow zone.
block.semiconductor-lab.electric_furnace: It heats things with electricity instead of fire, so no smoke gets in.

Resistance furnace: current through graphite rods turns into heat (Joule heat, P = I squared R), up to about 1500 C. 5 kW x 10 s per item. Fires refractory bricks and clay-graphite boats. With a hydrogen tube added it becomes the hydrogen furnace.
Nichrome wire (1906) needs nickel and chromium, which we don't have yet - but a graphite rod works as a heating element too. 1500 C is above the melting point of silicon (1414 C).
Omitted: hot graphite burns in air (C + O2 -> CO2), so real graphite-element furnaces run under inert gas or vacuum, and the rods are consumables. Here the rods never wear out.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: A stick of graphite. Electricity flows through it and makes it glow hot.
Heating element of the electric furnace [4-12] and electrode of the Acheson furnace [3-10]. Graphite conducts electricity but has some resistance, so current turns into heat.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.plac: Approximation: real carbon rods (arc lamp carbons, 19th c.) are carbon powder bound with pitch (coal tar) and baked. Pitch is not implemented, so 3 natural graphite make 2 rods.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: Graphite's resistance falls as it gets hotter (unlike metals), and it does not melt at normal pressure - it sublimes near 3600 C. That is why graphite heaters can go far above any metal wire.
item.semiconductor-lab.self_excited_dyna: A dynamo with no magnet inside. It makes its own magnet out of its own electricity.

1866-67, Varley, Siemens and Wheatstone (almost simultaneously): a steel core + 4 coils. Right-click a water wheel or steam engine to swap out its permanent-magnet dynamo: output x2 (a steam engine also burns coal twice as fast — same electricity per coal, twice the power per machine).

The core keeps a little leftover magnetism. Spinning makes a weak current, which goes through the field coils and makes the field stronger, which makes more current... it builds itself up in seconds (the 'dynamo-electric principle').

Permanent magnets of the 1860s were weak, so magneto machines could only turn part of the engine's power into electricity. Electromagnet fields made big generators possible — Varley filed a patent in December 1866, and Wheatstone presented the same idea to the Royal Society on the same day as Siemens in January 1867. Energy is still conserved: double the electricity needs double the steam.
message.semiconductor-lab.self_excited_d: Installed the self-excited dynamo: output x2
This generator already has a self-excited dynamo
This generator already has an electromagnet field built in
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_turbine.no: Steam spins a fan really fast. This is how most power plants still work.

Parsons 1884. Coal + water -> 500 kW. One coal lasts 18 s (9 MJ = 30% of the coal's heat; the steam engine gets 5%). Water: a bucket in the top slot (1 bucket = 2 coal), or a water source block beside it feeds it forever. Enough to run the Acheson furnace (500 kW) by itself.

No piston going back and forth, just a wheel of blades turning in one direction — so it can spin fast (Parsons' first: 18,000 rpm) and be built huge. Power plants sit by rivers and the sea because they need lots of cooling water.

Real plants are multi-stage (steam expands through many rows of blades) and use a condenser to turn the steam back into water under vacuum, which raises efficiency. Coal plants reach about 33-40% today, combined-cycle gas plants over 60%. Your electricity is still mostly made by spinning turbines.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_turbine.pl: Simplified: blades are not machined on a lathe ([8-01] not yet implemented); single stage, no condenser; feedwater from a river is not used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.lead_acid_batter: The same kind of battery as in a car. It stores electricity as a chemical change.

Planté 1859. Lead plates in sulfuric acid. Holds 1 MJ. Every face both charges and discharges (up to 10 kW each; only 85% of the charge is stored). On a cable network it charges when there is spare power and discharges when machines need more. Keeps its charge when broken. Right-click: charge level. Glows while discharging.

Charging: 2PbSO4 + 2H2O -> Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4. Discharging runs it backwards, so the acid gets weaker as the battery empties — mechanics check charge by measuring the acid's density. Planté made the PbO2 plate by charging and discharging bare lead sheets over and over ('forming').

The first rechargeable battery, and still in nearly every car 160+ years later because it can give a huge current to the starter motor and is cheap and recyclable (over 95% of the lead is recycled). Pure lead plates are soft, so grids were hardened with a few % antimony ([1-43]). Overcharging splits water into H2 + O2 — battery rooms need ventilation.
Simplified: no self-discharge, no voltage (12 V etc.); the case is glass (real: glass jars, later hard rubber / plastic).
message.semiconductor-lab.cable.network: Cable network: %s cables, longest path %s (loss %s%%), %s generators, %s machines, %s batteries, %s delivered
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: Joins machines into one electric grid. Long cables lose more power.

Real loss is P = I^2 R: doubling the voltage halves the current for the same power and cuts the loss to a quarter. That is why power lines run at hundreds of kV (transformer [4-10]). In this mod the whole network shares one 1 MW limit (like one trunk line) and the loss uses the longest path for every machine - both are simplifications.
item.semiconductor-lab.induction_coil.no: Copper wound round and round. It heats metal without touching it - the same principle as an induction (IH) cooktop.

High-frequency AC in the coil induces eddy currents (currents swirling inside the metal), and the metal heats itself through its own resistance (P = I²R). The higher the frequency, the more the current crowds to the surface (skin effect: depth δ = √(2ρ/ωμ)).

The principle is Faraday's electromagnetic induction (1831). Edwin Northrup in the USA applied for a patent on the high-frequency induction furnace in 1916 and demonstrated one in 1918. Real coils are hollow copper tubes with cooling water flowing inside, because the coil itself heats up from the current.
item.semiconductor-lab.electric_motor.no: Spins using electricity. There is one in every fan and washing machine.

A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force (F = BIL, the Lorentz force). A coil is pushed round by it, and the commutator (a switching part) keeps flipping the current direction. It is the same machine as a dynamo, just run the other way.

In 1821 Faraday made a wire circle a magnet using current (electromagnetic rotation), an important step that did not become a practical motor right away. At the 1873 Vienna Exhibition, workers connected two Gramme dynamos and one began to spin as a motor, showing that a generator can also be a motor.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note1: A stone that grabs iron. The ancestor of the compass.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note3: Inside magnetite, small magnetic domains (regions whose magnetism points one way) face random directions. The strong field from a lightning current is thought to line them up, turning the whole stone into a magnet.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note4: The Japanese word jishaku comes from the Chinese "loving stone", which pulls iron like a mother hugging her child. In Han-dynasty China a lodestone spoon called sinan pointed south. In 1600 William Gilbert wrote in De Magnete that the Earth itself is a great magnet.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note1: Spin it and electricity appears, like a bicycle light.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note3: A changing magnetic flux through a coil makes a voltage: EMF = −dΦ/dt (Faraday's law). A spinning coil gives alternating voltage, but the commutator swaps the connections every half turn to give direct current, which electrolysis needs.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note4: In 1832, the year after Faraday's discovery, Pixii in Paris built a hand-cranked magnet generator. Gramme's ring dynamo of 1871 finally gave smooth direct current usable in factories.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: Graphite is carbon atoms in stacked hexagonal sheets (sp2 bonds). Electrons free to move within the sheets (π electrons) let it conduct, but with far more resistance than metals (around 1000 times), so current heats it by Joule heating, P = I²R.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: A wire's resistance is R = ρL/A (longer means more, thicker means less). Copper's resistivity is about 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, second only to silver. Wire copper is electrolytically refined to 99.99%, because even small impurities raise the resistance a lot.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_wheel.note: Flowing water turns the wheel to make electricity.
Hydro power P = ρgQHη (ρ: water density, g: gravity, Q: flow, H: head, η: efficiency). One tonne of water per second falling 10 m gives about 98 kW, with no fuel burned and no CO2.

The world's first hydroelectric plant opened in Appleton, USA, in 1882. In Japan a spinning mill at Sankyozawa, Sendai, started one in 1888, and Kyoto's Keage plant (1891, on the Lake Biwa Canal) powered Japan's first electric tram in 1895.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_engine.not: Burns coal to boil water and makes electricity from the steam.

Heat engines have a ceiling (Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, in kelvin). With steam at about 150 °C (423 K) and a 40 °C (313 K) cold side the limit is about 26%; real engines lose more to leaks and friction. In this game one coal (30 MJ) gives 1.5 MJ of electricity (5%).

Newcomen's engine (1712) was about 1% efficient. In 1769 Watt multiplied that with a separate condenser (cooling the steam in another vessel). The unit of power, the watt, is named after him, and he invented "horsepower" to sell his engines.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.n: A glass bell on an iron plate. Pump the air out with a hand pump next to it.

Holds a pressure (Pa). Starts at 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. A hand pump next to it lowers the pressure each stroke (down to 1 kPa); a Sprengel mercury pump takes it down to 0.05 Pa. Air slowly leaks back in through the greased seal (about 0.1 Pa per minute). You cannot see the pressure - use a mercury gauge.

19th-century labs used a glass bell jar ground flat at the rim and greased onto a flat plate. The outside air pushes the bell down with about 1 kg on every square centimetre, which is what keeps it sealed.
Large or hot chambers later became welded mild steel, and ultra-high vacuum uses stainless steel baked at 150-250 C so gas trapped in the walls comes out first. Here only the glass stage exists.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.p: Omitted: the grease on the ground seal (tallow [2-09]).
message.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber: You can't see air pressure. Hold a mercury vacuum gauge and right-click.
block.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pump: Magdeburg hemispheres: with the air pumped out, 16 horses could not pull them apart.

Otto von Guericke's air pump (c. 1650). Place next to a vacuum chamber and right-click with an empty hand: each stroke removes 20% of the air (chamber : cylinder = 4 : 1). It never gets below about 1 kPa (1/100 atm). Costs a little hunger.

Each stroke follows Boyle's law: the chamber air spreads into the empty cylinder, the valve closes, and that share is pushed outside. The pressure falls like 0.8, 0.64, 0.51... so the first strokes do the most.

The limit comes from dead volume: air left in the gap between the piston and the valve at the end of the stroke expands back in, and the leather packing leaks. Guericke reached roughly a few hundred Pa to 1 kPa. Better vacuum needed Sprengel's mercury pump (1865) and the diffusion pump (1915).
Approximation: the real cylinder was cast brass/bronze ([1-05] not implemented) - steel here. The leather packing uses vanilla leather (rubber [2-29] not implemented).
message.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pu: Place a vacuum chamber next to the pump.
Whoosh... the piston still moves easily (lots of air left)
Whoosh... very heavy - the air outside pushes back on the piston
It won't go lower - this is the hand pump's limit (about 1 kPa)
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum_ga: Air pressure equals the weight of 76 cm of mercury.

A closed-end U-tube of mercury (Torricelli's mercury column, 1643). Right-click a vacuum chamber: the difference in mercury height is the pressure in mmHg (1 mmHg = 133 Pa, 1 atm = 760 mmHg). Below 1 mm it can't be read by eye.
One arm is sealed with nothing above the mercury (the 'Torricellian vacuum'); the other is open to the chamber. The chamber gas pushes its side down by exactly its pressure in mm of mercury.

For lower pressures came the McLeod gauge (1874, compresses a sample of gas with mercury so it can be read), the Pirani gauge (1906, how fast a hot wire cools) and the hot-cathode ionization gauge (1916, built like a vacuum tube).
message.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum: The mercury levels are within 1 mm - too low to read (below %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Everything is inside the glass, but it is still full of air. Seal it on a sealing station.
Glass bulb + tungsten wire filament + iron wire grid + iron plate. With air inside, the hot filament would burn out at once. Put it in a sealing station next to a pumped-down vacuum chamber.
Approximation: grid and plate are iron (nickel [1-37] not implemented). The lead-in wires through the glass (platinum / Dumet wire, glass-metal seal [5-12]) are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note1: Add one more electrode to a light bulb and you can control the flow of electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note: Lee de Forest's Audion (1906). The hot tungsten filament boils off electrons; the plate collects them; a small voltage on the grid between them controls a large current - an amplifier. Part of the HF oscillator.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note3: Fleming's diode (1904) used Edison's discovery that a hot filament gives off current. De Forest added the zig-zag grid. Before transistors, every radio, telephone repeater and early computer amplified with tubes like this.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note4: De Forest's first Audions were 'soft' - gas left inside made them erratic. Langmuir and Arnold (c. 1913) showed that a hard vacuum (about 10^-4 Pa) makes tubes stable, which needed diffusion pumps and getters (the silver film inside a tube is the getter that ate the last gas).
Pump the air out of the bulb, then melt the glass neck shut.

Place next to a vacuum chamber (it is the exhaust manifold). Tube assembly + chamber at 0.1 Pa or lower + 500 W x 10 s (filament heated to drive out gas) -> triode vacuum tube. A hand pump cannot reach 0.1 Pa - you need a Sprengel mercury pump. Each tube lets some air back into the chamber (5% of the gap to 1 atm) - wait for it to pump down again.

Real tube factories pumped each bulb through a glass tube at its top, heated the parts to drive out gas, then melted that tube shut with a flame. The little glass tip on old tubes and light bulbs is where it was sealed off.

Gas hides in the metal and glass surfaces. While pumping, the filament is run hot and the plate heated (later by induction) so the gas comes out before sealing; finally the getter is flashed to absorb what is left.
Approximation: the sealing-off flame (gas burner) is represented by electric power.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Tungsten only emits electrons (thermionic emission) above about 2000 °C. At that temperature in air it burns at once: 2W + 3O2 → 2WO3 (yellow smoke). Gas molecules would also get in the electrons' way.

De Forest's 1906 triode, the Audion, still held some gas (a "soft" vacuum) and behaved erratically. Around 1913 Langmuir and others pumped tubes to a high vacuum and made them stable. The silver mirror inside later tubes is the getter (barium) that soaks up leftover gas.
block.semiconductor-lab.sprengel_pump.no: A pump that carries air away bit by bit with falling drops of mercury.

Place it next to a vacuum chamber and load 4 mercury: it keeps pumping every second (no power, mercury is not used up). It reaches 0.05 Pa; at 0.1 Pa or below the sealing station can seal vacuum tubes. Roughing to 1 kPa with the hand pump first is a little faster.

Mercury drops falling down a narrow glass tube trap pockets of gas between them and push them down like little pistons. With no moving parts and no dead space it reaches pressures about ten thousand times lower than a hand pump - though the mercury's own vapour (about 0.2 Pa at 20 °C) remains.

Invented by Hermann Sprengel in London in 1865; his first pump emptied a half-litre vessel in about 20 minutes. In 1879 Swan and Edison exhausted their carbon-filament lamps with it, so the filaments glowed for a long time instead of burning out. Crookes ran several in series to study cathode rays in his discharge tubes - a path that led to the discovery of the electron.
Not enough mercury (%s / %s). Right-click with mercury
No vacuum chamber next to it
Mercury drops are falling: pumping the chamber next to it (down to 0.05 Pa)
block.semiconductor-lab.rotary_pump.note: A pump that spins a rotor with a motor and pushes air out steadily. Place it next to a vacuum chamber.

250 W electric. Pumps the adjacent vacuum chamber down to 1 Pa (about 17 s from 1 atm). It can also pump a chamber beyond an adjacent diffusion pump (as its backing pump). Recipe: rotor + 2 steel + motor + 2 mercury.

In 1905 Gaede built a 'rotary mercury pump' that carried air in pockets sealed by mercury on a rotating part, turning the vacuum pump from a hand tool into a motor-driven machine. Oil-sealed rotary pumps followed soon after (⚠️ around 1907).

As the off-centre (eccentric) rotor turns, the space between it and the casing grows to draw gas in and shrinks to push it out. Sealing the gaps with a liquid (mercury, oil) is the key. The lab's 'hum' is this pump.
block.semiconductor-lab.rotary_pump.plac: Approximation: stage 1 (mercury-sealed). Gaede's rotary mercury pump also used a separate backing pump; here it pumps directly from atmosphere. The 1 Pa limit is a game value. Oil stages (castor oil, silicone oil) come later.
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_pump.n: A pump that knocks the remaining air away with a wind of mercury vapor. No moving parts.

400 W heater. Place it next to both a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump (backing). It starts once the chamber is below 10 Pa and brings it down to about 0.004 Pa, where it balances the leak (high vacuum, enough for evaporation). Recipe: 3 soda-lime glass + 2 iron + 2 mercury + tungsten wire (heater).

In 1915 Gaede boiled mercury in an iron pot and blew the vapor through glass tubes: the diffusion pump. In 1916 Langmuir cooled the walls with water to condense the vapor (the condensation pump) and made it much faster. Now vacuum tubes and lamps could reach high vacuum.

A fast downward jet of mercury vapor knocks any gas molecules that wander into it downwards. At atmospheric pressure there are too many molecules and the jet breaks up, so a backing pump must lower the pressure first. From 1928, low-vapor-pressure oils replaced mercury [5-06].
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_pump.p: Approximation: Gaede heated with a Bunsen burner (here an electric heater). The cold trap that stops mercury vapor drifting into the chamber, the cooling water and the warm-up time are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note1: A machine that heats metal in a vacuum into vapor and coats glass with a thin layer of it.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note2: 300 W electric (tungsten wire heater). Place it next to a vacuum chamber; it runs only while the chamber is below 0.01 Pa (needs a diffusion pump [5-05]), 20 s per run. Crown glass + silver nugget -> half-silvered mirror; lens + fluorite -> coated lens [7-22]. Each run opens the chamber, so the pressure rises a little. Recipe: 2 W wire + 2 iron + copper cable + soda-lime glass.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note3: In 1912 Pohl and Pringsheim evaporated metals in vacuum to make mirror films (there were earlier attempts). In the 1930s John Strong evaporated aluminum onto telescope mirrors, making mirrors that tarnish less. The aluminum wiring of 1960s ICs was made the same way.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note4: Leftover air scatters the evaporated metal atoms. The distance a gas molecule travels before the next collision (mean free path) is about 6.6 mm divided by the pressure in Pa. At 0.01 Pa that is about 66 cm, longer than the bell jar, so atoms fly straight to the substrate.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.place: Omitted: film thickness control (the later quartz crystal thickness monitor [8-15]) and sputtering. For now silver and CaF2 can be deposited (aluminum, chromium and others once their prerequisites exist).
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.not: Put sulfuric acid or salt in the lower-left slot. (1) Water + sulfuric acid (not used up): 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2, 572 kJ = 115 s at 5 kW. (2) Water + 2 salt [6-05]: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH, about 640 kJ = 128 s. The + electrode gives oxygen from water, chlorine from brine.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: H2, made by splitting water. One bag ≈ 1 mol (≈24 L at 25 °C, 1 atm). 19th-century labs carried gases in rubberised-cloth bags. Store large amounts in a Gas Holder [6-02]. Later used as a protective furnace atmosphere and for ammonia (Haber–Bosch).
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note: O2, from the + electrode of the electrolyzer, half the volume of the hydrogen. One bag ≈ 1 mol. Keep it in a different holder from hydrogen: mixed, they make an explosive oxyhydrogen mixture. Later used for oxidising silicon (SiO2 film).
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: The lightest gas. A balloon filled with it floats up into the sky.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note1: The gas that makes things burn. About one fifth of the air is oxygen.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note1: In the age of gas lamps, gas tanks were sealed with water so the gas could not leak out.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note: A low-pressure tank: a bottomless iron bell over a tank of water (19th-century gasworks). Gas lifts the bell, and the bell's weight pushes the gas out. Holds one gas at a time (set by the first gas in, cleared when empty). Automatically takes the same gas from an adjacent electrolyzer. Capacity 1000 mol ≈ 24.5 m³ (25 °C, 1 atm). Mixing hydrogen and oxygen gives oxyhydrogen (2H2+O2→2H2O): bang.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note3: London's Gas Light and Coke Company (founded 1812) stored coal gas in water-sealed gasholders and piped it to street lamps. The huge cylindrical iron frames still stand at places like King's Cross, reused as a park and as flats.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note4: Gas pressure = bell weight ÷ bell area (a few kPa, a few % above atmospheric), so no compressor is needed, but the volume stays large. Squeezing gas small enough to carry is the job of the compressor and cylinder [6-03]. Hydrogen molecules are tiny and slowly escape through gaps in metal and dissolve a little in the seal water (ignored in game).
item.semiconductor-lab.empty_gas_cylinde: A thick steel bottle that can hold gas squeezed to 150 times air pressure.

A seamless steel cylinder (about 10 L). Put it in a compressor next to a gas holder: it is filled with 50 mol of that gas at about 150 atm. Low-pressure bags (about 1 mol) are still handy for small amounts.

Gas cylinders became practical in the 1880s: Brin's Oxygen Company in London (1886) sold compressed oxygen in metal cylinders, and the Mannesmann brothers' seamless steel tubes (late 1880s) made strong cylinders without a welded seam.
50 mol at 25 C and 150 atm takes V = nRT/P = 50 x 0.0821 x 298 / 150, about 8 L (ideal gas). Real cylinders are tested with water at 5/3 of the filling pressure and re-tested every few years.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_cylinder: In Japan, hydrogen cylinders are painted red so nobody mixes them up.
50 mol of H2 compressed to about 150 atm in a steel cylinder (about 1.2 m3 of gas at normal pressure). Flammable: 4-75% in air can explode.
Japan's High Pressure Gas Safety Act fixes cylinder colours: oxygen black, hydrogen red, carbon dioxide green, chlorine yellow, ammonia white, acetylene brown, others grey.

Hydrogen atoms are so small that they creep into steel and make it brittle (hydrogen embrittlement). Hydrogen cylinders use tougher, lower-strength steel, and modern 700-bar fuel-cell car tanks use carbon fibre with a plastic liner. (The colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard - red for H2, black for O2. Other countries differ: in Europe (EN 1089-3) oxygen is white and hydrogen red; in the US colours are not fixed by law.)
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_cylinder.n: In Japan, oxygen cylinders are painted black.
50 mol of O2 compressed to about 150 atm. Pure oxygen makes things burn violently: never put oil or grease on the valve.
The first big use of bottled oxygen was the limelight of theatres (an oxy-hydrogen flame heating lime) and then welding and cutting with the oxy-acetylene torch (1903). Hospitals followed.

At high pressure, oil and grease can ignite by themselves in oxygen (adiabatic compression heats the gas when a valve is opened quickly). Oxygen valves are cleaned to remove oil and opened slowly. (The colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard - red for H2, black for O2. Other countries differ: in Europe (EN 1089-3) oxygen is white and hydrogen red; in the US colours are not fixed by law.)
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note1: High-pressure cylinders were made in the 1880s, and people could carry gas around.
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note: An electric piston compressor. Place it next to a gas holder with at least 50 mol: empty cylinder + 50 mol + 5 kW x 124 s -> filled cylinder of that gas. The energy (620 kJ) is the work to squeeze 50 mol from 1 to 150 atm at constant temperature, nRT ln(150).
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note3: Squeezing gas heats it, so real compressors work in stages (for example 1 -> 6 -> 30 -> 150 atm) with water coolers between them. A bicycle pump gets warm for the same reason.
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note4: Isothermal work W = nRT ln(P2/P1) = 50 x 8.314 x 298 x ln150, about 621 kJ. Squeezing to 150 atm in one adiabatic stroke (no cooling) would need more work (about 1 MJ) and heat the gas to nearly 1000 C, which is why multi-stage cooling matters.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note1: Salt that turned into stone. It used to be a sea.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note2: Halite, NaCl 95-99%. Found in evaporite beds under deserts and badlands. Crush it in the crafting grid to get salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note3: When an ancient sea was cut off and dried up, its salts settled in layers. Salt beds can be hundreds of metres thick. Poland's Wieliczka mine has been worked since the 13th century and even has a chapel carved out of salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note4: Seawater precipitates salts in order as it evaporates: calcite -> gypsum -> halite -> potassium/magnesium salts. That is why rock salt beds often sit on top of gypsum. Salt is soft and flows slowly under pressure, forming salt domes that trap oil.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.placeho: Approximation: crushing gives salt 1:1. Removing impurities (gypsum, clay) by dissolving and recrystallising is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note1: The same salt you eat. Rock salt and sea salt are both NaCl.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note2: Sodium chloride NaCl. Raw material for chlor-alkali electrolysis [6-05] (brine -> chlorine + hydrogen + caustic soda).
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note3: Salt was so valuable that Roman soldiers were said to receive a salt allowance - the word 'salary' is often linked to it. In Japan, salt was made from seawater because there is no rock salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note4: Today about 40% of the salt mined worldwide goes to the chemical industry, mostly to chlor-alkali plants. Japan has no rock salt, so it imports solar salt from Mexico and Australia for that.
block.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt_ore.no: A layer of salt deep under the desert. Long ago this was a sea.
Evaporite bed. Generates only under deserts and badlands (y0-48), replacing stone in large lenses. Soft (Mohs 2.5): any pickaxe drops rock salt; silk touch keeps the block.
Rock salt is 'a sea turned into stone'. The Zechstein sea dried up about 255 million years ago and left salt under much of northern Europe.
Salt mines are dry and stable, so some old ones store nuclear waste or archives. Salt also conducts heat well and seals cracks by slowly flowing.
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.pla: Simplified (brine mode): the diaphragm / mercury cell / ion-exchange membrane that keeps chlorine away from the caustic soda is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorine_gas.note: A yellow-green, poisonous gas. Salt and electricity make it.

Cl2, from the + electrode when brine is electrolysed [6-05]. 1 bag = about 1 mol. Store it in a gas holder (mixing with hydrogen explodes: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl). Burn it with hydrogen to make hydrochloric acid [6-06].

Scheele made chlorine in 1774 from hydrochloric acid and manganese dioxide but thought it contained oxygen. In 1810 Davy showed it was an element and named it after the Greek 'chloros' (yellow-green).

Chlorine is heavier than air (2.5x), so it sinks into hollows. It became the first large-scale chemical weapon at Ypres in 1915 - and also the chlorination of drinking water (from 1908) that saved far more lives.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorine_cylinder: In Japan, chlorine cylinders are painted yellow.
50 mol of Cl2 filled by the compressor [6-03] from a gas holder.
Chlorine turns into a liquid at only about 7 atm at room temperature, so real chlorine cylinders contain liquid chlorine with gas on top - much more fits than in a hydrogen cylinder.

Cylinder colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard: hydrogen red, oxygen black, chlorine yellow. Dry chlorine does not attack steel, but wet chlorine does (it forms HCl), so cylinders must be kept dry.
Caustic soda. Strong enough to dissolve skin - handle with care.
NaOH, collects at the - electrode in brine electrolysis [6-05] (2 per run). Strong base: later used in the Bayer process for alumina [1-14] and for soap.
Chlorine and caustic soda always come out together in a fixed ratio (1 t Cl2 : 1.1 t NaOH). Plants must find buyers for both - this is called the 'chlor-alkali balance'.
Before electrolysis (1890s), caustic soda was made by boiling soda ash with slaked lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3. Castner and Kellner's mercury cell (1892) made electrolysis practical.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note1: Burns hydrogen in chlorine and dissolves the smoke in water to make hydrochloric acid.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note2: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl (burns at about 2000 C), then HCl gas is absorbed in water. 1 mol H2 + 1 mol Cl2 + 1/4 bucket of water (5 s) -> 1 hydrochloric acid. Gas from bags (1 mol), cylinders (50 mol) or an adjacent gas holder. No electricity needed. With no water (water slot empty), the HCl stays as dry gas: 1 mol H2 + 1 mol Cl2 -> 2 bags of hydrogen chloride gas, for trichlorosilane [1-16].
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note3: Burning hydrogen in chlorine gives a pale flame and white fumes of HCl. This 'synthetic hydrochloric acid' became the main use for the chlorine and hydrogen that chlor-alkali plants produced from the 1890s on.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note4: The burner nozzle is made of quartz (later graphite) because hot HCl eats metals. The mixture is only safe because the gases meet at the nozzle: premixed H2 + Cl2 explodes in sunlight. Earlier, HCl came from the Leblanc process (salt + sulfuric acid) and was simply vented as a pollutant until the 1863 Alkali Act.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.place: Approximation: one-block burner with a built-in absorber. Gas amounts are stoichiometric; cooling water is not needed.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrochloric_acid: A strong acid that dissolves metals. Your stomach makes a weak version of it.
HCl dissolved in water (about 25%, 2 mol HCl per bottle). Made in the HCl synthesis burner [6-06]. Used for tungstic acid [1-28] and germanium tetrachloride [1-34].
Alchemists called it 'spirit of salt' (made by heating salt with sulfuric acid). Concentrated hydrochloric acid gives off HCl gas that fumes in moist air. Gastric juice is about 0.1 mol/L HCl.

HCl gas dissolves enormously in water: about 450 L of gas per litre at 20 C, so you cannot make it more than about 38%. In semiconductor fabs, dilute HCl with hydrogen peroxide (RCA clean SC-2, 1965) removes metal contamination from wafers.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: Burning makes only water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, releasing about 286 kJ per bag (1 mol), exactly the electricity the electrolyzer spent splitting it. Mixed with air at 4-75% it explodes when lit.

Cavendish discovered it in 1766 as the "inflammable air" given off when acid meets metal. In 1783 Lavoisier named it hydrogène, "water-maker"; the Japanese name suiso (water element) translates that. The same year Charles flew in a hydrogen balloon.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note3: In sulfuric-acid electrolysis, + electrode: 2H2O → O2 + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻; − electrode: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H2. Four electrons give one O2 and two H2, so the oxygen is half the hydrogen's volume.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note4: Scheele and Priestley each discovered it in the 1770s. Lavoisier thought every acid contained it and named it oxygène, "acid-maker". That was wrong (hydrochloric acid, HCl, has no oxygen), but the Japanese name sanso (acid element) keeps the mistake alive.
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.not: Uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.

Pure water barely conducts, so sulfuric acid is added to supply ions (charged particles that carry current); the acid itself is not used up. Splitting water needs 1.23 V in theory, but about 2 V in practice because of losses at the electrodes.

In 1800, just after news of Volta's pile arrived, Nicholson and Carlisle electrolyzed water. In 1834 Faraday found the laws of electrolysis and coined (with Whewell's help) the words electrode, anode, cathode, ion and electrolyte.
block.semiconductor-lab.air_separation_u: Freezes air into a liquid and splits it into nitrogen, oxygen and argon.

Runs on electricity alone (the raw material is the air around it). 5 kW x 16 s separates 10 mol of air: about 8 bags of nitrogen, 2 of oxygen, and one bag of argon every ~11 runs. A gas holder next to it pulls from the outputs automatically.

Air is compressed to about 200 atm, cooled in a heat exchanger and then expanded through a small valve, which cools it (the Joule-Thomson effect). Repeating this liquefies it at about -194 °C.
