Distilling the liquid air stage by stage in a rectifying column sends low-boiling nitrogen (-196 °C) up and oxygen (-183 °C) down, while argon (-186 °C) collects in the middle.

Carl von Linde liquefied air in 1895 and separated oxygen with a rectifying column in 1902. Argon had been found in 1894 by Rayleigh and Ramsay, because nitrogen from air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made chemically. Its name is Greek for 'lazy' (it reacts with nothing). It later filled light bulbs and the furnaces that pull silicon crystals. Early plants used far more electricity than today's.
Omitted: the insulated cold box (real ones were wooden boxes packed with wool etc.), hours of cool-down at start-up, a separate argon column. Power uses the modern value (1900s plants used more).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrogen_gas.note: Four fifths of the air is this gas. Breathing it in does nothing to your body.

N2. Comes from the air separation unit [6-07]. 1 bag = about 1 mol. Works with gas holders and the compressor (nitrogen cylinder). It reacts with almost nothing, so it is used to blanket things you do not want oxidized.

The two atoms of N2 are held by a triple bond (N≡N, about 945 kJ/mol), so it hardly reacts at ordinary temperatures. Above about 1200 °C, though, it reacts with silicon to form silicon nitride (Si3N4) - so molten silicon is blanketed with argon instead.

Discovered in 1772 by Daniel Rutherford as air in which neither a candle nor a mouse could live. Lavoisier called it azote, 'lifeless' (still its French name). Plants cannot use nitrogen from the air directly; until the Haber-Bosch process [6-09] turned it into fertilizer, it set the limit on food.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note1: A gas that reacts with nothing, about 1% of the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note2: Ar. The air separation unit gives one bag per about 108 mol of air. Works with gas holders and the compressor (argon cylinder). Planned use: filling the furnace that pulls silicon crystals (CZ).
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note3: Argon is a noble gas (group 18): its outer electron shell is exactly full, so it bonds with almost nothing. Molten silicon (1414 °C) reacts with nitrogen and oxygen, but not with argon. It is about 1.4 times denser than air and lingers even in an open container.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note4: Discovered in 1894 by Rayleigh and Ramsay, who noticed that 'nitrogen' left after removing oxygen etc. from air was about 0.5% heavier than nitrogen made by chemical reactions. It is 0.93% of the air, yet nobody had noticed. Almost all argon on Earth comes from the decay of potassium-40 in rocks.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrogen_cylinder: In Japan, nitrogen cylinders are painted grey.
50 mol of N2 from a gas holder, filled by the compressor [6-03].

Nitrogen cannot be liquefied at room temperature however hard you squeeze it (it stays gas above its critical temperature, -147 °C). So the cylinder holds high-pressure gas; liquid nitrogen travels in insulated vacuum flasks.

The Japanese rules fix the colours for oxygen (black), hydrogen (red), liquefied CO2 (green), liquefied ammonia (white), liquefied chlorine (yellow) and acetylene (brown). Every other gas, nitrogen and argon included, is grey with the contents written on it.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_cylinder.no: Argon cylinders are grey too - read the lettering to tell them apart.
50 mol of Ar from a gas holder, filled by the compressor [6-03].

Argon's critical temperature is -122 °C, so like nitrogen it is high-pressure gas, not liquid, in a room-temperature cylinder. It is the most common shielding gas that protects metal from air during welding.

Argon comes out of air separation alongside oxygen and nitrogen, so it is by far the cheapest noble gas. It is inside light bulbs too: it slows the evaporation of the tungsten filament (Langmuir filled bulbs with nitrogen in 1913, later argon).
block.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth_bloc: Soft earth with white crystals in it, deep in limestone caves.
Only in dripstone caves (inside dripstone blocks). Dig with a shovel for 2 nitre earth; silk touch keeps the block.
During the War of 1812, saltpeter was mined from the cave earth of Mammoth Cave in the USA. Wooden pipes and vats from that time still remain in the cave.
Cave nitrates form when bacteria break down nitrogen from things like bat droppings (nitrification). They build up over centuries in dry cave earth that rain cannot wash out.
Approximation: placed only in dripstone caves (in reality it also came from old stable floors and walls; domestication [0-17] and nitre beds [6-10] come later).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth.note1: Earth containing nitrates. Soak it in water and they dissolve out.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth.note2: 4 + wood ash + water bucket -> nitre liquor (the bucket comes back).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth.note3: Old saltpeter diggers are said to have tasted the earth of stable floors and old walls: a bitter, cool taste meant plenty of saltpeter (⚠️ a tradition).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth.note4: Most of the nitrate in the earth is calcium nitrate Ca(NO3)2, which absorbs moisture and hardly crystallizes on its own.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_liquor.note: The clear liquid from soaking nitre earth in water with wood ash. Boil it down and white crystals appear.
4 nitre earth + wood ash + water bucket (the bucket comes back). Boil it down in a furnace for saltpeter.
Adding wood ash is old wisdom: its potassium carbonate settles the calcium out as calcium carbonate and turns the nitrate into potassium saltpeter.
Ca(NO3)2 + K2CO3 -> 2KNO3 + CaCO3(s). Saltpeter dissolves well in hot water but poorly in cold, so boiling down and cooling makes it crystallize first (recrystallization purifies it).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_liquor.plac: Approximation: made before the container system (IMP-33), so no bottle. The settled calcium carbonate is discarded.
item.semiconductor-lab.saltpeter.note1: White crystals. The raw material for nitric acid, and a fertilizer. ⚠ Helps things burn (oxidizer).
item.semiconductor-lab.saltpeter.note2: Potassium nitrate KNO3, made by boiling down nitre liquor in a furnace. Distilled with sulfuric acid it gives nitric acid [6-11]. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing solid (keep away from fire).
item.semiconductor-lab.saltpeter.note3: As a raw material of gunpowder, saltpeter changed history (China in the 9th-10th centuries, Europe around the 13th). It also has many peaceful uses: curing meat (keeping its color), fertilizer, and removing bubbles from glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.saltpeter.note4: In the 19th century Chilean desert nitre (sodium nitrate) was exported worldwide as fertilizer. From 1913 the Haber-Bosch process made ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen, which could be oxidized to nitric acid [6-09].
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.note1: A very strong acid that dissolves silver and copper. Kept in a glass bottle. ⚠ On skin it turns yellow and burns.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.note2: Distil saltpeter + sulfuric acid (bottle) + an empty glass bottle with the quartz still (returned): KNO3 + H2SO4 -> HNO3 + KHSO4. The sulfuric acid bottle comes back empty. React with silver for silver nitrate. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing liquid, corrosive to metals, skin corrosion, toxic if inhaled (industrial material only).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.note3: Its old name was aqua fortis ('strong water'). It dissolves silver but not gold, so it was used to part gold from silver (and test gold's purity). The first recipes appear in alchemical books of the late 13th-early 14th century; in the mid-17th century Glauber described making it from saltpeter and sulfuric acid (⚠️ the year 1648 is unconfirmed).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.note4: Nitric acid is both an acid and an oxidizer, so it dissolves copper and silver that ordinary acids cannot (releasing NO and NO2 gas). In semiconductors it is mixed with hydrofluoric acid in etchants (such as CP-4) that dissolve and polish silicon and germanium surfaces.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.place: Approximation: distillation in the crafting grid skips the heating. The byproduct potassium hydrogen sulfate and the brown NO2 gas are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.silver_nitrate.no: White crystals from dissolving silver in nitric acid. They turn black in light. ⚠ Leaves black stains on skin.

Silver nugget + nitric acid (the bottle comes back): 3Ag + 4HNO3 -> 3AgNO3 + NO + 2H2O. Material for photographic emulsions (silver halides) [B-02] and silver mirrors [7-05]. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing solid, skin corrosion, toxic to aquatic life.
It was once called lunar caustic and used in medicine, for example to burn off warts (in alchemy silver was the metal of the Moon).

Light reduces silver ions into tiny silver grains that look black. This property was the start of photography (Schulze showed in 1727 that it darkens in light ⚠️). Mixed with iodides or bromides it forms silver halides, which are far more light-sensitive.
item.semiconductor-lab.silver_nitrate.pl: Approximation: no container (in reality kept in light-proof brown bottles). Boiling down to crystals and the NO gas are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note: Fused silica (pure SiO2) survives high heat and adds no impurities. Ordinary glass would melt and leak sodium.
block.semiconductor-lab.oxyhydrogen_burn: Burn hydrogen and oxygen together and the flame gets hot enough to melt quartz.

Connect a hydrogen cylinder and an oxygen cylinder ([6-03] compressor). Vein quartz x1 + H2 4 mol + O2 2 mol (10 s) -> fused quartz. 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, flame about 2800 C; quartz (SiO2) melts at about 1713 C. One H2 cylinder = 12.5 quartz, one O2 cylinder = 25 (2:1 ratio). No electricity needed. Empty cylinders come out bottom right.

1801: Robert Hare (USA) built the oxyhydrogen blowpipe and melted platinum for the first time. In the late 1830s ⚠️ Marc Antoine Gaudin (France) melted rock crystal in the flame and drew threads of fused quartz. From 1899 Heraeus (Germany) made fused quartz industrially. The same flame lit theatres as 'limelight' (a block of quicklime glowing in it).

Hare kept the two gases in separate reservoirs and mixed them only at the nozzle tip: premixed H2 + O2 is knallgas and detonates. The flame is almost invisible (pale blue) and gives off only water vapour, so it does not contaminate quartz with carbon or sulfur. Heraeus later moved to electric melting; today synthetic fused silica is made by burning SiCl4 in an H2/O2 flame.
Approx: a 1-block bench burner. Gas per quartz is a game value (assumes ~10% of the flame's heat reaches the quartz). Gas left in the burner is lost if you break it.
item.semiconductor-lab.fused_quartz.note: Quartz melted into clear glass. Heat it red hot, drop it in water, and it still will not crack.
Pure SiO2 glass. Melt vein quartz in the oxyhydrogen burner (~2000 C). A furnace (~1000 C) is far too cold: quartz melts at about 1713 C. Made into quartz tubes for the zone refiner.

Gaudin melted quartz in an oxyhydrogen flame in the late 1830s ⚠️; Heraeus started industrial production in 1899. Ordinary glass is mostly SiO2 too, but soda and lime are added so it melts at about 1000 C.

Thermal expansion is only about 0.5 x 10^-6 per K (soda-lime glass ~9 x 10^-6), so it survives thermal shock. It transmits UV down to about 160-200 nm, which is why lithography lenses and photomask blanks are fused silica. With no sodium, it does not poison semiconductors.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note1: A glass tube made of the same stuff as rock crystal. It barely minds heat.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note3: Fused quartz is an almost pure SiO2 network that expands with heat only about 1/20 as much as ordinary glass (about 0.5×10⁻⁶ per K), so a red-hot tube can be dunked in water without cracking. It does not conduct electricity, so the induction coil's field passes straight through and only the germanium inside heats up.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note4: It began in the late 1830s ⚠️ when Gaudin melted tiny beads of quartz with an oxyhydrogen flame. Clear quartz tubing was first made industrially around 1900 in Germany (Heraeus), again with oxyhydrogen flames. In Pfann's zone refining the graphite boat sat inside a quartz tube filled with protective gas.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass_batch: Sand mixed with lead powder (litharge) and potash. Melted, it becomes a sparkling glass.
5 sand + 1 litharge + 1 potassium carbonate -> 5. By weight roughly SiO2 49%, PbO 36%, K2O 15% (close to real flint glass). Melt in a blast furnace for 20 s to get flint glass.
"Flint" comes from English glassmakers who used burnt, crushed flint pebbles instead of sand. Lead also lowers the melting temperature, making the glass easier to work.

PbO enters the glass network as a modifier. Heavy lead ions have easily distorted electron clouds (high polarizability), so light slows down more and the refractive index rises. Violet light is slowed even more than red, so dispersion grows too.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.note1: Heavy, sparkling glass with lead in it. It bends light strongly and splits it into rainbow colors.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.note2: Optical flint (lead glass, about 40% PbO). Refractive index about 1.6, high dispersion (Abbe number about 36-41). Combined with crown glass it makes an achromatic lens [7-04]. Lead is toxic - don't lick it.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.note3: In 1674 the Englishman George Ravenscroft patented a clear glass that did not cloud, usually counted as the start of lead crystal (⚠️ historians debate whether his early glass really contained lead). In the 18th century lead glass was used for lenses as flint glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.note4: A single lens focuses each color at a different point (chromatic aberration). Cementing a low-dispersion crown convex lens to a high-dispersion flint concave lens keeps the bending power but cancels the color error (Hall c. 1733, Dollond 1758). Lithography projection lenses also combine many glass types to cancel color and shape errors.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_glass.place: Omitted: removing bubbles and striae. Represented by the long melt time in the blast furnace (20 s).
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.note1: Glass remade evenly for lenses. It hardly splits light into colors.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.note2: Soda-lime glass remelted in a blast furnace and stirred to remove striae: optical glass. Refractive index about 1.52, low dispersion (Abbe number about 59). Combined with flint glass it makes an achromatic lens [7-04].
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.note3: The name comes from old window-glass making: a blown glass bubble was spun out into a flat disc (a 'crown'). Around 1805 the Swiss Guinand stirred molten glass with a fireclay rod to make optical glass free of bubbles and striae, and worked with Fraunhofer in Germany.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.note4: The Abbe number measures how little a glass spreads colors: the larger, the less color fringing. In 1884 Abbe, Schott and Zeiss set up a works in Jena and created new optical glasses with boron and barium. Today's standard lens glass BK7 is also a borosilicate crown.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_glass.place: Approximation: real optical crown is potash-lime or borosilicate glass (BK7). Here it is made from soda-lime glass (soda crown). Stirring is represented by the blast-furnace time (20 s).
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.note1: A red powder made by roasting iron. It is so fine that it can polish glass to a shine.
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.note2: Iron nugget -> furnace (roasted in air) -> iron(III) oxide Fe2O3. Used with the pitch lap to polish a ground lens clear.
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.note3: Red iron oxide has been a pigment since ancient times and was jeweller's rouge for polishing gems and metals. Newton polished his mirror with putty (tin oxide), but in the 19th century Lord Rosse used red iron oxide (⚠️ when it was first used for lenses is unconfirmed).
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.note4: From the 1940s cerium oxide CeO2 took over (⚠️). CeO2 does not just scrape: it bonds chemically with the SiO2 of the glass and pulls the surface away, so it polishes fast and flat (the idea behind chemical mechanical polishing, CMP, used to flatten chips today).
item.semiconductor-lab.rouge.placeholder: Approximation: real jeweller's rouge was often made by roasting green vitriol (iron sulfate). Here iron is roasted in air (the old crocus martis method).
item.semiconductor-lab.grinding_tool.not: An iron dish for grinding glass with sand into a lens shape. It can be used again and again.
3 iron ingots. Put it in the crafting grid with optical glass and sand to get a frosted lens blank (the tool comes back).
17th-century lens makers rubbed glass on a hollow iron or brass dish with wet sand or emery (corundum powder), changing from coarse to fine powder in many steps.

Rubbing two surfaces together in all directions wears down the high spots until they become spherical (the sphere is the only shape that fits itself however it slides). That is why old lenses were almost all spherical.
item.semiconductor-lab.grinding_tool.pla: Omitted: the many grinding steps from coarse sand to fine emery and the gauges that set the radius. The tool does not wear.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.note1: An iron dish covered with soft pitch, for polishing lenses. It can be used again and again.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.note2: 3 pitch + iron ingot. Put it in the crafting grid with a ground lens blank and rouge to get a clear lens (the lap comes back).
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.note3: A hard tool scratches. Pitch slowly flows to match the lens exactly and presses the polishing grains gently. Newton also wrote about polishing his mirror on pitch.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.note4: The shape of a polished surface is checked with Newton's rings, the interference fringes seen when a reference surface is laid on it. One fringe means a difference of half a wavelength (about 0.3 um). Projection lens [7-19] surfaces are now matched to a few nanometres.
item.semiconductor-lab.pitch_lap.placeho: Omitted: the lap does not wear. Adjusting the pitch hardness with temperature is also omitted.
Crown glass ground with sand into a convex lens shape. Still frosted and cloudy.
Crown glass + sand + grinding tool (comes back). The surface is full of tiny scratches that scatter light. Polish it with the pitch lap and rouge for a clear lens.
Ground glass looks cloudy because the bumpy surface scatters light in all directions. Wet it and the bumps fill in, so you can see through it a little.
The depth of the scratches left by grinding depends on the grain size. Polishing must remove more than that depth (a few um), which is why the powder is changed to finer and finer grades.
Flint glass ground with sand into a concave lens shape. Still frosted.
Flint glass + sand + grinding tool (comes back). Polish it with the pitch lap and rouge for a clear lens.
Lead glass is softer than ordinary glass and scratches easily, so it must be polished with special care.
A concave lens is ground on a convex tool. Convex and concave tools are rubbed against each other to make a matched pair of the same radius.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_lens.note1: A polished, clear convex lens. It brings light to a point, like a magnifying glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_lens.note2: Ground crown lens blank + rouge + pitch lap (comes back). Refractive index about 1.52. Combined with a flint concave lens it makes an achromatic lens [7-04].
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_lens.note3: Spectacles were invented in Italy in the late 13th century (convex lenses for reading). Lens is Latin for lentil, from the shape.
item.semiconductor-lab.crown_lens.note4: The focal length f of a convex lens depends on the surface radii and the refractive index (1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)). But n changes with color, so blue focuses nearer and red farther (chromatic aberration).
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_lens.note1: A polished, clear concave lens. It spreads light out.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_lens.note2: Ground flint lens blank + rouge + pitch lap (comes back). Refractive index about 1.6, strong color spreading. Cemented to a crown convex lens it makes an achromatic lens [7-04].
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_lens.note3: In 1758 Dollond patented an achromatic lens combining a crown convex lens and a flint concave lens (Hall had made one around 1733).
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_lens.note4: A concave lens alone forms no image, but its color error is opposite to that of a convex lens. Flint spreads colors strongly, so a weak concave flint lens can cancel the crown's color error. The pair stays a convex lens overall, but the color fringes vanish.
item.semiconductor-lab.achromatic_lens.n: Two lenses of different glass put together. The rainbow fringes disappear and the image is sharp.

Crown lens (convex) + flint lens (concave) + copper ingot (lens cell). Low-dispersion crown and high-dispersion flint cancel the color-by-color focus error (chromatic aberration). It becomes the objective of a refracting telescope.
Newton thought color fringes could not be removed with lenses and built a mirror telescope instead. Around 1733 Hall made an achromatic lens, and in 1758 Dollond patented it and made it widespread.

Achromatic means bringing two colors (usually red and blue) to one focus. The small leftover error (secondary spectrum) is reduced further with special materials such as fluorite (apochromats). Lithography projection lenses [7-19] combine many more glasses and use light of a single wavelength to avoid color problems.
item.semiconductor-lab.achromatic_lens.p: Omitted: the cement between the two lenses (Canada balsam from the 19th century). The real cell is brass.
item.semiconductor-lab.refracting_telesc: A tube for seeing far things large. Hold right-click to look through it (like the vanilla spyglass).

Achromatic lens (top, objective) + copper ingot (tube) + crown lens (bottom, eyepiece). Both are convex (Keplerian), so the image is upside down (fine for stars). Magnification = objective focal length / eyepiece focal length.

In 1608 Lippershey in the Netherlands applied for a telescope patent. In 1609 Galileo found mountains on the Moon and four moons of Jupiter with telescopes he made himself. The two-convex-lens design was proposed by Kepler in 1611.

Before achromatic lenses, telescopes were made extremely long so the color fringes were less noticeable. Hevelius's 17th-century telescope was about 45 m long and hung from a mast with ropes. Achromatic lenses made telescopes short and bright.
Approximation: the view (zoom and field) is the same as the vanilla spyglass, and the image is not flipped. The real tube is brass.
item.semiconductor-lab.prism.note1: A triangular glass that splits light into rainbow colors.
item.semiconductor-lab.prism.note2: Flint glass + sand + grinding tool + rouge + pitch lap (tools come back). Three flat faces are ground and polished. High-dispersion flint spreads the colors widely. The heart of the spectroscope.
item.semiconductor-lab.prism.note3: In 1666 Newton passed sunlight from a hole in a window shutter through a prism and showed that white light is a mixture of rainbow colors. A second prism passing a single color did not split it further.
item.semiconductor-lab.prism.note4: Light splits because the refractive index differs by color (dispersion); violet bends most. Ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet (shorter than about 350 nm), so UV spectroscopy uses quartz or fluorite prisms [7-15].
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.note: A tool that splits light into a rainbow to see which colored lines it has. Put something in a flame and look, and you can tell which elements it contains.

Use: hold a sample (salt, potash, slaked lime, boric acid...) in the other hand and right-click a lit campfire or fire -> element lines (flame test). Right-click the air under the open sky by day -> the Sun's dark lines. Recipe: prism + 2 crown lenses + 3 copper ingots.

In 1859 Kirchhoff and Bunsen found that each element gives lines of its own colors (spectral analysis). With it they discovered caesium the next year and rubidium the year after. In 1868 a line from an element unknown on Earth was seen in the Sun during an eclipse: helium.

Electrons in an atom can only sit on fixed energy steps, and stepping down they give off light with exactly the energy difference (a fixed wavelength). So the line positions are fingerprints of elements. The same element also absorbs those wavelengths (the Sun's dark lines). Spectroscopy is still used to find tiny impurities in semiconductor materials.
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.plac: Approximation: the real thing uses the soot-free flame of a Bunsen burner; here a campfire. Only strong visible lines are shown as text.
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.flam: An unbroken rainbow from red to violet (continuous spectrum): hot soot particles glowing
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.hold: -> Hold a sample in your other hand and look at the flame again
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.none: No clear lines (it does not glow at flame temperature, or does not evaporate)
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.line: Sodium Na: two bright yellow lines 589.0 nm, 589.6 nm (D lines)
Potassium K: deep red 766.5 nm, 769.9 nm and violet 404.4 nm (lilac flame)
Calcium Ca: orange-red band (~620 nm, CaOH), green band (~554 nm) and violet 422.7 nm
Boron B: green bands ~518 nm, 548 nm (BO2; the flame turns green)
Lead Pb: a weak violet line 405.8 nm (pale bluish flame)
Germanium Ge: its strong line is ultraviolet, 265.1 nm, invisible (glass prisms also block UV)
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.sun: ☀ Spectrum of sunlight: many thin dark lines across the rainbow (Fraunhofer lines)
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.sun_: C 656.3 nm (hydrogen), D 589 nm (sodium), b 517 nm (magnesium), F 486.1 nm (hydrogen), H/K 396.8/393.4 nm (calcium). Gas in the Sun's outer layers absorbs those colors
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.no_s: Point it at the air under open sky by day to see sunlight's spectrum (or at a lit campfire)
item.semiconductor-lab.speculum_charge.n: Copper and tin mixed 2 to 1. Melted, it becomes a shiny white alloy.
2 copper ingots + 1 tin ingot -> 3 (about 33% tin). Melt in a furnace for speculum metal.
Newton made his telescope mirror from 6 parts copper and 2 parts tin with a little arsenic. Each mirror maker kept their recipe secret.
Above about 30% tin, bronze turns from copper-red to silvery white, because Cu-Sn intermetallic phases (such as delta) increase; the alloy also becomes very hard and brittle.
item.semiconductor-lab.speculum_ingot.no: A white bronze with lots of tin. Polished well it becomes a mirror. Very hard and easy to crack.
Cu about 67%, Sn about 33%. Grind and polish it with the grinding tool, sand, rouge and pitch lap for a speculum mirror.
Until silvering glass was invented (mid-19th century), all large telescope mirrors were made of this metal. Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781 with a mirror he cast and polished himself.
Being brittle, a casting cracks if it cools unevenly. Lord Rosse's 1845 'Leviathan' had a speculum mirror about 1.8 m across weighing about 4 tonnes.
item.semiconductor-lab.speculum_ingot.pl: Approximation: melting in a furnace stands in for a crucible furnace (CHEMISTRY #38). Newton's arsenic is left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.speculum_mirror.n: A dish-shaped mirror made of polished metal. It brings light to a point.
Speculum metal + sand + grinding tool + rouge + pitch lap (tools come back). A concave mirror reflecting about 60% (silver: over 90%). The main mirror of a reflecting telescope.
In 1668 Newton built a telescope that gathers light with a mirror, avoiding the color fringes of lenses. About 15 cm long, it matched the magnification of the long refractors of the day.

A mirror bends every color the same way (the angle of reflection does not depend on wavelength), so it has no chromatic aberration. Today's large telescopes and EUV lithography [7-17] also gather light with mirrors, not lenses.
item.semiconductor-lab.speculum_mirror.p: Omitted: real speculum mirrors tarnished within months and had to be repolished (no tarnish or repolishing here).
item.semiconductor-lab.reflecting_telesc: A telescope that gathers light with a mirror. Hold right-click to look through it.

Speculum mirror (bottom of the tube) + 2 copper ingots (tube) + crown lens (eyepiece at the side). A small flat mirror in the tube sends the light out sideways, and you look in from the side. No color fringes.
In 1671 Newton showed his self-made reflecting telescope to the Royal Society, and was elected a Fellow the following year.
A mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made much larger than a lens. That is why telescope apertures grew with mirrors (now several to tens of metres).
Approximation: the view is the same as the vanilla spyglass. The small diagonal flat mirror (a little speculum flat in reality) is counted as part of the tube.
item.semiconductor-lab.wire_grating.note: Many thin copper wires lined up at equal gaps. Light passing through makes rainbows.

2 lead screws + copper ingot. Thin copper wire is wound in the threads of two screws to make a grating with spacing d = 0.004 inch (101.6 um). With a spectroscope it makes a grating spectroscope that measures wavelengths.
Around 1821 Fraunhofer used wires 0.002 inch thick at this spacing to make the first measurement of the wavelength of the Sun's dark D lines, to about one part in a thousand.

Light waves passing the gaps overlap and reinforce only at certain angles (interference). Since d sin(theta) = lambda (first order), knowing d and the angle fixes the wavelength with a ruler. The rainbow on the back of a CD is also a grating, with grooves 1.6 um apart.
item.semiconductor-lab.wire_grating.plac: Omitted: reflection gratings (grooves ruled in metal, needing a ruling engine [8-12]) are not here yet. Variation in wire thickness and count is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.grating_spectrosc: A spectroscope that measures the color of light as a wavelength number (nm).

Spectroscope + wire grating. Used like the spectroscope (sample in a flame, or the daytime sky). For each line it shows the first-order diffraction angle theta and the wavelength from lambda = d sin(theta).

A prism separates colors, but its angles depend on the glass, so it cannot give wavelength values. A grating fixes the wavelength from d and the angle alone, so it became a tool to measure them. In 1882 Rowland ruled gratings with about 570 grooves per mm using a ruling engine (⚠️ figures vary between sources).

The wavelengths of lithography light sources (mercury g-line 436 nm and i-line 365 nm [7-10], KrF 248 nm, ArF 193 nm) are told apart this way. Diffraction is also what limits the resolution of lithography (the Rayleigh formula).
diffraction angle theta = %s deg (%s') -> lambda = d sin(theta) = %s nm (d = %s um)
block.semiconductor-lab.mercury_lamp.not: A light made by passing electricity through mercury vapor. It gives bluish-white light and invisible ultraviolet.

Direct current, 385 W (110 V, 3.5 A). Shines at light level 15 while power comes in through cables. Through a spectroscope: mercury lines (g-line 436 nm, h-line 405 nm, i-line 365 nm and more). Mercury lamp tube + 2 iron + copper cable.

In 1901 the American Cooper Hewitt built a mercury lamp. It was more efficient than incandescent bulbs but its light was blue-green, so it was used in places like photography studios for black-and-white film. Early ones were started by tilting the tube so the mercury bridged the electrodes. In 1903-04 Küch (Heraeus, Germany) made the tube of quartz, giving a lamp rich in ultraviolet. Both ran on direct current.

Mercury's g-line (436 nm) and i-line (365 nm) became the light sources of 1980s-90s lithography steppers. Chip fabs are lit yellow so that only long wavelengths the resist does not react to are present. Low-pressure mercury lamps in quartz also give 254 nm UV used for sterilization.
block.semiconductor-lab.mercury_lamp.pla: Approximation: the starting method (tilting the tube, high-voltage ignition) and the dim warm-up time are omitted. UV output and its use for exposure come with the v0.3 lithography machine.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury_lamp_asse: A quartz tube with mercury and electrodes inside. Air is still in it, so it does not light.
Quartz tube + mercury + 2 tungsten wires (electrodes). Pump it below 0.1 Pa and seal it in the sealing station to get a mercury lamp tube (like a vacuum tube; needs the Sprengel mercury pump [5-15]).

Leftover air takes the discharge energy away into nitrogen and oxygen, and the mercury lines do not come out cleanly. Early mercury lamps were pumped with the same mercury pumps as light bulbs (oil rotary pumps came in 1905).

Ordinary glass blocks ultraviolet shorter than 300 nm. Quartz passes down to about 160 nm, so UV mercury lamps use quartz tubes. Küch melted rock crystal in an oxyhydrogen flame to make bubble-free quartz glass [7-02].
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury_lamp_tube: A pumped and sealed quartz tube. A drop of mercury rolls inside.
Made in the sealing station. With 2 iron and a copper cable it becomes a mercury lamp block.
Inside is almost nothing but mercury vapor. Mercury's vapor pressure at room temperature is about 0.25 Pa; when the lamp heats up the vapor increases and the light gets stronger.
Electrons from the electrodes hit mercury atoms and push an atom's electron up to a higher step. When it falls back, light with exactly the step's energy comes out (a line of fixed wavelength).
item.semiconductor-lab.spectroscope.line: Mercury Hg: yellow 579.1, 577.0 nm, green 546.1 nm, blue 435.8 nm (g-line), violet 404.7 nm (h-line)
The i-line at 365.0 nm is ultraviolet and invisible (paper fluoresces bluish-white under it). The first lithography steppers used these g and i lines
item.semiconductor-lab.half_silvered_mir: Glass that reflects half the light and lets half through. You see through it and see yourself too.
Crown glass with a very thin silver film (tens of nm ⚠️) from the vacuum evaporator. In the interferometer [7-09] it splits light into two paths and joins them again (a beam splitter).
An interrogation-room 'one-way mirror' works the same way: a mirror from the bright side, a window from the dark side.
A thicker silver film reflects more, a thinner one transmits more; an even split needs a film a few tens of nm thick. In Michelson's time (1881) it was made with a thin layer of chemical silvering.
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.no: A tool that splits light in two and recombines it, using light waves as a ruler to measure lengths smaller than a hundredth of a hair.

Half-silvered mirror + 2 speculum mirrors + lead screw + 2 iron. Right-click a lit mercury lamp -> with the green line (546.1 nm), it shows how many fringes pass when the screw turns once (0.5 mm) and the length worked out from them.

Michelson built this interferometer in 1881, and in 1887 with Morley tried to detect the 'ether wind' but found none, a clue that led to relativity. In 1907 Michelson became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Moving a mirror by d changes the light path by 2d (there and back), so 2d / lambda fringes pass; one fringe is half a wavelength (about 0.27 um). Today's lithography stages move while laser interferometers measure their position to nanometres. LIGO, which found gravitational waves, is a giant Michelson interferometer with 4 km arms.
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.pl: Approximation: the filter (colored glass) that isolates the green line is omitted. One screw turn = 0.5 mm is a game value. Michelson's half-silvered mirror was chemically silvered; here it is made by vacuum evaporation (which came later ⚠️).
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.la: 🌈 Interference fringes in mercury's green line (546.1 nm)
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.co: Moving the mirror %s mm with the screw, %s fringes passed
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.le: Length = %s fringes x %s nm / 2 = %s mm (light waves as the ruler)
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.wh: Flame light is a mixture of colors, so only a few fringes show where the two paths are equal, and they wash out. Point it at a lit mercury lamp
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.hi: Needs light of one color: right-click a lit mercury lamp
item.semiconductor-lab.coated_crown_lens: A lens with an invisibly thin film on its surface that reduces reflection. It glints slightly purple.
Vacuum evaporator: crown lens + fluorite (CaF2). With the film a quarter wavelength thick, light reflected from its top and bottom cancels. Reflection per surface about 4.3% -> about 2.2%.
In 1936 John Strong published a way to reduce reflection with vacuum-evaporated CaF2 films. In 1938 Katharine Blodgett stacked monolayers of a soap-like compound to make 'invisible glass'.

4% per surface means over half the light is lost with 20 surfaces, turning into glaring ghosts (stray light). A projection lens [7-19] with dozens of elements could not be made without coatings. The ideal film index is sqrt(glass index) ~ 1.23; MgF2 (1.38) is closer than CaF2 (1.43).
Approximation: a single layer only. CaF2 films are soft and scratch easily (in reality they were used only on inner lens surfaces).
item.semiconductor-lab.coated_flint_lens: A flint concave lens with an anti-reflection coating.
Vacuum evaporator: flint lens + fluorite (CaF2). Flint has a higher index (about 1.6), so its bare surface reflects more than crown (about 5%).
Around World War II, coated binoculars and periscopes stayed bright even at dusk.

A quarter-wave film works best for one color only. To cut reflection across colors, several films of different index are stacked (multilayers). EUV mirrors [7-17] use multilayers the other way round, to reflect strongly.
Approximation: a single layer only. CaF2 films are soft and scratch easily.
block.semiconductor-lab.bridgman_furnace: A furnace that cools molten fluorite slowly to grow one large crystal.

3 kW electric (induction heating). 4 fluorite + 1 argon bag -> CaF2 single crystal (90 s). Recipe: induction coil + HF oscillator + graphite rod (crucible) + 2 refractory bricks + quartz tube + lead screw (lowers the crucible slowly).

In 1925 the American Bridgman described growing single crystals by moving a crucible slowly from a hot zone to a cold one. In the 1930s Stockbarger made large CaF2 and LiF crystals in a vacuum furnace (⚠️ the year for CaF2 varies by source).

With a pointed crucible tip, only one of the first tiny crystals keeps growing, so the whole melt becomes one crystal (the same idea as necking in the CZ method). CaF2 melts at 1418 C. Oxygen or water would mix in CaO and block UV, so it is grown under argon or vacuum.
Approximation: the real crucible is lowered over several days (here 90 s). Natural fluorite is used directly (real optical grade uses purified raw material).
item.semiconductor-lab.caf2_crystal.note: A large, crystal-clear crystal of calcium fluoride. It also passes invisible ultraviolet well.
Bridgman furnace: 4 fluorite + argon. Grind and polish it into a CaF2 lens. It transmits UV down to about 130 nm (ordinary glass stops around 300 nm).
Clear, crack-free natural fluorite is very rare. Around 1886 Abbe used natural fluorite in microscope lenses to cut color fringes further (apochromats).

Projection lenses for ArF (193 nm) lithography combine fused silica and CaF2. 157 nm lithography relied on CaF2 alone, but large uniform crystals proved too hard to make and development stopped around 2003.
item.semiconductor-lab.caf2_lens.note1: A lens ground and polished from a calcium fluoride crystal. It passes ultraviolet too.
item.semiconductor-lab.caf2_lens.note2: CaF2 crystal + sand + grinding tool + rouge + pitch lap (tools come back). Index about 1.43, very low dispersion (Abbe number about 95). A material for projection lenses [7-19].
item.semiconductor-lab.caf2_lens.note3: 'Fluorite' lenses were used in high-end telephoto camera lenses, marked by white barrels (Canon, 1969 ⚠️).
item.semiconductor-lab.caf2_lens.note4: CaF2 is softer than glass, cracks easily with heat, and its index changes strongly with temperature, so it is hard to polish and mount. Being a crystal, its properties vary slightly with direction (birefringence), which also became a problem at 157 nm.
item.semiconductor-lab.caf2_lens.placeho: Approximation: grinding and polishing are done in one crafting step.
item.semiconductor-lab.hide_broth.note1: Animal hide boiled in water. It sets into a jelly when cool.
item.semiconductor-lab.hide_broth.note2: 2 leather + water bucket (the bucket comes back). Boil it down in a furnace and dry it for gelatin.
item.semiconductor-lab.hide_broth.note3: Hide glue made by boiling skin and bone has been used as an adhesive for thousands of years.
item.semiconductor-lab.hide_broth.note4: Collagen, the main protein of hide, unwinds its triple helix in hot water and becomes gelatin. When cooled the chains tangle again into a gel.
item.semiconductor-lab.hide_broth.placeh: Approximation: made the pre-container way, without a bottle. Liming the hide to remove hair and fat is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.gelatin.note1: The same stuff as in jelly. In photography it holds the light-sensitive silver grains evenly spread.
item.semiconductor-lab.gelatin.note2: Hide broth -> furnace. Mix with silver nitrate + salt for photographic emulsion.
item.semiconductor-lab.gelatin.note3: In 1871 Maddox proposed the 'dry plate' with silver salts spread in gelatin. Unlike wet plates it could be made in advance, and photography spread rapidly.
item.semiconductor-lab.gelatin.note4: Gelatin contained tiny amounts of sulfur compounds that help silver halide grains grow and become more sensitive. Sensitivity was said to vary with which cattle the hide came from (later understood as chemical sensitization).
item.semiconductor-lab.photo_emulsion.no: Light-sensitive silver grains spread in gelatin. Coated on glass it becomes a photographic plate.
Gelatin + silver nitrate + salt: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl (precipitated as very fine grains in the gelatin) + NaNO3. ⚠ Keep away from light.
Silver chloride emulsions are slow but very fine-grained, so thin lines come out sharp. Emulsions for photomasks were made far finer-grained than ordinary photographic ones.

Light makes a cluster of a few silver atoms (the latent image) in a grain, and the developer turns the whole grain into silver from there. Ordinary photographic emulsions are mostly silver bromide, which is faster (bromine is not implemented yet).
item.semiconductor-lab.photo_emulsion.pl: Approximation: real high-resolution mask plates were mostly silver bromide; silver chloride is used here because there is no bromine yet. Ripening the emulsion by warming is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.photo_plate.note1: Glass coated with photographic emulsion. Expose and develop it, and the lit areas turn black.
item.semiconductor-lab.photo_plate.note2: Soda-lime glass + photographic emulsion. The reduction camera [7-11] copies an original drawing onto it to make a photomask.
item.semiconductor-lab.photo_plate.note3: IC masks of the 1960s were made on high-resolution photographic plates (emulsion masks). The soft emulsion was soon scratched by contact printing and replaced after a number of uses.
item.semiconductor-lab.photo_plate.note4: Flatness matters for mask glass: it is pressed onto the wafer, so any bow leaves a gap that blurs the image. Later masks moved to quartz plates (chrome masks [7-12]).
item.semiconductor-lab.ferrous_sulfate.n: Pale green crystals. Used as a photographic developer.
Iron nugget + sulfuric acid (the bottle comes back): Fe + H2SO4 -> FeSO4 + H2. Turns exposed silver salt grains into silver (development). ⚠ Harmful if swallowed.
Once called green vitriol, it was a raw material for iron gall ink, dyeing and rouge (roasted into red iron oxide). It was also a developer for wet-plate photography.
Fe2+ readily gives up an electron to become Fe3+ (a reducing agent). The silver cluster of the latent image acts as a catalyst, so Ag+ is reduced and silver builds up only there.
item.semiconductor-lab.hypo_liquor.note1: Soda, sulfur dioxide and sulfur boiled in water. Boil it down for hypo (fixer) crystals.
item.semiconductor-lab.hypo_liquor.note2: Sodium carbonate + sulfur dioxide + sulfur powder + water bucket (the bucket comes back): Na2CO3 + SO2 -> Na2SO3 + CO2, Na2SO3 + S -> Na2S2O3.
item.semiconductor-lab.hypo_liquor.note3: Boiling sodium sulfite with sulfur is the classic way to make sodium thiosulfate.
item.semiconductor-lab.hypo_liquor.note4: The thiosulfate ion S2O3 2- is a sulfate ion with one oxygen replaced by sulfur.
item.semiconductor-lab.hypo_liquor.place: Approximation: no bottle. CO2 is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_thiosulfat: Photographic fixer. It dissolves the unexposed silver salt so the image no longer reacts to light.
Liquor -> furnace. Used after developing, it dissolves the remaining AgCl so the image no longer fades in light (fixing).
In 1819 Herschel found that thiosulfates dissolve silver salts, and in 1839 he recommended them for fixing photographs. It is still called 'hypo'.
AgCl + 2S2O3 2- -> [Ag(S2O3)2]3- + Cl- (a soluble complex ion). It is also used to remove chlorine from tap water.
block.semiconductor-lab.reduction_camera: A large camera that photographically shrinks a big drawing of a circuit onto a glass plate.

1 kW electric (illumination). Original drawing (not used up) + photographic plate + developer (ferrous sulfate) + fixer (hypo) -> photomask (30 s). Recipe: 2 achromatic lenses + mercury lamp tube + lead screw + 3 iron + copper cable.

Around 1960, IC originals were cut by hand from red film (rubylith) on large tables, then photographically reduced hundreds of times to make masks. The first IC layouts were literally cut out of film by hand.

Real reduction was done in two steps: the original was shrunk into a 'reticle', and a step-and-repeat camera printed it hundreds of times across a wafer-sized mask. Lens distortion and color fringes become mask errors directly, so special achromatic lenses were used.
Approximation: a single reduction step; step-and-repeat is omitted (a wafer is treated as one chip's content repeated). Developing and fixing happen in the same machine.
item.semiconductor-lab.photomask.note1: A glass plate carrying a circuit pattern: the master that transfers the pattern to a wafer with light.
item.semiconductor-lab.photomask.note2: Made from an original in the reduction camera (the pattern is copied exactly). Used in exposure machines. The soft emulsion wears out after 10 contact exposures.
item.semiconductor-lab.photomask.note3: Masks of the 1960s were photographic plates (emulsion masks). They were pressed right onto the wafer, so dust and scratches came quickly and masks were remade again and again.
item.semiconductor-lab.photomask.note4: Scratches and dust on a mask become defects on every chip (lower yield). Later, hard chrome-film masks [7-12] and projection printing that keeps the mask away from the wafer let a mask be used thousands of times.
item.semiconductor-lab.photomask.placeho: Approximation: the number of uses before wearing out (10) is a game value.
Extremely pure quartz glass made from chemicals. It also passes invisible ultraviolet well.
Put silicon tetrachloride in the oxyhydrogen burner: SiCl4 + 2H2O (water in the flame) -> SiO2 + 4HCl. Far fewer impurities (iron, aluminum...) than fused quartz made by melting natural vein quartz.
In 1934 Hyde at Corning in the USA invented making pure glass by hydrolyzing SiCl4 in a flame (the patent says 'an oxygen flame'). Optical fibres (1970) were later made this way too.

In ArF (193 nm) lithography, most of the projection lens and the photomask plate are synthetic quartz. Even traces of iron or water (OH) absorb UV, heat up and distort the lens, so purity decides performance.
Approximation: the HCl gas produced is not collected (real plants recover and reuse it).
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.vi: Floor vibration %s nm -> fringes jitter by +-%s: %s (%s)
item.semiconductor-lab.interferometer.sh: too shaky, you will miscount. Put the mercury lamp on an isolation table
item.semiconductor-lab.projection_lens.n: A lens that shrinks the mask pattern to 1/5 and projects it onto the wafer: a 'tower of glass' stacking many lenses.

Centered lens barrel + AR-coated crown lens. It inherits the barrel's lens offsets; the smaller they are, the finer it prints (CD = k1 lambda / NA). Right-click a lit mercury lamp for a test exposure; with an interferometer in the other hand it also measures the wavefront error.

In 1978 GCA released the DSW (g-line), a stepper that shrinks the mask and prints one chip at a time; Nikon and Canon followed. Because the mask is larger, its small dust and errors also shrink to 1/5.

Resolution is CD = k1 x lambda / NA (from Abbe's limit). Shorter lambda (g-line 436 nm -> i-line 365 -> KrF 248 -> ArF 193), larger NA and smaller k1 drove shrinking. Today's projection lenses have 20-30 elements and weigh over a tonne; EUV uses mirrors instead.
item.semiconductor-lab.projection_lens.p: Approximation: five lenses (real ones have 20-30). NA 0.35 is an early-1980s value (the 1978 GCA was about 0.28). The offset-to-aberration factor is a game value. No exposure tool yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.projection_lens.t: 🔦 Test exposure: CD = k1 %s x %s nm / NA %s = %s um
item.semiconductor-lab.projection_lens.o: reaches the g-line stepper target of %s um
item.semiconductor-lab.projection_lens.b: too blurred for the g-line stepper target of %s um (redo the barrel centering)
item.semiconductor-lab.projection_lens.s: Reduction 1/%s, NA %s, CD %s um at g-line
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note: Moves the coil slowly along the bar. Too fast and impurities cannot keep up.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note1: A long threaded rod: turn it and things move in a straight line.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note3: The distance moved per turn is the lead (pitch). Speed = lead × revolutions. A 1 mm lead screw turned once a minute moves 6 cm an hour, turning a motor's spin into a slow, precise straight-line motion.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note4: Around 1800 Henry Maudslay in England built an all-metal lathe whose tool carriage was driven by a lead screw, so accurate screws could be made identical again and again. The stages of today's chip lithography machines (ball screws) are its descendants.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note1: A machine that spins material and cuts it with a tool to make round parts.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note2: 750 W electric. Steel ingot -> pump rotor (30 s). Put a lead screw in the lower-left 'master screw' slot and steel -> 4 standard screws [8-02] (the lead screw is not used up). Parts made carry this lathe's size error. Recipe: 2 steel + lead screw + 2 iron + motor.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note3: Around 1797-1800 Henry Maudslay in England built an all-metal lathe whose tool carriage was moved by a lead screw. The shaking of the hand was gone, and identical screws and parts could be made in any number. He is called the father of machine tools.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note4: A lathe can remake its own lead screw more accurately (better screw -> better parts -> better screw). This cycle of machines making more accurate machines runs from precision engineering all the way to the nanometre stages of lithography machines.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.placeholde: Approximation: Maudslay's lathe was driven by hand, water wheel or steam; here by an electric motor. For now it only turns rotary pump rotors.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note1: A turned steel cylinder that spins inside a rotary pump.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note2: Turned from a steel ingot on the lathe. A part of the rotary pump [5-04]. It spins off-centre (eccentric), so the gap chamber grows and shrinks and pushes gas out.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note3: In 1905 Gaede built a 'rotary mercury pump' that moved air with a rotating part, turning the vacuum pump from a hand tool into a machine.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note4: The gap between rotor and casing is a few tens of micrometres. A larger gap lets gas leak back and spoils the vacuum, so the lathe's accuracy sets the pump's performance.
item.semiconductor-lab.simple_microscope: A tool with one small round lens that makes tiny, invisible things look big.

Crown lens + 2 copper. Hold a mask, original or wafer in your other hand and right-click to see whether one cell of its pattern is visible. With NA 0.2 it resolves about 1.4 um (masks up to contact and 1:1 projection printing).
In the 1670s the Dutch draper Leeuwenhoek used microscopes with a single tiny bead-like lens he ground himself (about 270x) and was the first to see microorganisms and bacteria in water.

The smaller and more strongly curved the lens, the higher the magnification, but it must be held right up to the eye. Leeuwenhoek kept his lens-making secret, and nobody else matched his lenses for a long time.
Approximation: NA 0.2 is a game value (⚠️ Leeuwenhoek's best lenses are said to have resolved about 1 um). The real mount was brass.
item.semiconductor-lab.compound_microsco: A microscope that magnifies in two stages, objective and eyepiece. Used to inspect fine lines on wafers and masks.

Achromatic lens (objective) + crown lens (eyepiece) + 2 copper + lead screw (focus) + iron. With NA 0.9 it resolves about 0.31 um (masks up to i-line steppers; lines finer than KrF cannot be seen with light).

In 1873 Abbe, working at the Zeiss works, showed that the finest line a microscope can resolve is about half the wavelength of light (d = lambda / 2NA), and that nothing finer can be seen with any lens. In 1878 he made oil-immersion lenses that raise the NA.

NA (numerical aperture) is how wide an angle of light the lens accepts. In air it cannot exceed 1, so to see finer you must shorten the wavelength (the UV microscope, 1904), fill the gap with oil or water (the same idea as immersion lithography [7-16]), or use electrons instead of light. Once chip lines became finer than the wavelength of light, inspection moved to electron microscopes.
Approximation: calculated with 550 nm, the middle of white light. Illumination techniques (Köhler) and oil immersion are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.standard_screw.no: A screw cut to exactly the same shape as all the others. It fits any machine's nut.
Turn steel on a lathe with a lead screw in its 'master screw' slot: 4 screws (the lead screw is not used up). It carries the lathe's size error (measure it with calipers or a micrometer [8-04]).

Once every workshop had its own thread shapes, and each screw and nut were made as a matched pair. In 1841 Whitworth proposed a 55-degree thread angle and a set number of threads per size, and screws across Britain became uniform.

Maudslay's lathe moved its tool carriage with a master lead screw, so it could cut any number of screws with exactly the same pitch. If part shapes are fixed, any part fits (interchangeable parts) - the foundation of later mass production and car assembly lines.
item.semiconductor-lab.standard_screw.pl: Approximation: the error range (+-25 um) is a game value. Thread forms (55 degrees etc.) are not distinguished.
item.semiconductor-lab.vernier_caliper.n: A tool that grips things between two jaws to measure length or thickness. A small scale lets you read fine fractions.
2 bronze. Hold a lathe part in your other hand and right-click: reads to 0.05 mm. It cannot grade parts (0.01 mm differences); that needs a micrometer.

In 1631 the Frenchman Pierre Vernier devised a sliding scale slightly offset from the main scale (the vernier) to read fractions between marks. Calipers of today's shape were sold by Brown & Sharpe in the USA around 1851.

If 20 vernier divisions span 19 mm of the main scale, each differs by 0.05 mm. Find where a vernier line exactly meets a main-scale line and you read that fraction (the eye is very sensitive to misaligned lines).
item.semiconductor-lab.vernier_caliper.p: Approximation: real calipers were brass (copper + zinc); here they are made of bronze.
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.note1: A tool that grips things by turning a screw and measures to 0.01 mm.
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.note2: Standard screw + steel + bronze. One turn advances 0.5 mm, divided by 50 marks around the thimble = 0.01 mm (the same 0.5 mm screw as the interferometer [7-09]). Grades lathe parts: A = error within 10 um, B = within 20 um, C = more.
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.note3: In 1848 the Frenchman Jean Laurent Palmer made a tool that measures 0.01 mm with a screw. It became possible once accurate screws could be made ([8-02]).
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.note4: Pressing too hard squashes both part and tool slightly and shifts the reading, so micrometers have a ratchet that slips at a set force. Steel also grows about 11 um per metre per degree, so precise measurement is done at 20 C.
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.placeh: Approximation: real frames are cast iron or steel; here the frame is bronze.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.note1: A platinum bar that is the model of 'one metre'. Right-click two blocks to learn the length between them.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.note2: 3 platinum ingots + theodolite (returned). Right-click a block for the first mark, another block for the length in metres and old units (shaku, toise). In Minecraft one block = 1 m.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.note3: After the French Revolution, the jumble of local length units was replaced by the metre: one ten-millionth of the meridian from the North Pole to the equator. Delambre and Méchain triangulated from Dunkirk to Barcelona in 1792-98, and in 1799 a platinum bar of that length was placed in the National Archives.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.note4: The bar was an end standard: 1 m between its two end faces. Platinum was chosen because it does not rust or warp easily. In 1889 a platinum-iridium international prototype (1 m between two lines) replaced it, and in 1893 Michelson measured it in wavelengths of light (about 1.55 million waves of cadmium red). The metre was redefined by a wavelength in 1960 and by the speed of light in 1983. Japan fixed the shaku in 1891 as 10/33 of a metre.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.placeho: Approximation: the meridian survey is represented by putting the theodolite in the recipe. Lengths are measured between block centers.
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.n: A plate cast from pig iron in a sand mold. It is slightly warped. Rubbing three together makes them perfectly flat.

4 pig iron + sand -> 1. Hold this plate in your main hand and another plate in the other hand, then right-click: one rouge laps the two together. Two plates alone end up fitting as convex and concave. Lapping three in turn (A-B, B-C, C-A) makes all three flat, and at 1 um or less a plate becomes a surface plate.

In the 1830s-40s Whitworth spread the method of lapping three plates against each other, which makes all three flat with no outside reference. If A fits B and A fits C, then B and C have the same shape; if B also fits C, both can only be flat.

You can make something flat without anything flatter. Whitworth preferred scraping to abrasive lapping: rub with red paint, then scrape the high spots the paint marks. Flatness, squareness, screws and scales were the start of machine tools that make machines.
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.p: Approximation: the real method was often scraping (here plates are lapped with rouge). Casting (melting and pouring into a sand mold) is folded into the recipe.
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.h: Hold the plate to lap against (cast plate or surface plate) in your other hand
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.n: You need an abrasive (rouge) in your inventory
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.l: 🪨 Lapped: this plate %s um (%s), other %s um (%s) / gap between them %s um
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.u: Warp: not lapped yet (as cast, +-20 to 60 um)
A heavy surface plate resting on rubber. Animals walking nearby hardly shake what sits on it.

Surface plate + vulcanized rubber. Whatever sits on it shakes 1/20 as much. When you measure a mercury lamp with the interferometer, animals, minecarts or pistons moving nearby make the fringes jitter; put the lamp on an isolation table to calm them.

Precise measurement is spoiled by footsteps and traffic (around a micrometre) and by temperature. A heavy table floated on springs passes little of the fine shaking. The standard temperature for length is 20 C (chosen by the CIPM in 1931); steel grows about 11 um per metre per degree.

Today's lithography tools sit on air springs with active isolation that moves to cancel shaking, in rooms held to a hundredth of a degree. A precise factory can stop work just because a truck goes by.
Approximation: vibration sizes are game values. No air springs (compressed air) or constant temperature (20 C room, air conditioning) yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.note1: A metal tube holding four lenses. Their centers are slightly off, so the image is blurred as it is.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.note2: 4 achromatic lenses + 2 steel + 2 standard screws. Hold the barrel in your main hand and a microscope in the other, then right-click: rotate it, watch the image wobble and nudge the worst lens. When every lens is within 1 um it is centered. A simple microscope cannot see fine offsets, and a moving piston nearby hides them (stand on an isolation table).
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.note3: If a lens center (optical axis) is off, the image circles when the barrel is rotated. Skilled workers tapped the lens until the wobble vanished and locked it with a retaining ring. It was the craft of Nikon, Canon and Zeiss.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.note4: Even the best lens blurs if assembled 0.001 mm off. Today's projection lenses align 20-30 elements to tens of nanometres, measuring the wavefront with interferometers as they are built.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.place: Approximation: four lenses (real projection lenses have 20-30). Each tap leaving 40% is a game value. 1950 is an approximate year.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.hold: Hold a microscope in your other hand, then right-click the lens barrel
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.wobbl: 🔬 Rotating the barrel, the image wobbles by %s um
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.canno: You cannot see any finer (limit %s um: microscope resolution %s um, floor vibration %s um)
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.tappe: Tapped lens %s into line -> offset %s um
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.done: ✨ All lens centers are within 1 um (centered)
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.unkno: Lens offsets: not inspected yet (20-80 um as assembled)
item.semiconductor-lab.centered_lens_bar: A tube whose four lens centers line up exactly. The image no longer wobbles when it turns.
A lens barrel brought within 1 um for every lens under the microscope. Material for the projection lens [7-19].
Good centering matters not only for blur but also for distortion. Copying a mask pattern onto a wafer in its true shape requires lenses on a common axis.
Even after assembly, temperature and vibration move lenses. That is why lithography tools sit on isolation tables in rooms held at 20 C ([8-07]).
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge_block_set.n: A box of steel blocks of exactly known length. Stack a few and you have a ruler of any length you like.

4 crucible steel + water bucket (quench) + rouge (finish). Right-click in the air to see how many blocks make a target length. With a micrometer in your other hand, right-click a lathe to bring its error within 1 um (a vernier caliper is too coarse).

In 1896 the Swede Johansson devised a set whose few blocks combine into tens of thousands of lengths to the micrometre. Henry Ford bought it in, and it underpinned interchangeable parts in American factories.
The faces are so flat that pressed and slid together they cling (wringing). Stacking adds almost no error, so blocks can be combined. Workshop gauges are set by comparing them with gauge blocks.
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge_block_set.p: Approximation: a 111-piece set (not the count of Johansson's first set). Finishing on a surface plate is folded into the recipe.
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge_block_set.n: Hold a micrometer in your other hand (a vernier caliper is too coarse)
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge_block_set.c: 🔧 Lathe error %s um -> %s um (set with gauge blocks and micrometer)
